key_definitions.framework agreement: An agreement concluded by a central purchasing body under which competition may be reopened or tasks allocated among economic operators party to the agreement.
key_definitions.ancillary purchasing activities: Supporting purchasing-related services that may be included in a public service contract for centralised purchasing activities.
key_definitions.mandatory public law provisions: Binding public law rules, in conformity with Union law, applicable to a contracting authority in its Member State and which may not be avoided through use of Article 39 mechanisms.

regulations.source_section: ## Procurement involving contracting authorities from different Member States

regulations.regulation_name: Directive 2014/24/EU on public procurement - Article 38(1) Occasional joint procurement

description.brief_summary: Article 38(1) authorizes two or more contracting authorities to agree to carry out certain specific procurement activities jointly. It also regulates the permissible duration and scope of the agreement governing such joint procurement.
description.detailed_explanation: The provision establishes a legal basis for occasional joint procurement among contracting authorities. It states that two or more contracting authorities may agree to perform certain specific procurements jointly. The section then specifies the types of procurement actions that may be jointly performed: '(a) the award of a contract under a dynamic purchasing system; (b) the conduct of a reopening of competition under a framework agreement; (c) the determination pursuant to points (a) or (b) of Article 33(4) of which of the economic operators, party to the framework agreement, shall perform a given task.' The provision further regulates the agreement underpinning the joint procurement, stating that it 'may either apply for an undetermined period, when fixed in the constitutive act of the joint entity, or may be limited to a certain period of time, certain types of contracts or to one or more individual contract awards.' This creates a structured but flexible framework for occasional collaboration between contracting authorities.
description.purpose: To enable contracting authorities to collaborate on specific procurement actions in a legally recognized manner and to provide flexibility in structuring the duration and scope of such cooperation.
description.legislative_intent: The lawmakers intended to facilitate efficient and coordinated public purchasing while ensuring that the joint arrangement is formally agreed and clearly delimited in duration or subject matter where appropriate.

what_it_covers: Agreements between two or more contracting authorities to perform specific procurements jointly
Award of a contract under a dynamic purchasing system
Reopening of competition under a framework agreement
Determination of which economic operator party to a framework agreement shall perform a given task under Article 33(4)(a) or (b)
Duration and scope parameters of the agreement governing joint procurement

target_entities: Joint entities established by contracting authorities
Economic operators party to a framework agreement (indirectly, where task allocation is determined)
who_it_applies_to.geographic_presence: Applies within the EU public procurement framework to contracting authorities subject to Directive 2014/24/EU

regulations.regulation_name: Directive 2014/24/EU on public procurement - Article 39(4) Joint procurement involving contracting authorities from different Member States

applicable_regions: Member States of the European Union

description.brief_summary: The provision authorizes contracting authorities from different EU Member States to collaborate in cross-border procurement by jointly awarding public contracts, concluding framework agreements, or operating dynamic purchasing systems. It further requires participating authorities to conclude an agreement governing the arrangement unless the necessary elements are already regulated by an international agreement between the Member States concerned.
description.detailed_explanation: The section establishes a legal basis for cross-border cooperation in public procurement among contracting authorities located in different Member States. It expressly permits several forms of joint procurement activity: joint award of a public contract, conclusion of a framework agreement, and operation of a dynamic purchasing system. It also extends, subject to the limits set out in the second subparagraph of Article 33(2), to the award of contracts based on a framework agreement or dynamic purchasing system. The provision then creates a conditional governance requirement. If the necessary elements of the joint arrangement have not already been regulated by an international agreement concluded between the Member States concerned, the participating contracting authorities are required to conclude their own agreement determining those elements. The text provided ends before listing the specific elements to be determined, so only the existence of the obligation to conclude such an agreement can be extracted with certainty from this section.
description.purpose: To facilitate lawful and structured cross-border public procurement cooperation between contracting authorities in different Member States.
description.legislative_intent: To enable joint procurement across Member States while ensuring that the participating authorities establish a clear legal and operational framework through an agreement where no international agreement already governs the necessary elements.

what_it_covers: Joint award of public contracts by contracting authorities from different Member States
Conclusion of framework agreements by contracting authorities from different Member States
Operation of dynamic purchasing systems by contracting authorities from different Member States
Award of contracts based on a framework agreement or dynamic purchasing system, to the extent permitted by the second subparagraph of Article 33(2)
Governance arrangements for cross-border joint procurement

who_it_applies_to.geographic_presence: Authorities must be from different EU Member States

what_it_does_not_cover: Situations where the necessary elements are already regulated by an international agreement concluded between the Member States concerned, insofar as the obligation to conclude a separate agreement is displaced

conditional_requirements: Contracting authorities from different Member States may jointly award a public contract.

The obligation to conclude an agreement applies only unless the necessary elements have already been regulated by an international agreement concluded between the Member States concerned.
documentation_requirements: A formal agreement between the participating contracting authorities is required where no applicable international agreement regulates the necessary elements.
timeline_requirements: The agreement must be concluded in connection with the joint procurement arrangement before reliance on an unregulated cross-border cooperation structure; no explicit deadline is stated in the provided text.

general_restrictions: Award of contracts based on the framework agreement or dynamic purchasing system is limited to the extent set out in the second subparagraph of Article 33(2).
The governance of the joint procurement arrangement cannot be left unspecified where no international agreement regulates the necessary elements.
operational_restrictions: Cross-border joint procurement must be structured either under an existing international agreement between the Member States concerned or under an agreement concluded by the participating contracting authorities.
geographic_restrictions: The provision applies specifically to contracting authorities from different Member States.

organizational_rights: Contracting authorities from different Member States are permitted to jointly award a public contract.
Contracting authorities from different Member States are permitted to conclude a framework agreement.
Contracting authorities from different Member States are permitted to operate a dynamic purchasing system.
Participating authorities may award contracts based on the framework agreement or dynamic purchasing system, subject to Article 33(2).
how_to_exercise_rights: Participate in a joint procurement arrangement with contracting authorities from different Member States.
Where no international agreement regulates the necessary elements, conclude an agreement among the participating contracting authorities determining those elements.
Ensure any award of contracts based on a framework agreement or dynamic purchasing system remains within the limits of the second subparagraph of Article 33(2).

general_exceptions: The obligation for participating contracting authorities to conclude their own agreement does not apply where the necessary elements have been regulated by an international agreement concluded between the Member States concerned.
conditional_exemptions: A separate inter-authority agreement is conditionally unnecessary if an international agreement already regulates the necessary elements.

organizational_measures: Establish a formal inter-authority agreement for the joint procurement arrangement where no international agreement already governs the necessary elements.
Verify whether an international agreement between the relevant Member States already regulates the necessary elements before proceeding without a separate agreement.
Confirm that any contracts awarded under a framework agreement or dynamic purchasing system comply with the limits referenced in Article 33(2).

complementary_regulations: Any international agreement concluded between the Member States concerned regulating the necessary elements of the joint procurement arrangement

implementation_steps: Identify whether the participating entities qualify as contracting authorities from different Member States.

regulations.regulation_name: Directive 2014/24/EU on public procurement - Preliminary market consultations

description.brief_summary: This provision allows contracting authorities to conduct market consultations before starting a procurement procedure in order to prepare the procurement and inform economic operators of procurement plans and requirements, subject to safeguards protecting competition and procurement principles.
description.detailed_explanation: The section establishes that, prior to launching a procurement procedure, contracting authorities are permitted to engage with the market. The stated purposes are twofold: preparing the procurement and informing economic operators about procurement plans and requirements. To support this, contracting authorities may seek or accept advice from independent experts, public authorities, or market participants. However, the use of such advice is conditional. It may be used in planning and conducting the procurement procedure only where it does not distort competition and does not violate the principles of non-discrimination and transparency. The provision therefore creates a permissive framework for pre-procurement engagement while imposing substantive limits designed to preserve fairness and equal treatment.
description.purpose: To enable better-informed and better-prepared procurement procedures while safeguarding fair competition, equal treatment, and transparency.
description.legislative_intent: The lawmakers intended to permit early market engagement so contracting authorities can understand market capabilities and shape procurements effectively, without allowing prior involvement by advisers or market participants to confer unfair competitive advantages.

Preparation of procurement procedures

timeline_requirements: Market consultations may occur before launching a procurement procedure.

operational_restrictions: Contracting authorities cannot operationalize consultation outcomes in a manner that gives unfair advantage or undermines equal treatment.

organizational_measures: Establish procedures for conducting pre-procurement market consultations.
Implement controls to assess whether external advice could distort competition.
Ensure procurement planning processes preserve non-discrimination and transparency when incorporating external advice.
training_requirements: Procurement personnel should be trained on how to engage with market participants without creating unfair competitive advantage or breaching transparency and equal treatment principles.
audit_requirements: Authorities should be able to demonstrate that consultation advice did not distort competition and did not violate non-discrimination and transparency.

enforcement_mechanisms: Not specified in this section.

Limit consultation objectives to procurement preparation and informing economic operators of plans and requirements.

Failing to preserve transparency about procurement requirements after receiving private market input.

regulations.regulation_name: Directive 2014/24/EU on public procurement - Allocation of responsibilities and applicable national law in joint procurement

description.brief_summary: This provision sets out how participating contracting authorities may allocate responsibilities and determine applicable national law in joint procurement, and requires that these matters be stated in procurement documents for jointly awarded public contracts.
description.detailed_explanation: The section provides that a participating contracting authority satisfies its obligations under the Directive when it purchases works, supplies, or services from a contracting authority responsible for the procurement procedure. It further states that, when determining responsibilities and applicable national law, participating contracting authorities may allocate specific responsibilities among themselves and determine which provisions of the national laws of any of their respective Member States will apply. This allocation of responsibilities and the applicable national law must be referred to in the procurement documents for jointly awarded public contracts. The provision therefore creates a governance framework for joint procurement, clarifying compliance responsibility and requiring transparency in procurement documentation regarding legal and operational allocation.
description.purpose: To provide legal certainty and operational clarity in joint procurement arrangements, especially where multiple contracting authorities and potentially multiple Member States are involved.
description.legislative_intent: The lawmakers intended to facilitate joint procurement by allowing participating authorities to structure responsibilities and choose applicable national law, while ensuring transparency through mandatory disclosure in procurement documents.

regulations.regulation_name: Prior involvement of candidates or tenderers

description.brief_summary: This article regulates how contracting authorities must handle situations where a candidate, tenderer, or related undertaking has previously advised the authority or otherwise participated in preparing the procurement procedure, in order to prevent distortion of competition and preserve equal treatment.
description.detailed_explanation: The section imposes a direct obligation on the contracting authority to act where a candidate or tenderer, or an undertaking related to them, has advised the authority or otherwise been involved in preparing the procurement procedure. The authority must take appropriate measures to ensure that competition is not distorted by that participant’s involvement. The text specifies that such measures include communicating to other candidates and tenderers relevant information exchanged in the context of, or resulting from, the prior involvement, and fixing adequate time limits for receipt of tenders. Exclusion of the involved candidate or tenderer is not the default response and is permitted only where there are no other means to ensure compliance with the principle of equal treatment. Before any exclusion, the affected candidate or tenderer must be given an opportunity to prove that its prior involvement is not capable of distorting competition. The authority must document the measures taken in the individual report required by Article 84. The section also includes a specific rule for joint entities established by several contracting authorities from different Member States, requiring the participating authorities, through a decision of the competent body of the joint entity, to agree on the applicable national procurement rules, choosing either the rules of the Member State where the joint entity has its registered office or the rules of the Member State where it carries out its activities.
description.purpose: To prevent unfair competitive advantage arising from prior involvement in procurement preparation, preserve equal treatment among tenderers, and provide a structured, proportionate mechanism for handling conflicts created by preparatory participation.
description.legislative_intent: The lawmakers intended to ensure that prior advisory or preparatory involvement does not automatically disqualify an economic operator, but is managed through transparency, procedural safeguards, and proportionate corrective measures, with exclusion used only as a last resort. The cross-border rule aims to provide legal certainty for joint entities created by contracting authorities from different Member States.

Involvement by undertakings related to a candidate or tenderer

mandatory_obligations: The contracting authority shall take appropriate measures to ensure that competition is not distorted by the participation of a candidate or tenderer that has advised the contracting authority or otherwise been involved in the preparation of the procurement procedure.

Such measures shall include the communication to the other candidates and tenderers of relevant information exchanged in the context of or resulting from the involvement of the candidate or tenderer in the preparation of the procurement procedure.
Such measures shall include the fixing of adequate time limits for the receipt of tenders.
Prior to any exclusion, candidates or tenderers shall be given the opportunity to prove that their involvement in preparing the procurement procedure is not capable of distorting competition.
The measures taken shall be documented in the individual report required by Article 84.

Where several contracting authorities from different Member States have set up a joint entity, the participating contracting authorities shall, by a decision of the competent body of the joint entity, agree on the applicable national procurement rules.
prohibited_actions: A contracting authority must not exclude the candidate or tenderer concerned unless there are no other means to ensure compliance with the duty to observe the principle of equal treatment.
A contracting authority must not proceed to exclusion before giving the affected candidate or tenderer an opportunity to prove that its prior involvement is not capable of distorting competition.
conditional_requirements: If a candidate or tenderer, or an undertaking related to them, has advised the contracting authority, whether in the context of Article 40 or not, the contracting authority must take appropriate anti-distortion measures.
If a candidate or tenderer has otherwise been involved in the preparation of the procurement procedure, the same anti-distortion measures apply.

If several contracting authorities from different Member States have set up a joint entity, they must agree on the applicable national procurement rules through the competent body of that joint entity.
If exclusion is being considered due to prior involvement, exclusion is lawful only where no other means exist to ensure equal treatment.
documentation_requirements: Document the measures taken in the individual report required by Article 84.
Maintain a record of the relevant information communicated to other candidates and tenderers.
Maintain a record of the opportunity given to the affected candidate or tenderer to prove that competition would not be distorted.
Maintain a record of the rationale showing why exclusion was necessary, if exclusion occurs, including why no other means could ensure equal treatment.
For joint entities, maintain the decision of the competent body selecting the applicable national procurement rules.
reporting_requirements: Include the measures taken in the individual report required by Article 84.
timeline_requirements: Relevant information must be communicated to other candidates and tenderers in time to preserve fair competition.
Adequate time limits must be fixed for the receipt of tenders.
The opportunity to prove absence of distortion must be given prior to any exclusion.

general_restrictions: Participation by a previously involved candidate or tenderer is restricted by the requirement that competition must not be distorted.
Exclusion is restricted to last-resort circumstances only.
The contracting authority’s discretion is constrained by the duty to observe the principle of equal treatment.
data_restrictions: Only relevant information exchanged in the context of or resulting from the prior involvement must be communicated to other candidates and tenderers.
operational_restrictions: The procurement procedure must be adjusted through appropriate measures where prior involvement exists.
Tender timelines may need to be extended or calibrated to offset any advantage arising from prior involvement.
Joint entities involving multiple Member States cannot proceed without agreeing on the applicable national procurement rules through the competent body.
geographic_restrictions: For joint entities established by contracting authorities from different Member States, the applicable procurement rules must be chosen from one of two specified Member States only: the Member State of the joint entity’s registered office or the Member State where the joint entity carries out its activities.

organizational_rights: The candidate or tenderer concerned has the right to be given an opportunity to prove that its involvement in preparing the procurement procedure is not capable of distorting competition.

Other candidates and tenderers have a right to receive relevant information exchanged in the context of or resulting from the prior involvement, insofar as this is part of the required measures to preserve fair competition.
how_to_exercise_rights: The affected candidate or tenderer exercises its right by presenting proof, before exclusion, that its prior involvement is not capable of distorting competition.

Other candidates and tenderers exercise their procedural position by receiving the relevant information disclosed by the contracting authority and using the adequate tender period to prepare their tenders.

general_exceptions: Exclusion is not required where other means exist to ensure compliance with equal treatment.
conditional_exemptions: A candidate or tenderer with prior involvement may remain in the procedure if the contracting authority can neutralize any competitive distortion through appropriate measures.
A candidate or tenderer may avoid exclusion by proving that its involvement in preparing the procurement procedure is not capable of distorting competition.

technical_measures: Implement a process for identifying prior advisory or preparatory involvement by candidates, tenderers, and related undertakings.
Implement a mechanism for controlled disclosure of relevant information to all other candidates and tenderers.
Implement tender timetable controls to ensure adequate time limits for receipt of tenders where prior involvement has occurred.
organizational_measures: Adopt procedures for assessing whether prior involvement creates a risk of distortion of competition.
Adopt procedures to determine and apply appropriate mitigation measures before considering exclusion.
Establish a documented decision-making process for exclusion that demonstrates why no other means could ensure equal treatment.
Establish a hearing or representation process allowing the affected candidate or tenderer to prove that competition is not distorted.
For joint entities, establish governance procedures enabling the competent body to decide the applicable national procurement rules.
training_requirements: Procurement staff should be trained to identify prior involvement, assess competitive distortion risks, apply equal-treatment safeguards, and document mitigation measures.
audit_requirements: Review the individual report under Article 84 to verify that all measures taken in response to prior involvement were documented.
Audit whether disclosures to other candidates and tenderers were made and whether adequate tender deadlines were set.
Audit whether exclusion decisions were preceded by an opportunity for the affected candidate or tenderer to respond.

enforcement.regulatory_authority: Not specified in this section; enforcement would ordinarily occur through the applicable public procurement oversight, review, or judicial mechanisms under EU and national procurement law.

penalties.reputational_consequences: Potential procurement challenge, annulment risk, and reputational harm for failure to preserve equal treatment and fair competition, though not expressly stated in this section.

enforcement_mechanisms: Documentation in the individual report under Article 84 creates an evidentiary basis for review.
Exclusion decisions and procedural fairness can be scrutinized through procurement review or challenge mechanisms.
Selection of applicable national procurement rules for joint entities can be reviewed against the decision of the competent body.

dates.compliance_deadline: Applies during preparation and conduct of the procurement procedure, including before any exclusion decision and before receipt of tenders.

complementary_regulations: Regulation (EC) No 1082/2006 of the European Parliament and of the Council on a European grouping of territorial cooperation (EGTC)

implementation_steps: Screen all candidates and tenderers, including related undertakings, for prior advisory or preparatory involvement.
Assess whether that involvement could distort competition.
Identify and disclose to other candidates and tenderers all relevant information exchanged in the context of or resulting from that involvement.
Adjust the tender timetable to provide adequate time limits for receipt of tenders.
Consider whether these measures sufficiently protect equal treatment.
If exclusion is contemplated, first give the affected candidate or tenderer an opportunity to prove that its involvement is not capable of distorting competition.
Exclude only if no other means can ensure compliance with equal treatment.
Document all measures and decisions in the individual report under Article 84.
Where a joint entity exists across Member States, obtain a decision from the competent body selecting the applicable national procurement rules from one of the two permitted Member States.
common_violations: Failing to identify prior involvement by a candidate, tenderer, or related undertaking.
Failing to disclose relevant preparatory information to other candidates and tenderers.
Setting insufficient time for other tenderers to respond after disclosure.
Automatically excluding a previously involved candidate without considering less restrictive measures.
Excluding a candidate without first giving it an opportunity to prove that competition is not distorted.
Failing to document the measures taken in the Article 84 individual report.
For joint entities, failing to formally agree on the applicable national procurement rules through the competent body.
best_practices: Use conflict and prior-involvement questionnaires at the start of the procurement process.
Create a standardized disclosure package for information that must be shared with all participants.
Record the reasoning for what information is considered relevant and disclosed.
Use a proportionality analysis before deciding on exclusion.
Provide a formal written opportunity for the affected candidate or tenderer to respond.
Maintain a complete audit trail in the individual report.
For cross-border joint entities, adopt a formal governance resolution identifying the chosen national procurement regime.
compliance_checklist: Has the contracting authority identified whether any candidate, tenderer, or related undertaking advised the authority or participated in preparing the procedure?
Have appropriate measures been taken to ensure competition is not distorted?
Has relevant information exchanged in the context of or resulting from the prior involvement been communicated to other candidates and tenderers?
Have adequate time limits for receipt of tenders been fixed?
If exclusion is considered, has the authority determined that no other means can ensure equal treatment?
Before exclusion, was the candidate or tenderer given an opportunity to prove that its involvement is not capable of distorting competition?
Have all measures taken been documented in the individual report required by Article 84?
If a joint entity involving authorities from different Member States exists, has the competent body decided the applicable national procurement rules?
Was the chosen national procurement regime either that of the Member State of the registered office or that of the Member State where the joint entity carries out its activities?

key_definitions.candidate: An economic operator seeking participation in a procurement procedure; not further defined in this section.
key_definitions.tenderer: An economic operator submitting a tender in a procurement procedure; not further defined in this section.
key_definitions.undertaking related to a candidate or te: An affiliated or connected undertaking linked to the candidate or tenderer; not further defined in this section.
key_definitions.contracting authority: The public authority conducting the procurement procedure and responsible for ensuring competition is not distorted.
key_definitions.appropriate measures: Measures required to ensure that competition is not distorted by prior involvement; expressly includes disclosure of relevant information and fixing adequate time limits for receipt of tenders.
key_definitions.principle of equal treatment: The duty that all candidates and tenderers must be treated fairly and without unjustified advantage; exclusion is permitted only where necessary to ensure compliance with this principle.
key_definitions.joint entity: An entity set up by several contracting authorities from different Member States, including EGTCs or other entities established under Union law.
key_definitions.competent body of the joint entity: The decision-making body that must determine the applicable national procurement rules for the joint entity.
key_definitions.relevant information: Information exchanged in the context of or resulting from the involvement of the candidate or tenderer in the preparation of the procurement procedure.
key_definitions.adequate time limits: Tender submission deadlines sufficient to mitigate any advantage arising from prior involvement; not numerically defined in this section.

regulations.regulation_name: Directive 2014/24/EU on public procurement - Article 42 (Technical specifications)

industry_sectors: Utilities where applicable under procurement frameworks

description.brief_summary: Article 42 sets out mandatory rules for drafting and using technical specifications in procurement documents. It requires specifications to define the characteristics of works, services, or supplies, permits formulation by performance/functional requirements or by reference to standards, mandates accessibility considerations for procurements intended for natural persons, prohibits unjustified brand- or source-specific references, and obliges contracting authorities to accept equivalent solutions and standards where tenderers prove equivalence.
description.detailed_explanation: The provision governs how contracting authorities must formulate technical specifications in procurement procedures. Technical specifications must be included in procurement documents and must define the required characteristics of the subject matter of the contract. These characteristics may include production or provision processes and life-cycle stage processes, provided they are linked to the contract subject matter and proportionate to contract value and objectives. The article requires technical specifications to ensure equal access for economic operators and to avoid unjustified barriers to competition. It prescribes permissible drafting methods: performance or functional requirements, references to standards in a specified order of preference, a combination of performance requirements with standards as presumptive evidence of conformity, or a mixed approach for different characteristics. It also allows specifications to address transfer of intellectual property rights. For procurements intended for use by natural persons, specifications must, except in duly justified cases, account for accessibility criteria for persons with disabilities or design for all users; where mandatory EU accessibility requirements exist, specifications must refer to them. The article further prohibits references to specific makes, sources, trademarks, patents, types, origins, or production methods that favor or eliminate certain undertakings or products, unless exceptionally justified because a sufficiently precise and intelligible description is otherwise impossible; any such reference must be accompanied by the words 'or equivalent'. Finally, where authorities use standards-based specifications or performance-based specifications, they may not reject tenders that prove equivalent compliance through appropriate means, including means of proof under Article 44.
description.purpose: To standardize the drafting of technical specifications in public procurement, preserve competition, prevent discriminatory procurement design, facilitate cross-border participation, and ensure accessibility and objective evaluation of tenders.
description.legislative_intent: The lawmakers intended to prevent contracting authorities from using technical specifications to distort competition or favor particular suppliers, while allowing sufficient flexibility to define procurement needs through performance criteria, standards, and equivalent solutions. The accessibility provisions indicate an intent to mainstream inclusive design in public procurement.

what_it_covers: Drafting of technical specifications in procurement documents
Definition of characteristics required of works, services, and supplies
Use of production methods and life-cycle process criteria
Use of performance or functional requirements
Use of standards and technical references
Accessibility criteria in procurements intended for natural persons
References to intellectual property rights transfer
Restrictions on make/source/trademark/patent/origin references
Acceptance of equivalent solutions and equivalent standards
Interaction with mandatory national technical rules compatible with Union law

entity_types: Authorities conducting procurement under EU public procurement rules
who_it_applies_to.geographic_presence: Applies within EU public procurement procedures governed by Union procurement law

what_it_does_not_cover: Specific penalties for non-compliance are not stated in this excerpt
Detailed evidentiary rules under Article 44 beyond cross-reference
Full definition of technical specifications in Annex VII point 1 is referenced but not reproduced in full

mandatory_obligations: Technical specifications as defined in point 1 of Annex VII shall be set out in the procurement documents.
The technical specification shall lay down the characteristics required of a works, service or supply.
Technical specifications shall afford equal access of economic operators to the procurement procedure.
Technical specifications shall not have the effect of creating unjustified obstacles to the opening up of public procurement to competition.
Without prejudice to mandatory national technical rules, to the extent compatible with Union law, technical specifications shall be formulated in one of the permitted ways listed in paragraph 3.

Where technical specifications are formulated in terms of performance or functional requirements, the parameters must be sufficiently precise to allow tenderers to determine the subject-matter of the contract and to allow contracting authorities to award the contract.

Where a contracting authority refers to technical specifications/standards under paragraph 3(b), the order of preference must be: national standards transposing European standards, European Technical Assessments, common technical specifications, international standards, other technical reference systems established by European standardisation bodies, and where those do not exist, national standards, national technical approvals or national technical specifications relating to design, calculation and execution of works and use of supplies.
Each reference to such standards/specifications shall be accompanied by the words 'or equivalent'.

For all procurement intended for use by natural persons, whether the general public or staff of the contracting authority, technical specifications shall, except in duly justified cases, be drawn up so as to take into account accessibility criteria for persons with disabilities or design for all users.

Where mandatory accessibility requirements are adopted by a legal act of the Union, technical specifications shall, as far as accessibility criteria for persons with disabilities or design for all users are concerned, be defined by reference thereto.

Where a contracting authority uses standards-based specifications under paragraph 3(b), it shall not reject a tender merely because the tendered works, supplies or services do not comply with the referenced technical specifications, if the tenderer proves by any appropriate means that the proposed solutions satisfy the requirements in an equivalent manner.

Where a contracting authority uses performance or functional requirements under paragraph 3(a), it shall not reject a tender for works, supplies or services complying with a national standard transposing a European standard, a European technical approval, a common technical specification, an international standard, or a technical reference system established by a European standardisation body, where those specifications address the laid down performance or functional requirements.

In its tender, the tenderer shall prove by any appropriate means, including those referred to in Article 44, that the work, supply or service in compliance with the standard meets the performance or functional requirements of the contracting authority.
prohibited_actions: Unless justified by the subject-matter of the contract, technical specifications shall not refer to a specific make or source.

Unless justified by the subject-matter of the contract, technical specifications shall not refer to a particular process which characterises the products or services provided by a specific economic operator.

Unless justified by the subject-matter of the contract, technical specifications shall not refer to trade marks, patents, types, or a specific origin or production where the effect is to favour or eliminate certain undertakings or certain products.
Contracting authorities may not reject equivalent tenders solely because they do not match the exact referenced technical specifications when equivalence is proven.
Contracting authorities may not reject tenders meeting performance/functional requirements through recognized standards when compliance is proven.
conditional_requirements: Characteristics in technical specifications may refer to a specific process or method of production or provision of the requested works, supplies or services, or to a specific process for another stage of the life cycle, only where such factors are linked to the subject-matter of the contract and proportionate to its value and objectives.
Technical specifications may specify whether transfer of intellectual property rights will be required.

Reference to a specific make, source, trademark, patent, type, origin, or production is permitted only on an exceptional basis where a sufficiently precise and intelligible description of the subject-matter pursuant to paragraph 3 is not possible.
Accessibility requirements may be omitted only in duly justified cases.
Mandatory national technical rules remain applicable only to the extent they are compatible with Union law.
documentation_requirements: Technical specifications must be included in the procurement documents.
Where standards or technical references are used, each reference must include the wording 'or equivalent'.

Tenderers must provide proof in their tender, by any appropriate means, including means of proof referred to in Article 44, to demonstrate equivalence or compliance with performance/functional requirements.
Where accessibility is not taken into account for procurement intended for natural persons, a duly justified case is required, implying justification should be documented.
If exceptional brand/source-specific references are used, the basis that a sufficiently precise and intelligible description was not possible should be documented.
timeline_requirements: Technical specifications must be set out at the procurement document stage.
Proof of equivalence or compliance must be provided in the tender.

general_restrictions: Technical specifications must not distort competition or create unjustified barriers to market access.
Specifications must be linked to the subject-matter of the contract and proportionate to value and objectives when process/life-cycle criteria are used.
operational_restrictions: Contracting authorities are restricted to the permitted methods of formulating technical specifications.
Authorities cannot structure specifications in a way that excludes equivalent solutions without lawful justification.
technical_restrictions: Brand-, source-, patent-, trademark-, type-, origin-, and production-specific references are restricted unless exceptionally justified.
Performance or functional parameters must be sufficiently precise.
Standards references must follow the prescribed order of preference.
Accessibility criteria must be integrated for procurements intended for natural persons except in duly justified cases.
geographic_restrictions: National technical rules may be used only insofar as they are compatible with Union law.

individual_rights: Natural persons who are intended users of procured works, supplies, or services benefit indirectly from a requirement that accessibility criteria or design for all users be taken into account.
organizational_rights: Economic operators have the right to equal access to the procurement procedure.
Tenderers have the right to offer equivalent solutions where standards-based specifications are used.
Tenderers have the right not to have their tenders rejected when they prove that recognized standards satisfy performance or functional requirements laid down by the contracting authority.
how_to_exercise_rights: Tenderers exercise equivalence rights by proving in their tender, by any appropriate means including means of proof under Article 44, that their proposed solution satisfies the requirements in an equivalent manner.

Tenderers exercise compliance rights under performance-based specifications by proving that the offered work, supply, or service complies with recognized standards addressing the required performance or functional requirements.

general_exceptions: Accessibility criteria need not be taken into account in duly justified cases.
Specific make/source/trademark/patent/type/origin/production references may be used exceptionally where a sufficiently precise and intelligible description of the subject-matter is not possible.
conditional_exemptions: Use of process or life-cycle criteria is allowed even where such factors do not form part of the material substance, provided they are linked to the subject-matter and proportionate to value and objectives.
National standards, approvals, or technical specifications may be used where higher-order European or international references do not exist.
public_interest_exceptions: Mandatory accessibility requirements adopted by a legal act of the Union override discretionary drafting and must be referenced.

technical_measures: Draft technical specifications using one of the authorized methods: performance/functional requirements, standards references, standards as presumption of conformity, or mixed formulation.
Ensure performance/functional parameters are sufficiently precise.
Include accessibility criteria or design-for-all requirements in procurements intended for natural persons unless duly justified otherwise.
Reference mandatory EU accessibility requirements where adopted.
Append 'or equivalent' to each standards/specification reference.
Allow and assess equivalent technical solutions and equivalent standards.
organizational_measures: Establish procurement drafting procedures to ensure equal access and avoid unjustified obstacles to competition.
Implement review controls to prevent unlawful brand-specific or supplier-specific specifications.
Maintain justification records for any exceptional use of specific make/source/trademark references or omission of accessibility criteria.
Train procurement staff on the hierarchy of standards references and equivalence assessment.
training_requirements: Procurement personnel should be trained on accessibility-by-design in procurement, equivalence assessment, and anti-discrimination in technical specifications.
audit_requirements: Review procurement documents to verify that technical specifications are included, properly formulated, non-discriminatory, and contain 'or equivalent' where required.
Audit tender evaluation decisions to ensure equivalent solutions and standards were not improperly rejected.

enforcement_mechanisms: Compliance is operationalized through procurement documentation requirements and tender evaluation obligations.
Tenderers may rely on proof of equivalence through appropriate means, including Article 44 evidence.

complementary_regulations: EU legal acts adopting mandatory accessibility requirements

implementation_steps: Insert technical specifications into procurement documents at the outset.
Define required characteristics of the works, services, or supplies.
Choose a lawful drafting method under paragraph 3.
If using performance/functional requirements, ensure precision sufficient for tendering and award.
If using standards references, follow the prescribed order of preference and add 'or equivalent' to each reference.
For procurements intended for natural persons, include accessibility or design-for-all criteria unless a documented justification exists.
Avoid references to specific brands, sources, patents, trademarks, types, origins, or production methods unless exceptional conditions are met and documented.
Set up evaluation criteria and evidence review processes to assess equivalence claims fairly.
Accept tenders demonstrating equivalent compliance through appropriate means, including Article 44 evidence.
common_violations: Omitting technical specifications from procurement documents.
Using vague performance requirements that are not sufficiently precise.
Failing to include 'or equivalent' after standards or brand-related references.
Specifying a brand or source without exceptional justification.
Ignoring accessibility criteria in procurements intended for natural persons without duly justified reasons.
Rejecting equivalent tenders solely because they do not match the exact cited standard.
Rejecting tenders compliant with recognized standards that satisfy performance requirements.
best_practices: Use performance-based specifications where possible to encourage innovation and competition.
Document the link between any process/life-cycle criteria and the contract subject matter, value, and objectives.
Maintain a standard checklist for accessibility review in all user-facing procurements.
Require evaluators to record reasons when accepting or rejecting equivalence evidence.
Use neutral, outcome-based language rather than supplier-specific descriptions.
compliance_checklist: Are technical specifications included in the procurement documents?
Do the specifications define the required characteristics of the contract subject matter?
If process or life-cycle criteria are used, are they linked to the subject matter and proportionate?
Do the specifications afford equal access and avoid unjustified obstacles to competition?
Are the specifications formulated using one of the permitted methods?
If standards are referenced, is the order of preference respected?
Does every such reference include 'or equivalent'?
For procurements intended for natural persons, are accessibility criteria or design-for-all requirements included, or is there a duly justified exception?
If mandatory EU accessibility requirements exist, are they referenced?
Are there any prohibited brand/source/trademark/patent/type/origin references without exceptional justification?
Do evaluation procedures allow proof of equivalence by appropriate means including Article 44 evidence?
Are tenders complying with recognized standards accepted where they meet performance/functional requirements?

key_definitions.technical specifications: Specifications set out in procurement documents that lay down the characteristics required of a works, service or supply.
key_definitions.performance or functional requirements: A method of formulating technical specifications by describing required outcomes or functions, including environmental characteristics, with sufficiently precise parameters.
key_definitions.equivalent: A solution or standard that satisfies in an equivalent manner the requirements defined by the contracting authority, even if it does not match the exact referenced specification.
key_definitions.accessibility criteria for persons with: Requirements intended to ensure procured works, supplies, or services are usable by persons with disabilities.
key_definitions.design for all users: An inclusive design approach requiring procurement specifications to consider usability by the widest range of users.

regulations.regulation_name: Directive 2014/24/EU on public procurement - Article 43 (Labels), paragraph 1(a)-(b)

description.brief_summary: This excerpt from Article 43 permits contracting authorities to require a specific label as proof that works, supplies, or services meet environmental, social, or other characteristics, but only if specified conditions are met, including that label requirements are linked to the subject matter of the contract and are based on objectively verifiable and non-discriminatory criteria.
description.detailed_explanation: The provision allows labels to be used in procurement as evidence of compliance with desired characteristics. Contracting authorities may include such label requirements in technical specifications, award criteria, or contract performance conditions when they seek works, supplies, or services with specific environmental, social, or other characteristics. However, the authority may only require a specific label if the label criteria concern characteristics linked to the subject matter of the contract and are appropriate to define those characteristics. In addition, the label requirements must be based on objectively verifiable and non-discriminatory criteria. The excerpt also indicates that the relevant specifications of the label, or where necessary parts thereof, must be linked to the subject matter of the contract and appropriate to define characteristics of that subject matter.
description.purpose: To permit the use of labels as practical proof mechanisms in procurement while preventing irrelevant, discriminatory, or unverifiable label requirements.
description.legislative_intent: The lawmakers intended to support sustainable and socially responsible procurement through labels, while ensuring that labels are used objectively and only where relevant to the contract.

what_it_covers: Use of labels in technical specifications
Use of labels in award criteria
Use of labels in contract performance conditions
Environmental, social, or other characteristics of procured works, supplies, or services
Conditions for lawful reliance on label requirements

who_it_applies_to.geographic_presence: Applies within EU public procurement procedures governed by Union procurement law

what_it_does_not_cover: The full set of Article 43 conditions is not included in this excerpt
Specific enforcement or penalties are not stated in this excerpt

mandatory_obligations: A specific label may be required as means of proof only where all stated conditions are fulfilled.

Label requirements must only concern criteria linked to the subject-matter of the contract and appropriate to define characteristics of the works, supplies, or services that are the subject-matter of the contract.
Label requirements must be based on objectively verifiable and non-discriminatory criteria.
prohibited_actions: Contracting authorities must not require a specific label where the label criteria are not linked to the subject-matter of the contract.
Contracting authorities must not rely on label requirements that are not appropriate to define characteristics of the contract subject matter.
Contracting authorities must not use label requirements based on criteria that are not objectively verifiable or that are discriminatory.
conditional_requirements: Where contracting authorities intend to purchase works, supplies, or services with specific environmental, social, or other characteristics, they may require a specific label in technical specifications, award criteria, or contract performance conditions, provided the stated conditions are met.
Relevant specifications of the label, or where necessary parts thereof, must be linked to the subject-matter of the contract and appropriate to define characteristics of that subject-matter.
documentation_requirements: If a label is required, the contracting authority should identify the relevant label specifications or parts thereof that are linked to the subject matter of the contract.
The authority should be able to demonstrate that the label criteria are objectively verifiable and non-discriminatory.
timeline_requirements: Label requirements must be embedded at the stage of drafting technical specifications, award criteria, or contract performance conditions.

general_restrictions: Use of labels is restricted to cases where all legal conditions are fulfilled.
operational_restrictions: Labels cannot be used as unrestricted procurement filters; they must be tied to contract-relevant characteristics.
technical_restrictions: Only label criteria linked to the subject matter and appropriate to define its characteristics may be used.
Criteria must be objectively verifiable and non-discriminatory.

organizational_rights: Economic operators are protected against irrelevant or discriminatory label requirements through the requirement that label criteria be linked to the subject matter and objectively verifiable.
how_to_exercise_rights: Operators may challenge label requirements that are not linked to the contract subject matter or that are discriminatory or not objectively verifiable.

technical_measures: Map each required label criterion to a contract characteristic.
Use only objectively verifiable and non-discriminatory label criteria.
organizational_measures: Establish internal review of label-based procurement requirements to confirm subject-matter linkage and non-discrimination.
Document why the label is an appropriate means of proof for the required characteristics.
training_requirements: Train procurement staff on lawful use of labels in technical specifications, award criteria, and contract performance conditions.
audit_requirements: Audit label requirements to ensure they are contract-linked, appropriate, objectively verifiable, and non-discriminatory.

enforcement_mechanisms: Compliance is reflected in procurement document design and review of label criteria.

implementation_steps: Determine whether the procurement seeks environmental, social, or other specific characteristics.
If using a label, identify the exact label criteria relevant to the contract subject matter.
Verify that each criterion is objectively verifiable and non-discriminatory.
Insert the label requirement only in technical specifications, award criteria, or contract performance conditions as appropriate.
common_violations: Requiring a label whose criteria extend beyond the contract subject matter.
Using labels with discriminatory or unverifiable criteria.
Treating labels as blanket eligibility requirements without linking them to contract characteristics.
best_practices: Use a criterion-by-criterion mapping between label requirements and contract needs.
Retain evidence showing objective verifiability and non-discrimination of the label criteria.
compliance_checklist: Is the procurement seeking specific environmental, social, or other characteristics?
Is the label being used as proof in technical specifications, award criteria, or contract performance conditions?
Do the label requirements concern only criteria linked to the subject matter of the contract?
Are those criteria appropriate to define characteristics of the contract subject matter?
Are the criteria objectively verifiable?
Are the criteria non-discriminatory?

key_definitions.label: A specified label that may be required as proof that works, services, or supplies correspond to required environmental, social, or other characteristics, subject to legal conditions.
key_definitions.objectively verifiable: Capable of being checked against objective evidence rather than subjective judgment.
key_definitions.non-discriminatory criteria: Criteria that do not unfairly favor or disadvantage particular economic operators.

regulations.regulation_name: Test reports, certification and other means of proof

description.brief_summary: Article 44 establishes the evidentiary rules that contracting authorities must follow when requesting proof that works, supplies, or services comply with procurement requirements. It permits the use of test reports and certificates, requires acceptance of equivalent certificates and labels, obliges authorities to accept alternative proof where certificates or labels are unavailable for reasons not attributable to the economic operator, and requires Member States to exchange relevant evidence upon request.
description.detailed_explanation: The section regulates how conformity with procurement requirements may be demonstrated in EU public procurement procedures. Contracting authorities are permitted to require a test report from a conformity assessment body or a certificate issued by such a body as proof that an economic operator's works, supplies, or services satisfy requirements or criteria contained in technical specifications, award criteria, or contract performance conditions. However, this discretion is limited by mandatory equivalence rules: if a specific conformity assessment body is named, certificates from equivalent other conformity assessment bodies must also be accepted. The section also addresses labels, including conditions under which label systems are acceptable, such as being established through an open and transparent procedure involving relevant stakeholders, being accessible to all interested parties, and having requirements set by an independent third party not controlled by the applicant economic operator. Where not all label requirements are required, the contracting authority must specify which requirements are relevant. The article further protects economic operators by requiring acceptance of other appropriate means of proof, such as a manufacturer's technical dossier, where the operator lacked access to certificates or test reports, or could not obtain them in time, provided the lack of access was not attributable to the operator and the alternative proof demonstrates compliance. Similar protection applies where a specific or equivalent label could not be obtained in time for reasons not attributable to the operator. Finally, Member States must provide each other, upon request, information relating to evidence and documents submitted under the relevant procurement provisions, with competent authorities of the Member State of establishment supplying the information in accordance with Article 86.
description.purpose: To ensure that proof of compliance in public procurement is reliable, non-discriminatory, and proportionate, while preventing unjustified exclusion of economic operators due to formalistic or overly restrictive evidentiary demands.
description.legislative_intent: The lawmakers intended to balance the contracting authority's need for objective proof of compliance with the principles of equal treatment, mutual recognition, competition, and cross-border access to procurement markets. The article is designed to prevent authorities from unfairly restricting participation by insisting on a single certifier or label where equivalent proof exists.

what_it_covers: Requests for test reports as proof of conformity
Requests for certificates from conformity assessment bodies
Acceptance of equivalent certificates
Use and acceptance of labels in procurement
Acceptance of equivalent labels
Acceptance of alternative means of proof
Technical dossiers from manufacturers
Definition of conformity assessment body
Information exchange between Member States regarding submitted evidence and documents

who_it_applies_to.geographic_presence: Applies within EU public procurement procedures and to economic operators established in Member States where evidence exchange is requested.

what_it_does_not_cover: Specific financial penalties for non-compliance
Detailed accreditation procedures under Regulation (EC) No 765/2008
General introductory procurement principles not expressly stated in this section

mandatory_obligations: Where contracting authorities require the submission of certificates drawn up by a specific conformity assessment body, they must also accept certificates from equivalent other conformity assessment bodies.

Contracting authorities must accept other appropriate means of proof than test reports or certificates where the economic operator had no access to such certificates or reports, or no possibility of obtaining them within the relevant time limits, provided the lack of access is not attributable to the economic operator and the operator proves compliance with the relevant requirements or criteria.
Contracting authorities requiring a specific label must accept all labels that confirm that the works, supplies or services meet equivalent label requirements.
Where contracting authorities do not require works, supplies or services to meet all of the label requirements, they must indicate which label requirements are referred to.

Where an economic operator demonstrably had no possibility of obtaining the specific label indicated by the contracting authority or an equivalent label within the relevant time limits for reasons not attributable to that operator, the contracting authority must accept other appropriate means of proof, which may include a technical dossier from the manufacturer, provided the operator proves that the works, supplies or services fulfil the requirements of the specific label or the specific requirements indicated by the contracting authority.

Member States must make available to other Member States, upon request, any information related to the evidence and documents submitted in accordance with Article 42(6), Article 43 and paragraphs 1 and 2 of this Article.
The competent authorities of the Member State of establishment of the economic operator must provide the requested information in accordance with Article 86.
prohibited_actions: Contracting authorities must not refuse certificates solely because they were not issued by the specific conformity assessment body named, if they are from an equivalent conformity assessment body.
Contracting authorities must not reject equivalent labels where those labels confirm equivalent label requirements.

Contracting authorities must not reject appropriate alternative proof where the operator could not obtain the required certificates, test reports, or labels in time for reasons not attributable to the operator and the operator proves substantive compliance.
Contracting authorities must not rely on unspecified label requirements when only some label requirements are intended to apply.
conditional_requirements: A contracting authority may require a test report from a conformity assessment body or a certificate issued by such a body as means of proof of conformity with requirements or criteria set out in technical specifications, award criteria, or contract performance conditions.
Acceptance of alternative proof is conditional on the economic operator having had no access to the certificates or test reports, or no possibility of obtaining them within the relevant time limits.
Acceptance of alternative proof is further conditional on the lack of access not being attributable to the economic operator.
Acceptance of alternative proof is further conditional on the economic operator proving that the works, supplies, or services meet the relevant requirements or criteria.

Acceptance of alternative proof for labels is conditional on the economic operator demonstrably having had no possibility of obtaining the specific label or an equivalent label within the relevant time limits for reasons not attributable to it.

Where labels are used, the relevant label system must satisfy stated characteristics, including open and transparent establishment, stakeholder participation, accessibility to all interested parties, and independence of the label requirements from decisive influence by the applying economic operator.
documentation_requirements: Test report from a conformity assessment body, where required by the contracting authority.
Certificate issued by a conformity assessment body, where required by the contracting authority.
Equivalent certificate from another conformity assessment body.
Technical dossier of the manufacturer as an alternative means of proof where certificates or reports are unavailable under the stated conditions.
Alternative proof demonstrating fulfilment of specific label requirements or specific requirements indicated by the contracting authority.
Evidence and documents submitted in accordance with Article 42(6), Article 43, and Article 44 paragraphs 1 and 2, which must be capable of being shared between Member States upon request.
reporting_requirements: Member States must provide requested information to other Member States regarding submitted evidence and documents.
Competent authorities of the Member State of establishment must provide such information in accordance with Article 86.

regulations.regulation_name: Directive 2014/24/EU on public procurement - Article 45 (Variants)

description.brief_summary: Article 45 regulates the use of variants in procurement procedures. It allows contracting authorities to authorise or require variants, but only if this is clearly indicated in the contract notice or invitation to confirm interest. It also requires variants to be linked to the subject-matter of the contract, obliges authorities to define minimum requirements and presentation rules in procurement documents, and limits consideration to variants that meet those minimum requirements.
description.detailed_explanation: The section establishes a structured legal framework for accepting alternative tender solutions ('variants') in public procurement. Contracting authorities are given discretion to permit or mandate variants, but that discretion is constrained by transparency obligations: the authority must expressly state in the contract notice, or where a prior information notice is used as a call for competition, in the invitation to confirm interest, whether variants are authorised or required. If no such indication is given, variants cannot be authorised. The article further requires a substantive connection between any variant and the subject-matter of the contract, preventing unrelated alternative offers. Where variants are authorised or required, the procurement documents must specify the minimum requirements applicable to those variants and any specific presentation requirements, including whether a non-variant tender must also be submitted. The authority must also ensure that the award criteria selected are capable of being applied both to compliant variants and to conforming non-variant tenders. Finally, only variants that satisfy the stated minimum requirements may be taken into consideration in the evaluation process.
description.purpose: To ensure transparency, equal treatment, comparability, and legal certainty when contracting authorities allow or require alternative tender solutions.
description.legislative_intent: The lawmakers intended to permit innovation and flexibility in procurement while preventing arbitrary acceptance of alternative bids and ensuring that all economic operators understand in advance whether and how variants may be submitted and assessed.

regulations.regulation_name: Setting time limits and treatment of variants in public supply or service contract award procedures

description.brief_summary: The section imposes two concrete obligations on contracting authorities in public procurement procedures for supply or service contracts. First, where variants have been authorized or required, authorities may not reject a variant solely because its acceptance would result in the contract being classified as a service contract instead of a supply contract, or vice versa. Second, when setting deadlines for tenders and requests to participate, authorities must consider the complexity of the contract and the time needed to prepare tenders, subject to the minimum deadlines established elsewhere.
description.detailed_explanation: The first rule addresses procurement procedures in which contracting authorities permit or mandate variants. In such cases, the authority is expressly prohibited from rejecting a variant for the sole reason that, if selected, it would alter the legal classification of the procurement outcome between a public supply contract and a public service contract. This means classification change alone cannot be used as the exclusive basis for rejection. The second rule governs deadline-setting. Contracting authorities, when determining the time limits for receipt of tenders and requests to participate, must actively assess two factors: the complexity of the contract and the time required for economic operators to prepare tenders. This obligation is expressly stated to operate 'without prejudice to the minimum time limits set out in Articles 27 to 31,' meaning authorities must both consider these practical factors and comply with the mandatory minimum deadlines established in those referenced provisions.
description.purpose: To ensure fair treatment of variants in procurement procedures and to ensure that tendering deadlines are realistic and proportionate to the complexity of the procurement while preserving mandatory minimum procedural safeguards.
description.legislative_intent: The lawmakers intended to prevent arbitrary exclusion of innovative or alternative offers merely because they would change the formal contract type, and to promote effective competition by requiring sufficient time for market participants to prepare responsive tenders.

regulations.regulation_name: Directive 2014/24/EU on public procurement - Article 46 Division of contracts into lots

industry_sectors: Utilities procurement where applicable under national transposition

description.brief_summary: Article 46 regulates how contracting authorities may divide contracts into lots and sets procedural safeguards to ensure transparency, equal treatment, and adequate time for tender preparation. It also requires disclosure when contracts are not subdivided into lots, governs whether tenders may be submitted for one or multiple lots, and allows limits on the number of lots awarded to a single tenderer if disclosed in advance and governed by objective, non-discriminatory criteria.
description.detailed_explanation: The section establishes a structured framework for lot-based procurement. First, contracting authorities are permitted to award contracts as separate lots and to define the size and subject matter of those lots. Second, where tender preparation requires a site visit or on-the-spot inspection of supporting procurement documents, the authority must set tender deadlines longer than the minimum deadlines in Articles 27 to 31 so that all interested economic operators can obtain the information needed to prepare tenders. Third, except where subdivision into lots is mandatory under paragraph 4, contracting authorities must state the main reasons for deciding not to subdivide a contract into lots, and those reasons must appear either in the procurement documents or in the individual report under Article 84. Fourth, authorities must state in the contract notice or invitation to confirm interest whether tenders may be submitted for one, several, or all lots. Fifth, even where multiple-lot tenders are allowed, authorities may cap the number of lots that may be awarded to one tenderer, but only if the maximum number is stated in the contract notice or invitation to confirm interest and the procurement documents specify the objective and non-discriminatory criteria or rules for determining which lots will be awarded if the award criteria would otherwise result in one tenderer receiving more than the maximum. Finally, the section also contains mandatory rules requiring extension of tender deadlines where additional information requested in good time is not supplied by the specified deadline, or where significant changes are made to procurement documents; the extension must be proportionate to the importance of the information or change, and no extension is required where the information was not requested in good time or is insignificant for preparing responsive tenders.
description.purpose: To promote access to public procurement, especially for smaller operators, ensure transparency in lotting decisions, prevent arbitrary allocation of multiple lots, and guarantee sufficient time for tenderers to prepare informed and responsive tenders.
description.legislative_intent: The lawmakers intended to encourage competition and SME participation through lot division, while preserving contracting authority discretion. They also intended to ensure equal treatment and procedural fairness by requiring disclosure of lotting decisions, advance notice of lot submission rules, objective allocation criteria, and deadline extensions where tender preparation is materially affected.

regulations.regulation_name: Prior information notices

description.brief_summary: The provision regulates how contracting authorities may publicize intended planned procurements through prior information notices, including required content, publication methods, and notification obligations tied to buyer profile publication.
description.detailed_explanation: The section establishes a formal mechanism by which contracting authorities may disclose their procurement intentions before launching procurement procedures. It permits the use of a prior information notice and requires that such notices include specified information from Annex V part B section I. It further limits publication methods to either publication by the Publications Office of the European Union or publication by the contracting authorities on their buyer profiles in accordance with Annex VIII point 2(b). Where the buyer profile route is used, the contracting authority must additionally send a notice of that publication to the Publications Office of the European Union in accordance with Annex VIII, and that notice must contain the information set out in Annex V part A. The section therefore creates a structured publication and notification framework intended to ensure transparency, standardization of notice content, and centralized awareness of procurement planning activity.
description.purpose: To ensure transparency and advance market awareness of planned procurements through standardized and controlled publication of prior information notices.
description.legislative_intent: The lawmakers intended to create a harmonized EU-level process for announcing planned procurements, ensuring that economic operators receive consistent information and that publication occurs through recognized channels with prescribed content.
