regulations.regulation_name: Directive 2014/24/EU on public procurement - Article 50 Contract award notices

industry_sectors: Utilities where applicable under related regimes

description.brief_summary: Article 50 requires contracting authorities to send contract award notices within specified deadlines, defines content and publication obligations, establishes special rules for prior information notices used as calls for competition, permits grouped notices for framework agreements and dynamic purchasing systems, and allows withholding of certain information from publication in limited circumstances.
description.detailed_explanation: The section imposes a core transparency obligation on contracting authorities to notify the outcome of procurement procedures by sending a contract award notice no later than 30 days after conclusion of a contract or framework agreement following the award decision. The notice must contain the information specified in Annex V Part D and be published according to Article 51. The section also creates a special procedural mechanism for sub-central contracting authorities using restricted procedures or competitive procedures with negotiation: they may use a prior information notice as the call for competition only if the notice specifically identifies the subject matter, states that the contract will be awarded without further publication and invites expressions of interest, includes the required Annex V Part B information, and is sent for publication within a defined time window before invitations are sent. Where a prior information notice served as the call for competition and the authority decides not to award further contracts during the covered period, the contract award notice must expressly state that fact. For framework agreements under Article 33, authorities are not required to send a separate notice for each contract based on the agreement, and Member States may allow quarterly grouped notices, which must be sent within 30 days after quarter-end. For dynamic purchasing systems, authorities must send a contract award notice within 30 days after each contract award, but may also group such notices quarterly, again with a 30-day post-quarter deadline. The section further prohibits publication of certain notices on a buyer profile, while allowing additional national-level publication under Article 52 on a buyer profile. It also limits the period covered by a prior information notice to 12 months from transmission for publication, except that prior information notices for social and other specific services under Article 75(1)(b) may cover a longer period. Finally, it permits withholding certain information from publication where disclosure would impede law enforcement, be contrary to the public interest, harm legitimate commercial interests, or prejudice fair competition.
description.purpose: To ensure transparency, accountability, and market information in public procurement while balancing confidentiality, competition, and administrative efficiency.
description.legislative_intent: The lawmakers intended to create a standardized and timely publication regime for procurement outcomes, facilitate competition through clear notice rules, reduce administrative burden in recurring procurement mechanisms such as framework agreements and dynamic purchasing systems, and protect sensitive information where publication would cause public or commercial harm.

regulations.regulation_name: Directive 2014/24/EU on public procurement - Contract notices requirements

description.brief_summary: The section establishes mandatory rules for the use, content, format, transmission, and publication of contract notices in public procurement procedures. It requires contract notices to serve as the means of calling for competition in all procedures, subject to prejudice language, and imposes detailed obligations regarding standard forms, electronic submission, publication timing, and cost allocation.
description.detailed_explanation: The section imposes concrete obligations on contracting authorities regarding contract notices. First, it states that contract notices shall be used as a means of calling for competition in respect of all procedures, indicating a general mandatory mechanism for initiating competition. Second, notices referred to in Articles 48, 49 and 50 must include the information set out in Annex V and must use the format of standard forms, including standard forms for corrigenda. Third, the Commission is tasked with establishing those standard forms through implementing acts adopted under the advisory procedure in Article 89(2). Fourth, notices referred to in Articles 48, 49 and 50 must be drawn up and transmitted electronically to the Publications Office of the European Union and published in accordance with Annex VIII. Finally, publication must occur no later than five days after the notices are sent, and the costs of publication by the Publications Office are borne by the Union.
description.purpose: To ensure transparent, standardized, timely, and centrally published procurement notices that effectively call for competition across EU public procurement procedures.
description.legislative_intent: The lawmakers intended to harmonize procurement notice practices across the EU, improve transparency and accessibility of tender opportunities, ensure consistent notice content and formatting, and centralize publication through the Publications Office of the European Union.

regulations.regulation_name: Publication at national level

description.brief_summary: The section regulates when and how procurement notices referred to in Articles 48, 49 and 50 may be published at national level, including sequencing relative to publication under Article 51, content consistency, language requirements, and buyer-profile publication conditions for prior information notices.
description.detailed_explanation: The section imposes a structured publication regime for procurement notices. First, notices and their contents may not be published nationally before publication pursuant to Article 51, unless the contracting authority has not been notified of publication within 48 hours after confirmation of receipt of the notice under Article 51. Second, notices published nationally must not contain information beyond what was dispatched to the Publications Office of the European Union or published on a buyer profile, and they must indicate the date of dispatch to the Publications Office or the date of publication on the buyer profile. Third, notices referred to in Articles 48, 49 and 50 must be published in full in the official language or languages of the institutions of the Union chosen by the contracting authority, and only those language versions are authentic; a summary of important elements must also be published in the other official languages of the institutions of the Union. Fourth, prior information notices may not be published on a buyer profile before dispatch to the Publications Office of the European Union of the notice announcing that form of publication, and such notices must indicate the date of dispatch. The section also assigns a continuing publication responsibility to the Publications Office of the European Union for the full text and summary of certain prior information notices and calls for competition establishing a dynamic purchasing system.

description.legislative_intent: The lawmakers intended to prevent premature or inconsistent national publication, preserve the primacy and integrity of EU-level publication, ensure multilingual accessibility, and maintain traceability of publication actions.

regulations.regulation_name: Directive 2014/24/EU on public procurement - Article 53 Electronic availability of procurement documents

industry_sectors: Social and other specific services procurement

description.brief_summary: Article 53 requires contracting authorities to provide unrestricted, full, direct, and free electronic access to procurement documents from the relevant publication or invitation date, to identify the internet address where those documents are available, and to provide additional information within specified deadlines. Where electronic access cannot be provided for specified legal reasons or confidentiality reasons, documents may be transmitted by other means, but the tender submission deadline must generally be extended by five days.
description.detailed_explanation: The section imposes concrete procedural obligations on contracting authorities in EU public procurement. As a default rule, procurement documents must be made available electronically, without restriction, in full, directly, and free of charge, starting from the date of publication of the notice under Article 51 or from the date an invitation to confirm interest is sent. The notice or invitation must expressly state the internet address where the documents can be accessed. If certain procurement documents cannot be made available electronically for reasons referenced in the second subparagraph of Article 22(1), or because the authority intends to apply Article 21(2) concerning confidentiality, the authority may use non-electronic means for those documents, but must disclose this in the notice or invitation. In confidentiality cases, the authority must also explain the protective measures required and how access to the documents can be obtained. In both categories of exception, the deadline for submission of tenders must be prolonged by five days, except in duly substantiated urgency cases under Article 27(3), Article 28(6), and the fourth subparagraph of Article 29(1). The article also requires contracting authorities, where requested in good time, to provide all participating tenderers with additional information relating to specifications and supporting documents no later than six days before the tender receipt deadline, or four days in accelerated procedures. The section further includes evidentiary obligations and publication-related rules: contracting authorities must be able to prove the dates on which notices are dispatched; the Publications Office of the European Union must confirm receipt and publication of notices and indicate the publication date, with that confirmation serving as proof of publication; notices not otherwise subject to mandatory publication may still be published if sent electronically to the Publications Office in the prescribed Annex VIII format and procedures. The excerpt also includes publication-duration rules for prior information notices and calls for competition establishing a dynamic purchasing system.
description.purpose: To ensure transparency, equal access, and timely availability of procurement information, while accommodating limited exceptions for technical or confidentiality reasons and preserving fair competition through deadline extensions.
description.legislative_intent: The lawmakers intended to modernize procurement through electronic access, reduce barriers to participation, standardize access to procurement documents across the EU, and ensure that any departure from electronic access does not disadvantage economic operators.

mandatory_obligations: Contracting authorities shall by electronic means offer unrestricted and full direct access free of charge to the procurement documents from the date of publication of a notice in accordance with Article 51 or the date on which an invitation to confirm interest was sent.
The text of the notice or the invitation to confirm interest shall specify the internet address at which the procurement documents are accessible.

Where requested in good time, contracting authorities shall supply to all tenderers taking part in the procurement procedure additional information relating to the specifications and any supporting documents not later than six days before the time limit fixed for the receipt of tenders.
In an accelerated procedure referred to in Article 27(3) and Article 28(6), the additional-information period shall be four days.
Contracting authorities shall be able to supply proof of the dates on which notices are dispatched.

Where contracting authorities intend to apply Article 21(2) and therefore cannot offer unrestricted and full direct electronic access to certain procurement documents, they shall indicate in the notice or invitation to confirm interest which measures aimed at protecting the confidential nature of the information they require and how access can be obtained to the documents concerned.
prohibited_actions: Failing to provide unrestricted, full, direct, and free electronic access to procurement documents as a default rule from the required date, unless one of the specified exceptions applies.

Failing to extend the tender submission deadline by five days when non-electronic transmission is used under the specified exceptions, unless a duly substantiated urgency exception applies.
conditional_requirements: Where unrestricted and full direct access free of charge by electronic means to certain procurement documents cannot be offered for one of the reasons set out in the second subparagraph of Article 22(1), contracting authorities may indicate in the notice or the invitation to confirm interest that the procurement documents concerned will be transmitted by other means than electronic means in accordance with paragraph 2 of this Article.

In such a case, the time limit for the submission of tenders shall be prolonged by five days, except in the cases of duly substantiated urgency referred to in Article 27(3), Article 28(6) and in the fourth subparagraph of Article 29(1).

Where unrestricted and full direct access free of charge by electronic means to certain procurement documents cannot be offered because contracting authorities intend to apply Article 21(2), they must indicate the confidentiality-protection measures and how access can be obtained.

In such confidentiality cases, the time limit for the submission of tenders shall be prolonged by five days, except in the cases of duly substantiated urgency referred to in Article 27(3), Article 28(6) and in the fourth subparagraph of Article 29(1).

In the case of prior information notices, publication is maintained for 12 months or until receipt of a contract award notice under Article 50 indicating that no further contracts will be awarded during the 12-month period covered by the call for competition.

For public contracts for social and other specific services, the prior information notice referred to in Article 75(1)(b) shall continue to be published until the end of its originally indicated period of validity or until receipt of a contract award notice under Article 50 indicating that no further contracts will be awarded during the period covered by the call for competition.
In the case of calls for competition setting up a dynamic purchasing system, publication continues for the period of validity of the dynamic purchasing system.

Contracting authorities may publish notices for public contracts that are not subject to the publication requirement laid down in the Directive, provided that those notices are sent to the Publications Office of the European Union by electronic means in accordance with the format and procedures for transmission indicated in Annex VIII.
documentation_requirements: Proof of the dates on which notices are dispatched must be capable of being supplied by contracting authorities.

reporting_requirements: Notices for publication, including voluntary notices, must be sent to the Publications Office of the European Union by electronic means in the required format and procedures where applicable.
timeline_requirements: Electronic access to procurement documents must be available from the date of publication of a notice in accordance with Article 51 or from the date on which an invitation to confirm interest was sent.

regulations.regulation_name: Article 54(c)

description.brief_summary: This provision requires disclosure to a tenderer that submitted an admissible tender of certain award-related information, specifically the characteristics and relative advantages of the selected tender and the identity of the successful tenderer or the parties to the framework agreement.
description.detailed_explanation: The subsection identifies a category of recipient—"any tenderer that has made an admissible tender"—and specifies the information that must be communicated to that recipient. The required disclosure consists of: (1) the characteristics of the tender selected, (2) the relative advantages of that selected tender, and (3) the name of the successful tenderer or, where applicable, the parties to the framework agreement. The text is framed as a concrete procedural requirement within an award or post-award communication process in procurement. Although the excerpt is incomplete and does not restate the actor or timing, the wording clearly establishes a mandatory informational entitlement for admissible tenderers.
description.purpose: To ensure transparency in procurement award decisions and enable unsuccessful but admissible tenderers to understand why another tender was selected.
description.legislative_intent: To promote fairness, accountability, and informed review of procurement decisions by requiring meaningful disclosure of the basis for award and the identity of the winning party or framework participants.

regulations.regulation_name: Directive 2014/24/EU on public procurement - Article 54 (Invitations to candidates)

description.brief_summary: Article 54 establishes detailed rules for invitations issued by contracting authorities to selected candidates in specified procurement procedures. It requires simultaneous written invitations, prescribes inclusion of electronic access references and procurement documents in certain cases, requires inclusion of Annex IX information, and permits withholding certain award-related information under narrowly defined circumstances.
description.detailed_explanation: The section imposes procedural obligations on contracting authorities conducting restricted procedures, competitive dialogue procedures, innovation partnerships, and competitive procedures with negotiation. In those procedures, selected candidates must be invited simultaneously and in writing either to submit tenders or, for competitive dialogue, to participate in the dialogue. Where a prior information notice is used as a call for competition under Article 48(2), economic operators that expressed interest must likewise be invited simultaneously and in writing to confirm continuing interest. The invitations must contain a reference to the electronic address where procurement documents are directly available electronically. If unrestricted and full direct access free of charge was not provided for the reasons allowed under Article 53(1), and the documents have not otherwise already been made available, the invitations must be accompanied by the procurement documents. The invitations must also include the information listed in Annex IX. The section further grants contracting authorities discretion to withhold certain information relating to contract award, framework agreement conclusion, or admission to a dynamic purchasing system where disclosure would impede law enforcement, be contrary to the public interest, prejudice legitimate commercial interests of a particular economic operator, or prejudice fair competition.
description.purpose: To ensure equal treatment, transparency, and procedural fairness in procurement by standardizing how invitations are issued and what information they must contain, while preserving limited confidentiality where disclosure would cause specific harms.
description.legislative_intent: The lawmakers intended to create a uniform and non-discriminatory invitation process in multi-stage procurement procedures, ensure candidates receive equivalent information at the same time, support electronic access to procurement documents, and balance transparency with protection of public interest, law enforcement, commercial confidentiality, and competition.

regulations.regulation_name: Public procurement contract award principles and pre-award verification requirements

description.brief_summary: The section establishes mandatory conditions for awarding public contracts. Contracting authorities must award contracts based on criteria laid down under Articles 67 to 69 and must first verify, in accordance with Articles 59 to 61, that specified conditions are fulfilled. Additional procedural principles prohibit premature award, require eventual declaration of an award where a call and participation exist, impose a 70-day maximum period between publication and award announcement, and prohibit contract commencement before an award to a participant.
description.detailed_explanation: The provision imposes a structured sequence for lawful contract award. First, the substantive basis for award must be the award criteria established under Articles 67 to 69. Second, before awarding, the contracting authority must perform verification in accordance with Articles 59 to 61. The section then adds explicit compliance principles governing the timing and validity of the award process. An award cannot occur before publication of the call or before at least one candidate has participated in the procedure. If a call has been published and at least one candidate has participated, the procedure must culminate in an award declaration. The elapsed time between publication of the call and announcement of the awarded candidate must not exceed 70 days. Finally, operational commencement of the contract is prohibited unless a participant has actually been awarded the contract. These are concrete procedural obligations and prohibitions directed primarily at contracting authorities.
description.purpose: To ensure transparent, fair, and procedurally valid public procurement awards by requiring use of lawful award criteria, prior verification of bidder-related conditions, and orderly sequencing of publication, participation, award, and contract commencement.
description.legislative_intent: The lawmakers intended to prevent arbitrary or premature awards, ensure that procurement procedures are based on predefined criteria and verification steps, avoid indefinite or stalled procedures, and ensure that contracts only begin after a lawful award has been made to a participating candidate.

regulations.regulation_name: Directive 2014/24/EU on public procurement - Article 55 (Informing candidates and tenderers)

industry_sectors: Utilities and infrastructure procurement where applicable under public procurement regimes

description.brief_summary: Article 55 requires contracting authorities to promptly inform candidates and tenderers of decisions concerning framework agreements, contract awards, and admission to dynamic purchasing systems, including reasons for certain negative decisions. It also requires authorities, upon written request, to provide specified reasons to unsuccessful candidates within 15 days.
description.detailed_explanation: The provision establishes procedural transparency obligations in EU public procurement. Contracting authorities must communicate procurement outcomes 'as soon as possible' to each candidate and tenderer. The communication must cover decisions on concluding a framework agreement, awarding a contract, or admitting participants to a dynamic purchasing system. The authority must also include the grounds for decisions not to conclude a framework agreement, not to award a contract where there has been a call for competition, to recommence the procedure, or not to implement a dynamic purchasing system. In addition, where a candidate or tenderer submits a written request, the authority must respond as quickly as possible and no later than 15 days after receipt, including at minimum the reasons for rejection of an unsuccessful candidate's request to participate. The extract also contains substantive criteria indicating when a tender is compliant and references exclusion and selection criteria under Articles 45, 57, 58, and 65, which inform the decision-making context.
description.purpose: To ensure transparency, accountability, and procedural fairness in public procurement by requiring timely notification and reason-giving to affected economic operators.
description.legislative_intent: The lawmakers intended to reduce arbitrariness in procurement decisions, enable unsuccessful participants to understand and potentially challenge decisions, and promote equal treatment and confidence in EU procurement procedures.

Framework agreement conclusion decisions
Contract award decisions

Reasons for non-award or procedural restart

description.brief_summary: The extract includes adjacent procurement rules stating that contracting authorities may refuse to award a contract to the most economically advantageous tender if it breaches applicable obligations under Article 18(2), may in open procedures examine tenders before verifying exclusion and selection criteria, and may request missing or incomplete information or documentation subject to equal treatment and transparency.
description.detailed_explanation: Although the section title concerns informing candidates and tenderers, the provided text also contains substantive procedural rules from a neighboring article. These rules establish that a contracting authority may decide not to award a contract to the tenderer submitting the most economically advantageous tender where the authority has established non-compliance with applicable obligations referred to in Article 18(2). In open procedures, authorities may examine tenders before verifying whether exclusion grounds are absent and selection criteria are fulfilled under Articles 57 to 64. If they use this sequencing option, they must ensure verification is carried out impartially and transparently so that no contract is awarded to a tenderer that should have been excluded or that does not meet the selection criteria. The extract further provides that where submitted information or documentation is incomplete, erroneous, or missing, authorities may request economic operators to submit, supplement, clarify, or complete the relevant information or documentation within an appropriate time limit, unless national implementing law provides otherwise, and only if equal treatment and transparency are fully respected.
description.purpose: To provide flexibility in procurement evaluation while preserving legality, equal treatment, transparency, and integrity of award decisions.
description.legislative_intent: The lawmakers intended to allow efficient tender examination and correction of documentary deficiencies without undermining fair competition or awarding contracts to ineligible operators.

regulations.regulation_name: Article 57 - Exclusion criteria in procurement procedures

industry_sectors: All sectors participating in public procurement
Private companies bidding for public contracts

description.brief_summary: Article 57 establishes mandatory exclusion grounds for economic operators in procurement procedures. In the excerpt provided, exclusion applies where a person convicted by final judgment holds specified governance, representation, decision-making, or control roles within the economic operator, and where the operator has been finally determined to be in breach of tax or social security payment obligations.
description.detailed_explanation: The section imposes mandatory exclusion obligations on contracting authorities in procurement procedures. First, it extends the exclusion obligation beyond the economic operator as an abstract entity to situations where the person convicted by final judgment is closely connected to the operator through governance or control functions. Specifically, exclusion must also apply if the convicted person is a member of the administrative, management, or supervisory body of the economic operator, or if that person has powers of representation, decision, or control within the operator. Second, the section requires exclusion where the contracting authority is aware that the economic operator has failed to meet obligations relating to taxes or social security contributions, but only where that breach has been formally established by a judicial or administrative decision that is both final and binding under the legal provisions of either the country of establishment of the operator or the Member State of the contracting authority.
description.purpose: To protect the integrity of public procurement by preventing participation by operators linked to serious criminal convictions through controlling persons and by excluding operators that have definitively failed to comply with tax or social security obligations.
description.legislative_intent: The lawmakers intended to ensure that contracting authorities do not award public contracts to operators whose governance structure includes convicted persons in positions of influence or to operators with definitively established tax or social security non-compliance, thereby promoting fairness, legality, and trust in procurement markets.

organizational_measures: Implement governance screening to identify whether any member of the administrative, management, or supervisory body has been convicted by final judgment.
Implement due diligence procedures to identify persons with powers of representation, decision, or control and assess whether any such person has been convicted by final judgment.
Maintain procedures to monitor and verify tax compliance status relevant to procurement eligibility.
Maintain procedures to monitor and verify social security contribution compliance status relevant to procurement eligibility.
Establish internal review processes for recognizing and acting upon final and binding judicial or administrative decisions.
training_requirements: Procurement compliance personnel should be trained to identify mandatory exclusion triggers related to governance-linked convictions and final tax/social security breach decisions.
audit_requirements: Contracting authorities should audit procurement eligibility assessments to ensure exclusion decisions are made where awareness and final binding determinations exist.
Economic operators should periodically review governance structures and compliance records to detect exclusion risks.

enforcement.regulatory_authority: Contracting authorities applying EU public procurement rules; underlying judicial or administrative bodies establish the relevant final and binding decisions.

penalties.administrative_penalties: Exclusion from participation in a procurement procedure.
penalties.reputational_consequences: Loss of eligibility to participate in public procurement may adversely affect commercial reputation and market access, though not expressly stated in the excerpt.

enforcement_mechanisms: Mandatory exclusion by the contracting authority.
Reliance on final judgments for conviction-based exclusion linkage.
Reliance on final and binding judicial or administrative decisions for tax or social security breach-based exclusion.
Contracting authority awareness of the breach as a trigger for action.

dates.compliance_deadline: Compliance is required at the time of participation in the procurement procedure when the exclusion conditions are met.

implementation_steps: Identify all members of the administrative, management, and supervisory bodies of the economic operator.
Identify all persons with powers of representation, decision, or control within the operator.
Check whether any such person has been convicted by final judgment.
Assess whether the contracting authority is aware of any breach of tax or social security obligations by the operator.
Verify whether any such breach has been established by a judicial or administrative decision.
Confirm that the decision is final and binding.
Confirm that the decision is valid under the legal provisions of the operator's country of establishment or the Member State of the contracting authority.
Exclude the operator from the procurement procedure where the conditions are satisfied.
common_violations: Failing to screen controlling or governing persons for final criminal convictions.
Ignoring convictions of persons who are not directors in title but who have powers of representation, decision, or control.
Allowing an operator to participate despite awareness of a final and binding tax breach decision.
Allowing an operator to participate despite awareness of a final and binding social security breach decision.
Failing to verify whether a judicial or administrative decision is final and binding.
best_practices: Use structured beneficial ownership and governance questionnaires during procurement qualification.
Require declarations and supporting evidence regarding convictions of relevant governing and controlling persons.
Require up-to-date tax and social security compliance evidence where legally appropriate.
Maintain documented decision trails showing how exclusion grounds were assessed.
Cross-check legal status of foreign decisions under the country of establishment and the contracting authority's Member State rules.
compliance_checklist: Has the operator identified all members of its administrative, management, and supervisory bodies?
Has the operator identified all persons with powers of representation, decision, or control?
Has any such person been convicted by final judgment?
Is the contracting authority aware of any tax payment breach by the operator?
Is the contracting authority aware of any social security contribution breach by the operator?
Has the breach been established by a judicial or administrative decision?
Is that decision final and binding?
Is the decision in accordance with the legal provisions of the country of establishment or the Member State of the contracting authority?
If any mandatory exclusion condition is met, has the operator been excluded from the procurement procedure?

key_definitions.economic operator: An entity participating or seeking to participate in a procurement procedure.
key_definitions.contracting authority: The public authority or body conducting the procurement procedure and responsible for applying exclusion rules.
key_definitions.final judgment: A conviction that has become final and is no longer subject to ordinary challenge, as referenced in the excerpt.
key_definitions.administrative body: A governing body of the economic operator falling within the excerpt's specified roles triggering exclusion linkage.
key_definitions.management body: A management-level governing body of the economic operator whose members are covered by the exclusion rule.
key_definitions.supervisory body: An oversight body of the economic operator whose members are covered by the exclusion rule.
key_definitions.powers of representation: Authority to act on behalf of the economic operator.
key_definitions.powers of decision: Authority to make decisions within the economic operator.
key_definitions.powers of control: Authority to control or direct the economic operator.
key_definitions.breach of obligations relating to the pa: Failure to comply with legally required tax payment obligations.
key_definitions.breach of obligations relating to social: Failure to comply with legally required social security contribution obligations.
key_definitions.judicial or administrative decision havi: A formal determination by a court or administrative authority that is conclusive and enforceable under the relevant legal provisions.

regulations.source_section: ## C r i t e r i a f o r q u a l i t a t i v e s e l e c t i o n

regulations.regulation_name: Directive 2014/24/EU on public procurement - Article 57 (Exclusion grounds)

industry_sectors: All sectors participating in public tenders

description.brief_summary: Article 57 establishes when contracting authorities must exclude, may exclude, or may be required by Member States to exclude economic operators from procurement procedures. It covers criminal convictions, tax and social security breaches, insolvency, grave professional misconduct, anti-competitive conduct, conflicts of interest, prior involvement in procurement preparation, poor prior contract performance, misrepresentation, and undue influence. It also provides derogations, self-cleaning rights, and maximum exclusion periods.
description.detailed_explanation: The section imposes mandatory exclusion where a contracting authority has established, through verification under Articles 59, 60 and 61 or otherwise, that an economic operator has been convicted by final judgment for specified criminal offences. It also allows or requires exclusion for breaches of tax or social security obligations, subject to reinstatement where the operator has paid or entered into a binding payment arrangement. In addition, contracting authorities may exclude operators for a broad set of integrity, competition, conflict, insolvency, and performance-related grounds. The section further requires exclusion at any time during the procedure if mandatory grounds become apparent, and permits exclusion at any time for discretionary grounds. Economic operators may in certain cases avoid exclusion by demonstrating reliability through remedial 'self-cleaning' measures, except where a final judgment excludes them for a defined period. Member States must define implementing conditions and maximum exclusion periods, subject to EU law and specified caps.
description.purpose: To protect the integrity, fairness, legality, and reliability of public procurement procedures by preventing participation by operators involved in serious criminality, non-compliance, misconduct, anti-competitive behavior, or unreliable contract performance.
description.legislative_intent: The lawmakers intended to harmonize exclusion grounds across Member States, ensure equal treatment and integrity in procurement, allow proportionate treatment in exceptional cases, and create a structured mechanism for rehabilitation through self-cleaning while preserving public interest and competition.

what_it_covers: Participation in procurement procedures
Mandatory exclusion grounds based on final criminal convictions
Discretionary exclusion grounds based on misconduct or risk indicators
Tax and social security compliance in procurement
Exclusion timing during procurement procedures
Derogations from exclusion
Self-cleaning and rehabilitation evidence
Maximum exclusion periods
Member State implementation rules

entity_types: Public bodies acting as contracting authorities
Private companies bidding for public contracts
Public undertakings participating as economic operators
Consortia or other tendering entities where qualifying as economic operators
who_it_applies_to.geographic_presence: Applies within EU public procurement procedures and to economic operators participating in such procedures, including cross-border bidders from Member States and potentially other operators where procurement rules apply.

what_it_does_not_cover: Detailed evidentiary procedures under Articles 59, 60 and 61 beyond their reference
Detailed substantive definitions of the listed criminal offences beyond cross-references
General procurement selection criteria outside the exclusion grounds discussed here

mandatory_obligations: Contracting authorities shall exclude an economic operator from participation in a procurement procedure where they have established, by verifying in accordance with Articles 59, 60 and 61, or are otherwise aware that the economic operator has been the subject of a conviction by final judgment for one of the listed criminal reasons.

Contracting authorities shall at any time during the procedure exclude an economic operator where it turns out that the economic operator is, in view of acts committed or omitted either before or during the procedure, in one of the situations referred to in paragraphs 1 and 2.
Where self-cleaning measures are considered insufficient, the economic operator shall receive a statement of the reasons for that decision.

For self-cleaning, the economic operator shall prove that it has paid or undertaken to pay compensation in respect of any damage caused by the criminal offence or misconduct, clarified the facts and circumstances in a comprehensive manner by actively collaborating with the investigating authorities, and taken concrete technical, organisational and personnel measures appropriate to prevent further criminal offences or misconduct.
Member States shall specify the implementing conditions for this Article by law, regulation or administrative provision and having regard to Union law.

Member States shall, in particular, determine the maximum period of exclusion if no self-cleaning measures as specified in paragraph 6 are taken by the economic operator to demonstrate its reliability.
Where the period of exclusion has not been set by final judgment, the period shall not exceed five years from the date of the conviction by final judgment in the cases referred to in paragraph 1.
Where the period of exclusion has not been set by final judgment, the period shall not exceed three years from the date of the relevant event in the cases referred to in paragraph 4.
prohibited_actions: Economic operators subject to mandatory exclusion grounds must not be allowed to participate in the procurement procedure.

An economic operator excluded by final judgment from participating in procurement or concession award procedures shall not be entitled to make use of the self-cleaning possibility during the period of exclusion resulting from that judgment in the Member States where the judgment is effective.
Contracting authorities must not refrain from excluding an operator where mandatory grounds under paragraphs 1 and 2 are established, except where a valid derogation applies.
conditional_requirements: Contracting authorities may exclude, or may be required by Member States to exclude, an economic operator where the contracting authority can demonstrate by any appropriate means that the economic operator is in breach of obligations relating to the payment of taxes or social security contributions.

The tax/social security exclusion ground shall no longer apply when the economic operator has fulfilled its obligations by paying or entering into a binding arrangement with a view to paying the taxes or social security contributions due, including, where applicable, any interest accrued or fines.

Member States may provide for a derogation from mandatory exclusion under paragraphs 1 and 2, on an exceptional basis, for overriding reasons relating to the public interest such as public health or protection of the environment.

Member States may also provide for a derogation from the mandatory exclusion provided in paragraph 2 where an exclusion would be clearly disproportionate, in particular where only minor amounts of taxes or social security contributions are unpaid.

Member States may also provide for a derogation from the mandatory exclusion provided in paragraph 2 where the economic operator was informed of the exact amount due following its breach at such time that it did not have the possibility of taking corrective payment measures before the deadline for requesting participation or, in open procedures, the deadline for submitting its tender.

Contracting authorities may exclude, or may be required by Member States to exclude, any economic operator where the contracting authority can demonstrate by any appropriate means a violation of applicable obligations referred to in Article 18(2).

Contracting authorities may exclude, or may be required by Member States to exclude, any economic operator where the operator is bankrupt, subject to insolvency or winding-up proceedings, has assets administered by a liquidator or by the court, is in an arrangement with creditors, has suspended business activities, or is in any analogous situation arising from a similar procedure under national laws and regulations.

Notwithstanding the insolvency ground, Member States may require or may provide for the possibility that the contracting authority does not exclude an economic operator in that situation where the contracting authority has established that the operator will be able to perform the contract, taking into account applicable national rules and measures on continuation of business.

Contracting authorities may exclude, or may be required by Member States to exclude, any economic operator where the contracting authority can demonstrate by appropriate means that the operator is guilty of grave professional misconduct rendering its integrity questionable.

Contracting authorities may exclude, or may be required by Member States to exclude, any economic operator where the contracting authority has sufficiently plausible indications to conclude that the operator has entered into agreements with other economic operators aimed at distorting competition.

Contracting authorities may exclude, or may be required by Member States to exclude, any economic operator where a conflict of interest within the meaning of Article 24 cannot be effectively remedied by other less intrusive measures.

Contracting authorities may exclude, or may be required by Member States to exclude, any economic operator where a distortion of competition from prior involvement of the economic operators in the preparation of the procurement procedure, as referred to in Article 41, cannot be remedied by other, less intrusive measures.

Contracting authorities may exclude, or may be required by Member States to exclude, any economic operator where the operator has shown significant or persistent deficiencies in the performance of a substantive requirement under a prior public contract, prior contract with a contracting entity, or prior concession contract which led to early termination, damages, or other comparable sanctions.

Contracting authorities may exclude, or may be required by Member States to exclude, any economic operator where the operator has been guilty of serious misrepresentation in supplying information required for verification of the absence of grounds for exclusion or fulfilment of selection criteria, has withheld such information, or is not able to submit supporting documents required pursuant to Article 59.

Contracting authorities may exclude, or may be required by Member States to exclude, any economic operator where the operator has undertaken to unduly influence the decision-making process of the contracting authority, to obtain confidential information conferring undue advantages in the procurement procedure, or to negligently provide misleading information that may have a material influence on decisions concerning exclusion, selection or award.

At any time during the procedure, contracting authorities may exclude, or may be required by Member States to exclude, an economic operator where it turns out that the operator is, in view of acts committed or omitted either before or during the procedure, in one of the situations referred to in paragraph 4.

Any economic operator in one of the situations referred to in paragraphs 1 and 4 may provide evidence that measures taken are sufficient to demonstrate its reliability despite the existence of a relevant ground for exclusion.
If self-cleaning evidence is considered sufficient, the economic operator concerned shall not be excluded from the procurement procedure.
The measures taken by the economic operator shall be evaluated taking into account the gravity and particular circumstances of the criminal offence or misconduct.
documentation_requirements: Verification of exclusion grounds must be carried out in accordance with Articles 59, 60 and 61 where applicable.

Economic operators seeking to rely on self-cleaning must provide evidence of compensation paid or undertaken, factual clarification, active collaboration with investigating authorities, and concrete technical, organisational and personnel measures.
Where an operator is unable to submit supporting documents required pursuant to Article 59, this may itself constitute a discretionary exclusion ground.
Where self-cleaning measures are rejected as insufficient, a statement of reasons must be provided to the economic operator.
reporting_requirements: No standalone external reporting obligation is expressly stated in this section.
A reasoned statement must be communicated to the economic operator when self-cleaning measures are deemed insufficient.
timeline_requirements: Mandatory exclusion under paragraphs 1 and 2 applies at any time during the procurement procedure if the relevant situation becomes apparent.
Discretionary exclusion under paragraph 4 may be applied at any time during the procurement procedure if the relevant situation becomes apparent.

For proportionality derogation in tax/social security cases, timing is relevant where the operator was informed of the exact amount due too late to take corrective measures before the deadline for requesting participation or, in open procedures, before the deadline for submitting the tender.
Maximum exclusion period, where not set by final judgment, shall not exceed five years from the date of conviction by final judgment for paragraph 1 cases.
Maximum exclusion period, where not set by final judgment, shall not exceed three years from the date of the relevant event for paragraph 4 cases.
An operator excluded by final judgment cannot use self-cleaning during the period of exclusion resulting from that judgment in the Member States where the judgment is effective.

general_restrictions: Participation in procurement procedures is restricted for economic operators meeting mandatory or discretionary exclusion grounds.
Contracting authorities are constrained to exclude operators in mandatory cases and may be constrained by Member State law to exclude in discretionary cases.
Self-cleaning is unavailable to operators excluded by final judgment during the effective exclusion period.
data_restrictions: Operators must not withhold information required for verification of exclusion grounds or selection criteria.
Operators must not provide misleading information that may materially influence exclusion, selection, or award decisions.
Operators must be able to submit supporting documents required under Article 59.
operational_restrictions: Operators in bankruptcy, insolvency, winding-up, creditor arrangement, suspended business, or analogous situations may be excluded from procurement participation.
Operators whose prior involvement in procurement preparation distorts competition may be excluded if less intrusive remedies are unavailable.
Operators with conflicts of interest that cannot be effectively remedied by less intrusive measures may be excluded.
Operators with significant or persistent deficiencies in prior contract performance leading to early termination, damages, or comparable sanctions may be excluded.
technical_restrictions: No direct technical system restrictions are imposed, but self-cleaning may require concrete technical measures to prevent further criminal offences or misconduct.
geographic_restrictions: The inability to use self-cleaning after exclusion by final judgment applies in the Member States where the judgment is effective.

organizational_rights: Economic operators in situations referred to in paragraphs 1 and 4 may provide evidence that remedial measures are sufficient to demonstrate reliability despite a ground for exclusion.
If self-cleaning evidence is sufficient, the economic operator has the right not to be excluded from the procurement procedure.
Where self-cleaning measures are considered insufficient, the economic operator has the right to receive a statement of reasons for that decision.
Under Member State derogation rules, operators may benefit from exceptional public-interest derogations or proportionality-based derogations in tax/social security cases.
Under Member State rules concerning insolvency situations, an operator may avoid exclusion if the contracting authority establishes that it can still perform the contract.
how_to_exercise_rights: Submit evidence of self-cleaning measures demonstrating compensation, factual clarification, active cooperation with investigating authorities, and preventive technical, organisational, and personnel measures.
Rely on payment or a binding arrangement to pay taxes or social security contributions due, including interest or fines where applicable, to neutralize the tax/social security exclusion ground.
Invoke applicable Member State derogations for overriding public interest or disproportionality where the legal conditions are met.

general_exceptions: The tax/social security exclusion ground no longer applies when the economic operator has fulfilled its obligations by paying or entering into a binding arrangement to pay the amounts due, including interest or fines where applicable.

Member States may provide derogations from mandatory exclusion under paragraphs 1 and 2 on an exceptional basis for overriding reasons relating to the public interest such as public health or protection of the environment.
conditional_exemptions: Member States may provide a derogation from mandatory exclusion under paragraph 2 where exclusion would be clearly disproportionate.
Examples of disproportionality include cases where only minor amounts of taxes or social security contributions are unpaid.
A further example is where the operator was informed of the exact amount due so late that it had no possibility of taking corrective payment measures before the participation or tender deadline.

Member States may require or permit contracting authorities not to exclude an operator in an insolvency-type situation if the authority establishes that the operator will be able to perform the contract, taking into account national continuation-of-business rules and measures.
public_interest_exceptions: Overriding reasons relating to the public interest, such as public health or protection of the environment, may justify derogation from mandatory exclusion under paragraphs 1 and 2.

technical_measures: For self-cleaning, economic operators must take concrete technical measures appropriate to prevent further criminal offences or misconduct.
organizational_measures: For self-cleaning, economic operators must take concrete organisational measures appropriate to prevent further criminal offences or misconduct.
Contracting authorities must maintain procedures to verify exclusion grounds in accordance with Articles 59, 60 and 61.
Contracting authorities must assess whether less intrusive measures can remedy conflicts of interest or distortions of competition before excluding on those grounds.
Contracting authorities must evaluate self-cleaning measures in light of the gravity and particular circumstances of the offence or misconduct.
Member States must establish implementing conditions for Article 57 through law, regulation, or administrative provision.
security_measures: No explicit security measures are prescribed, except insofar as technical and organisational measures are required to prevent further offences or misconduct.
audit_requirements: No formal audit requirement is expressly stated, but contracting authorities must verify and evaluate exclusion grounds and self-cleaning evidence.

enforcement.regulatory_authority: Contracting authorities apply the exclusion rules in procurement procedures; Member States establish implementing conditions and may mandate exclusions or derogations.

penalties.administrative_penalties: Exclusion from participation in procurement procedures; inability to rely on self-cleaning during a final-judgment exclusion period; possible continuation of exclusion for up to the maximum periods set under Member State rules subject to EU caps.
penalties.reputational_consequences: Exclusion based on criminality, misconduct, misrepresentation, anti-competitive conduct, or poor performance may adversely affect procurement reputation and future tender eligibility.

enforcement_mechanisms: Verification in accordance with Articles 59, 60 and 61.
Awareness by the contracting authority of relevant convictions or exclusion situations.
Demonstration by any appropriate means for certain grounds such as tax/social security breaches or Article 18(2) violations.
Assessment of sufficiently plausible indications for anti-competitive agreements.
Evaluation of self-cleaning evidence and issuance of reasons where insufficient.
Application of exclusion at any time during the procurement procedure when relevant facts emerge.

complementary_regulations: Convention on the fight against corruption involving officials of the European Communities or officials of Member States of the European Union Article 3
Council Framework Decision of 13 June 2002 on combating terrorism

implementation_steps: Screen all bidders for mandatory criminal conviction grounds using the verification mechanisms under Articles 59, 60 and 61.
Assess tax and social security compliance and determine whether any unpaid amounts have been settled or are subject to a binding payment arrangement.

Check for discretionary exclusion grounds including insolvency, professional misconduct, anti-competitive agreements, conflicts of interest, prior involvement, poor prior performance, misrepresentation, and undue influence.
Before excluding for conflict of interest or prior involvement, assess whether less intrusive remedial measures can effectively address the issue.
Where Member State law provides derogations, document whether public-interest or disproportionality exceptions apply.
Allow operators to submit self-cleaning evidence where eligible and evaluate the sufficiency of compensation, cooperation, factual clarification, and preventive measures.
Provide a written statement of reasons when self-cleaning evidence is rejected.
Track exclusion periods and ensure they do not exceed the statutory maximum where no final judgment period is set.
common_violations: Failing to exclude an operator with a final criminal conviction for a listed offence.
Excluding an operator for tax/social security arrears even though the operator has paid or entered into a binding payment arrangement.
Excluding for conflict of interest or prior involvement without first considering less intrusive remedies.
Accepting misleading or incomplete exclusion-related information from bidders.
Failing to provide reasons when self-cleaning evidence is deemed insufficient.
Applying exclusion periods longer than the maximum allowed where no final judgment sets the period.
best_practices: Maintain a structured exclusion assessment checklist aligned to each paragraph and subparagraph of Article 57.
Document the evidentiary basis for each exclusion decision, including the legal ground and supporting facts.
Use a proportionality assessment for tax/social security cases where Member State law permits derogation.
Establish a formal self-cleaning review process with criteria for compensation, cooperation, remediation, and prevention.
Coordinate legal, procurement, and compliance teams when assessing grave professional misconduct, anti-competitive conduct, or undue influence.
compliance_checklist: Has the contracting authority verified whether the operator has a final conviction for any listed offence?
Has the authority checked tax and social security payment status?
If taxes/social contributions are unpaid, has the operator paid or entered into a binding arrangement including interest/fines where applicable?
Do any Member State derogations apply for public interest or disproportionality?
Is the operator bankrupt, insolvent, in winding-up, under creditor arrangement, or in an analogous situation?
Can the operator still perform the contract under applicable national continuation-of-business rules?
Is there evidence of grave professional misconduct?
Are there sufficiently plausible indications of anti-competitive agreements?
Is there a conflict of interest that cannot be remedied by less intrusive measures?
Has prior involvement in procurement preparation distorted competition in a way that cannot be remedied by less intrusive measures?
Has the operator shown significant or persistent deficiencies in prior contract performance leading to early termination, damages, or comparable sanctions?
Has the operator misrepresented, withheld, or failed to provide required exclusion/selection information or Article 59 documents?
Has the operator attempted to unduly influence the authority, obtain confidential information, or negligently provide materially misleading information?
Has the authority reassessed exclusion grounds at any time during the procedure as new facts emerge?
If self-cleaning evidence was submitted, was it evaluated against compensation, cooperation, clarification, and preventive measures?
If self-cleaning was rejected, was a statement of reasons issued?
Is the exclusion period within the maximum allowed by law?

key_definitions.contracting authority: The public authority or entity conducting the procurement procedure and responsible for applying exclusion rules.
key_definitions.economic operator: An entity participating in a procurement procedure whose eligibility may be assessed under exclusion grounds.
key_definitions.mandatory exclusion: Exclusion that contracting authorities are required to apply when specified grounds are established.
key_definitions.discretionary exclusion: Exclusion that contracting authorities may apply, or may be required by Member States to apply, in specified situations.
key_definitions.final judgment: A conviction that is final and triggers mandatory exclusion for listed criminal offences.
key_definitions.self-cleaning: Evidence-based remedial process by which an economic operator demonstrates reliability despite an exclusion ground.
key_definitions.grave professional misconduct: Professional misconduct serious enough to render the operator's integrity questionable.
key_definitions.conflict of interest: A conflict within the meaning of Article 24 that may justify exclusion if it cannot be effectively remedied by less intrusive measures.
key_definitions.distortion of competition: An unfair competitive advantage or anti-competitive effect, including from prior involvement in procurement preparation or agreements with other operators.
key_definitions.binding arrangement: A formal arrangement entered into by the operator with a view to paying taxes or social security contributions due, including interest or fines where applicable.

regulations.regulation_name: Council Framework Decision 2008/841/JHA on the fight against organised crime - Article 2 definition reference

industry_sectors: All sectors participating in public tenders

description.brief_summary: This external legal instrument is referenced solely to define 'participation in a criminal organisation' as a mandatory exclusion ground in procurement.
description.detailed_explanation: The section does not reproduce the substantive requirements of the Framework Decision, but expressly incorporates Article 2 as the definitional source for the offence of participation in a criminal organisation. Within the procurement context, a final judgment for this offence triggers mandatory exclusion under Article 57.
description.purpose: To provide a harmonized legal definition for one of the criminal offences that triggers mandatory procurement exclusion.
description.legislative_intent: To ensure consistent interpretation of the criminal organisation offence across Member States when applying procurement exclusion rules.

what_it_covers: Definition of participation in a criminal organisation for procurement exclusion purposes

who_it_applies_to.geographic_presence: Relevant wherever EU procurement exclusion rules are applied.

what_it_does_not_cover: The full substantive criminal law regime is not detailed in this section.

mandatory_obligations: Contracting authorities must treat a final judgment for participation in a criminal organisation, as defined in Article 2 of Council Framework Decision 2008/841/JHA, as a mandatory exclusion ground under Article 57.

general_restrictions: Economic operators convicted by final judgment for participation in a criminal organisation are restricted from procurement participation under Article 57.

general_exceptions: Any exceptions arise under Article 57 derogations and self-cleaning rules, not from this referenced definition itself.

organizational_measures: Contracting authorities should map criminal conviction checks to the referenced offence definition.

enforcement.regulatory_authority: Applied by contracting authorities through Article 57 procurement exclusion decisions.

penalties.administrative_penalties: Mandatory exclusion from procurement where the conviction ground is established.
penalties.reputational_consequences: Association with organised crime convictions may impair procurement eligibility and reputation.

enforcement_mechanisms: Use of the referenced criminal law definition when assessing final judgments under Article 57.

implementation_steps: When reviewing criminal convictions, confirm whether the offence falls within the Article 2 definition referenced by Article 57(1)(a).
common_violations: Failing to recognize a qualifying final judgment as a mandatory exclusion ground.
best_practices: Maintain legal cross-reference guidance for procurement teams on offences incorporated by reference.
compliance_checklist: Is there a final judgment?
Does the conviction correspond to participation in a criminal organisation as defined in Article 2 of Framework Decision 2008/841/JHA?

key_definitions.participation in a criminal organisation: As defined in Article 2 of Council Framework Decision 2008/841/JHA and incorporated by reference into Article 57(1)(a).

regulations.regulation_id: Convention on the fight against corruption involving officials of the European Communities or officials of Member States of the European Union Article 3
regulations.regulation_name: Convention on the fight against corruption involving officials of the European Communities or officials of Member States of the European Union - Article 3 definition reference

industry_sectors: All sectors participating in public tenders

description.brief_summary: This Convention is referenced as the definitional source for corruption constituting a mandatory procurement exclusion ground.
description.detailed_explanation: The section identifies corruption, as defined in Article 3 of the Convention, as one of the offences that triggers mandatory exclusion when established by final judgment. The section itself does not restate the Convention's substantive anti-corruption rules, but uses the Convention to define the relevant offence for procurement purposes.
description.purpose: To anchor the procurement exclusion ground for corruption in an established EU legal definition.
description.legislative_intent: To ensure consistent treatment of corruption convictions across Member States in public procurement.

what_it_covers: Definition of corruption for procurement exclusion purposes

who_it_applies_to.geographic_presence: Relevant in EU procurement procedures.

what_it_does_not_cover: The full anti-corruption regime of the Convention is not detailed in this section.

mandatory_obligations: Contracting authorities must treat a final judgment for corruption, as defined in Article 3 of the Convention, as a mandatory exclusion ground under Article 57.

general_restrictions: Economic operators convicted by final judgment for corruption are restricted from procurement participation under Article 57.

general_exceptions: Any exceptions arise under Article 57 derogations and self-cleaning rules, not from this referenced definition itself.

organizational_measures: Contracting authorities should align corruption conviction screening with the referenced Article 3 definition.

enforcement.regulatory_authority: Applied by contracting authorities through Article 57 procurement exclusion decisions.

penalties.administrative_penalties: Mandatory exclusion from procurement where the conviction ground is established.
penalties.reputational_consequences: Corruption-related exclusion may significantly impair procurement reputation and eligibility.

enforcement_mechanisms: Use of the referenced corruption definition when assessing final judgments under Article 57.

implementation_steps: Assess whether any final corruption conviction falls within the Article 3 definition referenced by Article 57.
common_violations: Failing to exclude a bidder with a qualifying final corruption conviction.
best_practices: Provide procurement teams with legal guidance on corruption offences incorporated by reference.
compliance_checklist: Is there a final judgment?
Does the conviction correspond to corruption as defined in Article 3 of the Convention?

key_definitions.corruption: As defined in Article 3 of the Convention on the fight against corruption involving officials of the European Communities or officials of Member States of the European Union and incorporated by reference into Article 57(1)(b).

regulations.regulation_name: Directive 2014/24/EU on public procurement - Article 58 (Selection criteria)

description.brief_summary: Article 58 regulates the selection criteria that contracting authorities may impose on economic operators in public procurement procedures. It limits such criteria to suitability to pursue the professional activity, economic and financial standing, and technical and professional ability, and requires that all participation requirements be transparent, objective, non-discriminatory, related to the subject matter of the contract, and proportionate.
description.detailed_explanation: The section establishes detailed legal constraints on how contracting authorities may assess and select economic operators. It permits consideration of financial ratios such as the ratio between assets and liabilities only where the procurement documents specify the methods and criteria for such consideration, and those methods and criteria must be transparent, objective, and non-discriminatory. It identifies the permissible categories of selection criteria as: suitability to pursue the professional activity, economic and financial standing, and technical and professional ability. It further restricts contracting authorities to imposing only those criteria referred to in the relevant paragraphs as participation requirements, and obliges them to limit requirements to what is appropriate to ensure that a candidate or tenderer has the legal and financial capacities and the technical and professional abilities necessary to perform the contract. All such requirements must be related and proportionate to the subject matter of the contract. The section also contains specific rules for contracts divided into lots, allowing minimum yearly turnover requirements to be set by reference to groups of lots where several lots may be awarded for simultaneous execution. For framework agreements awarded after reopening competition, and for dynamic purchasing systems, the maximum yearly turnover requirement must be calculated using specified valuation methods tied to the expected maximum size of contracts or the estimated value of the framework agreement. With respect to technical and professional ability, contracting authorities may require evidence of necessary human and technical resources and experience, including sufficient experience demonstrated by suitable references from past contracts. They may also infer lack of required professional ability where conflicting interests are established that may negatively affect contract performance. In supplies requiring siting or installation work, services, or works, professional ability may be evaluated by reference to skills, efficiency, experience, and reliability. Finally, contracting authorities must indicate required participation conditions, including minimum levels of ability and appropriate means of proof, in the contract notice or invitation to confirm interest.
description.purpose: To ensure that selection criteria in public procurement are lawful, fair, proportionate, and directly connected to the ability of economic operators to perform the contract.
description.legislative_intent: To prevent arbitrary, excessive, discriminatory, or irrelevant participation requirements while allowing contracting authorities to verify that bidders possess the necessary legal, financial, technical, and professional capacity.

what_it_covers: Selection criteria in public procurement procedures
Assessment of economic and financial standing
Assessment of technical and professional ability
Use of financial ratios in selection
Turnover requirements
Procurement divided into lots
Framework agreements with reopened competition

industry_sectors: Utilities where applicable through procurement frameworks

description.brief_summary: Article 59 establishes the ESPD as a self-declaration mechanism that contracting authorities must accept at the request-to-participate or tender stage as preliminary evidence that an economic operator is not subject to exclusion grounds and satisfies applicable selection criteria and, where relevant, objective rules and criteria.
description.detailed_explanation: The section imposes procedural obligations on contracting authorities and Member States regarding the use of the European Single Procurement Document. At submission stage, contracting authorities must accept the ESPD instead of certificates issued by public authorities or third parties. The ESPD functions as preliminary evidence that the economic operator is not in an exclusion situation under Article 57, meets selection criteria under Article 58, and where applicable satisfies objective rules and criteria under Article 65. The ESPD must also include equivalent information for entities whose capacities are relied upon under Article 63. Contracting authorities retain the power to request supporting documents during the procedure where necessary for proper conduct, and before award they must require up-to-date supporting documents from the successful tenderer, subject to a specific exception for certain framework agreement contracts. Economic operators are exempt from submitting supporting documents where the contracting authority can obtain them directly from a free national database or already possesses them. Member States must ensure cross-border consultation of relevant databases under the same conditions and must maintain in e-Certis a complete and current list of such databases. Where certificates are not issued or do not cover all required cases, substitute evidence in the form of declarations on oath or solemn declarations is permitted, and Member States must provide official declarations to that effect through e-Certis. The Commission is also required to review practical application of the ESPD and report by a specified date.
description.purpose: To simplify and standardize evidence of eligibility and qualification in EU public procurement, reduce administrative burden, facilitate cross-border participation, and improve access to procurement opportunities across Member States.
description.legislative_intent: The lawmakers intended to replace repetitive documentary submissions at early procurement stages with a harmonized self-declaration, while preserving the contracting authority’s ability to verify evidence when necessary and ensuring interoperability of national databases across the internal market.

description.brief_summary: Article 60(3) specifies that proof of an economic operator’s economic and financial standing may generally be provided by one or more references listed in Annex XII Part I, and where the operator cannot provide the requested references for a valid reason, it may use another document that the contracting authority considers appropriate.
description.detailed_explanation: This provision governs acceptable evidence for demonstrating economic and financial standing in procurement procedures. It establishes a general rule that proof may be provided through one or more references listed in Annex XII Part I. It also creates a flexibility mechanism: if an economic operator is unable, for any valid reason, to provide the references requested by the contracting authority, the operator may instead prove its economic and financial standing by any other document that the contracting authority considers appropriate. The rule therefore balances standardization of evidence with proportionality and accessibility for operators who cannot produce the standard references.
description.purpose: To define acceptable evidence of economic and financial standing while preventing unjust exclusion of operators who cannot provide standard references for valid reasons.
description.legislative_intent: To ensure contracting authorities can assess financial reliability using recognized forms of evidence, while preserving flexibility and equal access to procurement for operators with legitimate documentary constraints.
