regulations.regulation_name: Directive 2014/24/EU on public procurement - provisions on recognition of equivalent certificates and reduction of tenders or solutions

industry_sectors: Utilities where applicable under procurement frameworks

description.brief_summary: The provision ensures non-discriminatory access to public procurement for economic operators from other Member States by prohibiting mandatory local registration or certification and requiring recognition of equivalent evidence. It also regulates how contracting authorities may reduce the number of tenders or solutions during certain procurement procedures, requiring use of pre-stated award criteria and preservation of genuine competition.
description.detailed_explanation: This section imposes concrete obligations on contracting authorities in EU public procurement. First, it states that economic operators established in other Member States cannot be compelled to undergo domestic registration or certification merely to participate in a public contract. Instead, contracting authorities must recognize equivalent certificates issued by bodies established in other Member States and must also accept other equivalent means of proof. This creates a mutual-recognition and equivalence framework intended to remove unjustified barriers to cross-border participation. Second, where a contracting authority chooses to reduce the number of tenders to be negotiated under Article 29(6) or the number of solutions to be discussed under Article 30(4), the reduction must be carried out using the award criteria already stated in the procurement documents. In the final stage, the remaining number must be sufficient to ensure genuine competition, provided there are enough tenders, solutions, or qualified candidates available.
description.purpose: To prevent discriminatory or protectionist procurement practices, facilitate cross-border participation by economic operators from other Member States, and ensure that any narrowing of competition in negotiated or solution-based procedures is transparent, objective, and competition-preserving.
description.legislative_intent: The lawmakers intended to promote equal treatment, mutual recognition, transparency, and effective competition in EU procurement markets by removing unnecessary national administrative barriers and constraining discretionary reduction of participants through pre-disclosed criteria.

what_it_covers: Participation conditions for economic operators from other Member States in public contracts
Recognition of certificates issued by bodies in other Member States
Acceptance of equivalent means of proof
Reduction of the number of tenders to be negotiated
Reduction of the number of solutions to be discussed
Use of award criteria in down-selection during procurement procedures
Maintenance of genuine competition at the final stage of the procedure

target_entities: Bodies issuing certificates in Member States
entity_types: Private companies participating in public tenders
who_it_applies_to.geographic_presence: Applies where economic operators are from Member States other than the Member State of the contracting authority, within EU public procurement procedures.

what_it_does_not_cover: Specific penalty amounts for non-compliance
Detailed evidentiary standards for what constitutes equivalence beyond the obligation to accept equivalent certificates and proof
Procedures outside the referenced procurement contexts of Article 29(6) and Article 30(4)
General introductory policy statements

mandatory_obligations: Contracting authorities must not oblige economic operators from other Member States to undergo registration or certification in order to participate in a public contract.
Contracting authorities must recognize equivalent certificates from bodies established in other Member States.
Contracting authorities must accept other equivalent means of proof.
Where contracting authorities reduce the number of tenders to be negotiated under Article 29(6), they must do so by applying the award criteria stated in the procurement documents.
Where contracting authorities reduce the number of solutions to be discussed under Article 30(4), they must do so by applying the award criteria stated in the procurement documents.
In the final stage, the number of tenders, solutions, or qualified candidates remaining must make for genuine competition, insofar as there are enough tenders, solutions, or qualified candidates.
prohibited_actions: Requiring economic operators from other Member States to undergo domestic registration as a condition of participation.
Requiring economic operators from other Member States to undergo domestic certification as a condition of participation.
Refusing to recognize equivalent certificates from bodies established in other Member States.
Refusing to accept other equivalent means of proof where equivalence is established.
Reducing the number of tenders or solutions using criteria other than the award criteria stated in the procurement documents.
Reducing participant numbers to a level that undermines genuine competition when sufficient tenders, solutions, or qualified candidates exist.
conditional_requirements: If a contracting authority exercises the option of reducing the number of tenders to be negotiated under Article 29(6), the reduction must be based on the award criteria stated in the procurement documents.

If a contracting authority exercises the option of reducing the number of solutions to be discussed under Article 30(4), the reduction must be based on the award criteria stated in the procurement documents.
The obligation to maintain a final number sufficient for genuine competition applies insofar as there are enough tenders, solutions, or qualified candidates.
documentation_requirements: Procurement documents must state the award criteria that will be applied if the contracting authority reduces the number of tenders or solutions.
Equivalent certificates from bodies established in other Member States must be accepted as valid documentary evidence where relevant.
Other equivalent means of proof must be accepted where certificates are not provided but equivalent proof is offered.
timeline_requirements: The award criteria used for reduction must be stated in the procurement documents before the reduction decision is applied.
Recognition of equivalent certificates and acceptance of equivalent proof must occur during participation assessment in the procurement process.
The requirement for genuine competition applies at the final stage of the procedure.

general_restrictions: Contracting authorities are restricted from imposing national registration or certification requirements on economic operators from other Member States as a participation condition.
Contracting authorities are restricted to using only the award criteria stated in the procurement documents when reducing the number of tenders or solutions.
operational_restrictions: Down-selection decisions in negotiated or solution-discussion stages cannot be made on undisclosed, arbitrary, or ad hoc criteria.
Final-stage participant reduction cannot be carried out in a way that eliminates genuine competition where sufficient participants exist.
geographic_restrictions: The prohibition on mandatory registration or certification specifically protects economic operators from other Member States.

organizational_rights: Economic operators from other Member States have the right not to be obliged to undergo local registration or certification solely to participate in a public contract.
Economic operators from other Member States have the right to have equivalent certificates from bodies established in other Member States recognized by contracting authorities.
Economic operators have the right to submit other equivalent means of proof, which contracting authorities must accept.
Participants in procedures involving reduction of tenders or solutions have the right to have such reduction carried out only on the basis of award criteria stated in the procurement documents.
Participants have the right to a final-stage process that preserves genuine competition where sufficient tenders, solutions, or qualified candidates exist.
how_to_exercise_rights: Submit equivalent certificates issued by bodies established in another Member State during the procurement process.
Provide alternative equivalent means of proof where local registration or certification is not held.
Review procurement documents to verify the stated award criteria governing any reduction in tenders or solutions.
Challenge procurement decisions if a contracting authority imposes domestic registration/certification requirements or uses unstated criteria for reduction.

general_exceptions: The requirement to maintain a final number that makes for genuine competition is qualified by the phrase 'in so far as there are enough tenders, solutions or qualified candidates.'
conditional_exemptions: If there are not enough tenders, solutions, or qualified candidates, the final number may be lower than would otherwise be necessary for genuine competition.

organizational_measures: Establish procurement procedures that do not require domestic registration or certification from cross-border bidders as a participation prerequisite.
Implement an equivalence assessment process for certificates issued by bodies in other Member States.
Implement a process for evaluating and accepting other equivalent means of proof.
Ensure procurement documents clearly state the award criteria that will govern any reduction in tenders or solutions.
Maintain procedural controls to ensure final-stage reductions preserve genuine competition where sufficient participants exist.
training_requirements: Procurement staff should be trained on mutual recognition of certificates and acceptance of equivalent proof from other Member States.
Procurement staff should be trained to apply only pre-disclosed award criteria when reducing tenders or solutions.
Procurement staff should be trained on competition-preserving obligations at the final stage of negotiated or solution-based procedures.
audit_requirements: Contracting authorities should be able to demonstrate that any reduction of tenders or solutions was based on award criteria stated in the procurement documents.
Contracting authorities should retain evidence showing recognition of equivalent certificates and acceptance or assessment of equivalent means of proof.
Contracting authorities should document how the final number of participants was sufficient to ensure genuine competition, where enough participants existed.
certification_requirements: No domestic registration or certification may be required from economic operators from other Member States solely for participation.
Equivalent certificates from bodies established in other Member States must be recognized.

enforcement.regulatory_authority: National procurement oversight bodies, review bodies, courts, and other competent authorities responsible for enforcing Directive 2014/24/EU in Member States

penalties.administrative_penalties: Not specified in this section; remedies and sanctions depend on Member State implementation and procurement review mechanisms.
penalties.reputational_consequences: Potential procurement challenge findings, annulment of decisions, and reputational harm for discriminatory or non-transparent procurement practices.

enforcement_mechanisms: Bidder challenges before procurement review bodies or courts
Administrative review of procurement procedures
Judicial scrutiny of discriminatory participation requirements
Review of procurement documents and down-selection decisions for compliance with stated award criteria

dates.compliance_deadline: Subject to Member State transposition of Directive 2014/24/EU, generally by 2016-04-18

related_regulations.parent_legislation: Directive 2014/24/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 26 February 2014 on public procurement
complementary_regulations: National public procurement laws implementing Directive 2014/24/EU
superseded_regulations: Directive 2004/18/EC, to the extent replaced by Directive 2014/24/EU

implementation_steps: Remove any procurement rule or template requiring foreign bidders to obtain domestic registration or certification solely to participate.
Create internal guidance for recognizing equivalent certificates from bodies established in other Member States.
Define a documented method for assessing 'other equivalent means of proof.'
Ensure procurement documents expressly state the award criteria that will be used if the number of tenders or solutions is reduced.
When reducing tenders or solutions, apply only the stated award criteria and document the scoring or rationale.
Before finalizing reductions, verify whether enough tenders, solutions, or qualified candidates exist to maintain genuine competition.
common_violations: Demanding local registration before allowing a foreign economic operator to participate.
Rejecting foreign certificates without assessing equivalence.
Refusing alternative equivalent proof without justification.
Using unstated or subjective criteria to reduce the number of tenders or solutions.
Reducing the field to too few participants despite having enough qualified tenders, solutions, or candidates to preserve competition.
best_practices: Use procurement documentation that expressly acknowledges acceptance of equivalent certificates and equivalent means of proof.
Maintain a transparent equivalence assessment record for each foreign certificate or proof submitted.
Predefine and publish clear award criteria and any methodology relevant to reduction decisions.
Document the competitive rationale for the final number of participants retained.
compliance_checklist: Does the procedure avoid requiring domestic registration or certification from economic operators from other Member States?
Are equivalent certificates from bodies established in other Member States recognized?
Are other equivalent means of proof accepted?
If reduction of tenders or solutions is used, are the applicable award criteria stated in the procurement documents?
Was the reduction carried out strictly using those stated award criteria?
At the final stage, does the remaining number ensure genuine competition where enough tenders, solutions, or qualified candidates exist?

key_definitions.economic operators: Entities seeking to participate in a public contract, including suppliers, service providers, and contractors.
key_definitions.contracting authorities: Public bodies or authorities conducting procurement procedures subject to the directive.
key_definitions.equivalent certificates: Certificates issued by bodies established in other Member States that are comparable in substance to domestic certificates required or recognized in the procurement process.
key_definitions.other equivalent means of proof: Alternative evidence demonstrating equivalent compliance or qualification where a specific certificate is not held.
key_definitions.award criteria: The criteria stated in the procurement documents used to evaluate tenders and, in this context, to reduce the number of tenders or solutions.
key_definitions.genuine competition: A final-stage level of participation sufficient to preserve real competitive pressure, insofar as enough tenders, solutions, or qualified candidates exist.

regulations.regulation_id: Contract award criteria (unnumbered article section; paragraphs 1, 2, 4, 5; reference to Article 68)
regulations.regulation_name: Contract award criteria for public contracts

industry_sectors: Public contracting across all sectors using public contracts

description.brief_summary: The section establishes mandatory rules for how contracting authorities must evaluate and award public contracts. Contracts must be awarded on the basis of the most economically advantageous tender, using price or cost and potentially price-quality criteria linked to the subject matter of the contract. Award criteria must not give unrestricted discretion, must preserve effective competition, must be verifiable, and must be weighted or ranked in procurement documents.
description.detailed_explanation: The section imposes a structured framework for contract award decisions by contracting authorities. First, it requires that public contracts be awarded on the basis of the 'most economically advantageous tender', subject to national rules on regulated prices for certain supplies or remuneration for certain services. Second, it defines how that tender is to be identified: by reference to price or cost, using a cost-effectiveness approach such as life-cycle costing under Article 68, and potentially including the best price-quality ratio. The price-quality ratio may be assessed using criteria linked to the subject matter of the contract, including qualitative, environmental, and social aspects. The text gives examples of permissible criteria, including quality-related features and, in certain circumstances, the organisation, qualification, and experience of staff assigned to contract performance. Third, it limits the discretion of contracting authorities by requiring that award criteria not confer unrestricted freedom of choice, that they ensure effective competition, and that they be accompanied by specifications enabling effective verification of tenderers' information. Where there is doubt, the authority must effectively verify the accuracy of information and proof submitted. Fourth, it requires transparency in procurement documents by obliging the authority to specify the relative weighting of each chosen criterion, unless the award is based on price alone. If objective reasons make weighting impossible, the criteria must instead be listed in decreasing order of importance.
description.purpose: To ensure that public contract awards are made objectively, transparently, competitively, and on economically sound grounds rather than arbitrary preference.
description.legislative_intent: The lawmakers intended to prevent arbitrary or opaque award decisions, promote fair competition among tenderers, ensure that award criteria are genuinely connected to the contract and capable of verification, and improve value for money in public procurement through structured evaluation methods.

what_it_covers: Award of public contracts
Selection and formulation of award criteria
Evaluation of tenders
Use of price, cost, and price-quality criteria
Disclosure of weighting of award criteria in procurement documents
Verification of tender information and supporting proof
Use of life-cycle costing as a cost-effectiveness approach

who_it_applies_to.geographic_presence: Applies within EU public procurement contexts governed by the underlying procurement framework

what_it_does_not_cover: National laws, regulations, or administrative provisions concerning the price of certain supplies
National laws, regulations, or administrative provisions concerning the remuneration of certain services
Detailed life-cycle costing methodology beyond the reference to Article 68

mandatory_obligations: Contracting authorities shall base the award of public contracts on the most economically advantageous tender.
The most economically advantageous tender shall be identified from the point of view of the contracting authority on the basis of the price or cost.
Where a cost-based approach is used, it shall use a cost-effectiveness approach, such as life-cycle costing in accordance with Article 68.
Where the best price-quality ratio is used, it shall be assessed on the basis of criteria linked to the subject matter of the public contract.
Award criteria shall ensure the possibility of effective competition.
Award criteria shall be accompanied by specifications that allow the information provided by tenderers to be effectively verified.
In case of doubt, contracting authorities shall verify effectively the accuracy of the information and proof provided by the tenderers.

The contracting authority shall specify in the procurement documents the relative weighting given to each of the criteria chosen to determine the most economically advantageous tender, except where the tender is identified on the basis of price alone.
Where weighting is not possible for objective reasons, the contracting authority shall indicate the criteria in decreasing order of importance.
prohibited_actions: Contracting authorities must not use award criteria that have the effect of conferring an unrestricted freedom of choice on the contracting authority.
conditional_requirements: If the most economically advantageous tender is identified using the best price-quality ratio, the assessment criteria may include qualitative, environmental, and/or social aspects, provided they are linked to the subject matter of the contract.

Organisation, qualification, and experience of staff assigned to performing the contract may be used as award criteria only where the quality of the staff assigned can have a significant impact on the level of performance of the contract.
Relative weighting of criteria need not be specified where the award is identified on the basis of price alone.
If weighting cannot be provided for objective reasons, criteria must be listed in decreasing order of importance.
Where doubt exists regarding information or proof submitted by tenderers, the contracting authority must effectively verify its accuracy.
documentation_requirements: Procurement documents must specify the relative weighting assigned to each chosen award criterion, except where award is based on price alone.
If weightings are expressed as a range, the range must have an appropriate maximum spread.
Where weighting is not possible for objective reasons, procurement documentation must indicate the criteria in decreasing order of importance.
Award criteria must be accompanied by specifications enabling effective verification of tenderers' information.
timeline_requirements: Relative weighting or, where applicable, decreasing order of importance must be specified in the procurement documents before tender evaluation as part of the procurement documentation.
Verification of tenderer information must occur in case of doubt during the assessment process.

general_restrictions: Award decisions are restricted to the framework of the most economically advantageous tender.
Criteria used must be linked to the subject matter of the public contract when assessing the best price-quality ratio.
The authority's discretion is restricted; criteria cannot allow unrestricted freedom of choice.
data_restrictions: Information provided by tenderers must be capable of effective verification through accompanying specifications.
operational_restrictions: Contracting authorities cannot rely on unverifiable or overly discretionary criteria.
Authorities must structure evaluation criteria to preserve effective competition.
Authorities must disclose weighting or ranking methodology in procurement documents, subject to the stated exception.
technical_restrictions: Where ranges are used for criterion weighting, they must have an appropriate maximum spread.
geographic_restrictions: The rule applies within the EU procurement legal framework, without prejudice to national rules on regulated prices or remuneration in certain sectors.

organizational_rights: Tenderers have an implied right to compete under award criteria that preserve effective competition.
Tenderers have an implied right to evaluation under criteria that are specified, linked to the contract, and capable of verification.
Tenderers have an implied right to transparency regarding criterion weighting or ranking in procurement documents, except where award is based on price alone.
how_to_exercise_rights: Tenderers may rely on the procurement documents to understand the weighting or order of importance of award criteria.
Tenderers may challenge procurement procedures where criteria confer unrestricted discretion, are not linked to the subject matter, are not properly disclosed, or are not verifiable.

general_exceptions: The rules apply 'without prejudice to national laws, regulations or administrative provisions concerning the price of certain supplies or the remuneration of certain services.'
conditional_exemptions: The obligation to specify relative weighting does not apply where the most economically advantageous tender is identified on the basis of price alone.
Where weighting is not possible for objective reasons, the authority may indicate criteria in decreasing order of importance instead of assigning weightings.
public_interest_exceptions: National legal provisions on regulated prices or remuneration remain unaffected.

technical_measures: Develop evaluation methodologies that use price or cost as the basis for identifying the most economically advantageous tender.
Where using cost-effectiveness, implement life-cycle costing methods consistent with Article 68 if applicable.
Design specifications and evaluation tools that allow effective verification of tenderer-submitted information.
If using weighting ranges, ensure the ranges have an appropriate maximum spread.
organizational_measures: Establish internal procurement procedures requiring award on the basis of the most economically advantageous tender.
Adopt governance controls to ensure award criteria do not confer unrestricted discretion.
Require procurement teams to document criterion weighting or ranking in procurement documents.
Implement review procedures for verifying tender information where doubts arise.
Ensure criteria selected for best price-quality ratio are linked to the subject matter of the contract.
training_requirements: Procurement staff should be trained on drafting lawful award criteria.
Procurement evaluators should be trained on how to verify tenderer information and supporting proof.
Staff should be trained on when personnel qualifications and experience may lawfully be used as award criteria.
audit_requirements: Audit procurement files to confirm that weighting or ranking was disclosed in procurement documents.
Audit whether award criteria were linked to the subject matter of the contract.
Audit whether verification steps were taken where doubts about tender information arose.
Audit whether criteria preserved effective competition and avoided unrestricted discretion.

penalties.administrative_penalties: Not specified in this section; non-compliance may expose the procurement procedure to administrative challenge, annulment, or corrective measures under the broader procurement regime.
penalties.reputational_consequences: Non-transparent or arbitrary award criteria may undermine confidence in the contracting authority and expose it to procurement disputes.

enforcement_mechanisms: Review of procurement documents for disclosed weighting or ranking of criteria
Scrutiny of whether criteria are linked to the subject matter of the contract
Assessment of whether criteria permit effective competition
Examination of whether the authority verified tender information where doubts existed
Procurement challenge or review procedures under the broader legal framework

dates.compliance_deadline: Applies at the time procurement documents are prepared and throughout tender evaluation and award.

complementary_regulations: National laws, regulations, or administrative provisions concerning the price of certain supplies
National laws, regulations, or administrative provisions concerning the remuneration of certain services

implementation_steps: Define award methodology around the most economically advantageous tender.
Choose whether evaluation will be based on price alone, cost, or best price-quality ratio.
If using cost, determine whether life-cycle costing under Article 68 is appropriate.
Select only criteria linked to the subject matter of the contract.
Ensure criteria do not give evaluators unrestricted discretion.
Draft specifications that enable verification of all tenderer claims relevant to award criteria.
Publish the relative weighting of each criterion in procurement documents, or if objectively impossible, list criteria in decreasing order of importance.
If using weighting ranges, ensure the maximum spread is appropriate.
During evaluation, verify the accuracy of tenderer information and proof whenever doubts arise.
Document all verification and evaluation decisions.
common_violations: Using vague or subjective criteria that confer unrestricted freedom of choice
Failing to link quality, environmental, or social criteria to the subject matter of the contract
Omitting criterion weighting from procurement documents when required
Using staff qualification or experience as an award criterion where staff quality does not significantly affect contract performance
Failing to verify tenderer claims when doubts arise
Using unverifiable criteria or lacking specifications needed to test tenderer assertions
Applying undisclosed weighting or changing criterion importance after publication
best_practices: Use clear, measurable, contract-linked award criteria.
Document the rationale for each criterion and its weighting.
Where weighting is impossible, record the objective reasons supporting use of decreasing order of importance.
Create verification protocols for tenderer claims, including documentary proof checks.
Ensure evaluators understand the distinction between selection criteria and award criteria.
Use life-cycle costing where long-term cost implications are material.
compliance_checklist: Is the contract award based on the most economically advantageous tender?
Has the authority identified the tender on the basis of price or cost?
If cost is used, is a cost-effectiveness approach applied?
If best price-quality ratio is used, are all criteria linked to the subject matter of the contract?
Do the award criteria avoid conferring unrestricted freedom of choice?
Do the criteria preserve effective competition?
Are there specifications enabling effective verification of tenderer information?
Is there a process to verify tender information where doubts arise?
Are the relative weightings of each criterion stated in the procurement documents, unless award is based on price alone?
If ranges are used, do they have an appropriate maximum spread?
If weighting is not possible for objective reasons, are criteria listed in decreasing order of importance?
If staff qualifications/experience are used, is there a significant impact on contract performance justifying their use?

key_definitions.most economically advantageous tender: The tender identified from the point of view of the contracting authority on the basis of price or cost, using a cost-effectiveness approach, and which may include the best price-quality ratio.
key_definitions.cost-effectiveness approach: An approach to identifying the most economically advantageous tender based on cost considerations, such as life-cycle costing in accordance with Article 68.
key_definitions.best price-quality ratio: An award basis assessed using criteria linked to the subject matter of the contract, including qualitative, environmental and/or social aspects.
key_definitions.award criteria: The criteria chosen by the contracting authority to determine the most economically advantageous tender.
key_definitions.effective competition: A condition that award criteria must ensure, preventing criteria from being structured in a way that unduly restricts or distorts competition.
key_definitions.relative weighting: The comparative importance assigned by the contracting authority to each award criterion in the procurement documents.
key_definitions.decreasing order of importance: An alternative ranking of criteria required where objective reasons make numerical weighting impossible.
key_definitions.linked to the subject-matter of the publ: A requirement that criteria used for assessing the best price-quality ratio must relate directly to the contract being procured.
key_definitions.verification: The effective checking of the accuracy of information and proof provided by tenderers, especially in case of doubt.

regulations.regulation_id: Directive 2014/24/EU Article 68 and related extracted provisions
regulations.regulation_name: Directive 2014/24/EU on public procurement - Life-cycle costing

description.brief_summary: These provisions regulate how contracting authorities may use life-cycle costing in public procurement and what cost elements may be included. They also require transparency in procurement documents and impose objective, accessible, and non-discriminatory conditions on methods used to monetize environmental externalities.
description.detailed_explanation: The section provides detailed rules for the use of life-cycle costing as part of procurement evaluation. It states that life-cycle costing shall, to the extent relevant, cover parts or all of specified categories of costs over the life cycle of a product, service, or works. These include costs borne by the contracting authority or other users, such as acquisition costs, use costs including energy and other resource consumption, maintenance costs, and end-of-life costs such as collection and recycling. It also permits inclusion of costs imputed to environmental externalities linked to the product, service, or works during its life cycle, but only where their monetary value can be determined and verified. Examples include greenhouse gas emissions, other pollutant emissions, and other climate change mitigation costs. Where contracting authorities assess costs using a life-cycle costing approach, they are required to specify in the procurement documents both the data to be provided by tenderers and the method that will be used to determine life-cycle costs based on those data. Any method used to assess costs imputed to environmental externalities must satisfy cumulative conditions: it must be based on objectively verifiable and non-discriminatory criteria; if not established for repeated or continuous application, it must not unduly favor or disadvantage certain economic operators; it must be accessible to all interested parties; and the required data must be capable of being provided with reasonable effort by normally diligent economic operators, including operators from third countries party to the GPA or other international agreements binding on the Union. Where a common Union legislative method for calculating life-cycle costs has been made mandatory, that common method must be applied. The section also notes that the list of such legislative acts is set out in Annex XIII and may be updated by delegated acts.
description.purpose: To ensure that procurement decisions based on life-cycle costing are transparent, comparable, objective, and capable of incorporating environmental externalities in a verifiable and non-discriminatory manner.
description.legislative_intent: The lawmakers intended to enable contracting authorities to move beyond simple purchase price and evaluate total cost over the life cycle, while preventing arbitrary or discriminatory methodologies and promoting harmonized calculation methods where mandated at Union level.

what_it_covers: Use of life-cycle costing in procurement evaluations
Permissible cost categories over the life cycle
Environmental externality costing
Procurement document disclosure obligations
Mandatory use of common Union calculation methods where applicable

who_it_applies_to.geographic_presence: Applies within EU public procurement governed by Member State implementation of Directive 2014/24/EU

what_it_does_not_cover: Specific penalty amounts for non-compliance
Detailed formulas for all life-cycle costing methods unless mandated by separate Union legislation

mandatory_obligations: Life-cycle costing shall, to the extent relevant, cover parts or all of specified costs over the life cycle of a product, service or works.
Where contracting authorities assess costs using a life-cycle costing approach, they shall indicate in the procurement documents the data to be provided by the tenderers.

Where contracting authorities assess costs using a life-cycle costing approach, they shall indicate in the procurement documents the method the contracting authority will use to determine the life-cycle costs on the basis of those data.
The method used for the assessment of costs imputed to environmental externalities shall be based on objectively verifiable and non-discriminatory criteria.
Where the environmental externality assessment method has not been established for repeated or continuous application, it shall not unduly favour or disadvantage certain economic operators.
The method used for the assessment of costs imputed to environmental externalities shall be accessible to all interested parties.

The data required by the environmental externality assessment method must be capable of being provided with reasonable effort by normally diligent economic operators, including economic operators from third countries party to the GPA or other international agreements by which the Union is bound.
Whenever a common method for the calculation of life-cycle costs has been made mandatory by a legislative act of the Union, that common method shall be applied for assessment of life-cycle costs.
prohibited_actions: Using an environmental externality costing method that is not based on objectively verifiable and non-discriminatory criteria.
Using a non-standard environmental externality costing method that unduly favours or disadvantages certain economic operators.
Failing to disclose required tenderer data and the life-cycle costing method in procurement documents when using life-cycle costing.
Failing to apply a mandatory common Union method where one has been established by legislative act.
conditional_requirements: Environmental externality costs may be included only provided their monetary value can be determined and verified.
Life-cycle costing shall cover specified cost categories only to the extent relevant.
The obligation to apply a common method arises only where a legislative act of the Union has made such method mandatory.
documentation_requirements: Procurement documents must specify the data to be provided by tenderers.
Procurement documents must specify the method the contracting authority will use to determine life-cycle costs.
Where environmental externalities are costed, the methodology must be documented in a way that demonstrates objective verifiability, non-discrimination, accessibility, and reasonable data burden.
reporting_requirements: No standalone reporting requirement is expressly stated in this extracted life-cycle costing provision.
timeline_requirements: The required data and method must be indicated in the procurement documents before tender evaluation.
Mandatory common Union methods must be applied whenever such methods have been made mandatory.

general_restrictions: Only relevant life-cycle cost elements should be covered.
Environmental externality costs are restricted to those whose monetary value can be determined and verified.
data_restrictions: Required data must be such that normally diligent economic operators can provide them with reasonable effort.
operational_restrictions: Contracting authorities are constrained to use disclosed methods when applying life-cycle costing.
Contracting authorities cannot substitute their own method where a mandatory common Union method exists.
technical_restrictions: Methodologies for environmental externality costing must be objectively verifiable.
Methodologies must be accessible to all interested parties.
geographic_restrictions: The accessibility and reasonable-effort standard extends to economic operators from third countries party to the GPA or other international agreements binding on the Union.

organizational_rights: Interested parties have the right to access the method used for assessment of costs imputed to environmental externalities.
Economic operators, including certain third-country operators, are entitled to methodologies that do not unduly favor or disadvantage competitors.
how_to_exercise_rights: Review procurement documents for disclosed data requirements and life-cycle costing methodology.
Challenge inaccessible, discriminatory, or unverifiable methodologies through procurement remedies available under applicable law.

general_exceptions: Life-cycle costing covers specified cost categories only 'to the extent relevant.'
conditional_exemptions: Environmental externality costs need not be included unless their monetary value can be determined and verified.
A common Union method applies only where made mandatory by legislative act.

technical_measures: Develop or adopt a life-cycle costing methodology capable of calculating acquisition, use, maintenance, end-of-life, and where applicable environmental externality costs.
Ensure environmental externality valuation methods are objectively verifiable and technically reproducible.
Provide accessible methodological documentation to all interested parties.
organizational_measures: Include life-cycle costing data requirements and methodology in procurement documents.
Verify whether a mandatory Union common method exists before launching the procurement.
Establish internal review to ensure methodologies are non-discriminatory and proportionate in data demands.
training_requirements: Procurement staff should be trained on permissible life-cycle cost categories and conditions for environmental externality costing.
Staff should be trained to identify when Annex XIII or other Union legislation mandates a common calculation method.
audit_requirements: Maintain an audit trail showing why included cost categories were relevant and how the methodology met the required conditions.
Retain evidence that required data could be provided with reasonable effort by normally diligent operators.

enforcement.regulatory_authority: Enforced through Member State public procurement oversight and remedies systems; the European Commission has a role regarding delegated acts updating Annex XIII.

penalties.administrative_penalties: Potential procurement law consequences such as annulment, challenge, or corrective action under national implementation, not specified in the excerpt.
penalties.reputational_consequences: Potential challenge to procurement transparency and fairness.

enforcement_mechanisms: Review of procurement documents and award methodology
Bidder challenges under procurement remedies
Administrative oversight under Member State procurement regimes

amendment_history: The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts under Article 87 to update the Annex XIII list when new legislation makes a common method mandatory or existing acts are repealed or modified.

related_articles: Article 67 (award criteria, referenced contextually in the section)
complementary_regulations: Government Procurement Agreement (GPA), as referenced for third-country operators
Other international agreements by which the Union is bound

implementation_steps: Determine whether life-cycle costing will be used in the procurement.
Identify relevant cost categories across acquisition, use, maintenance, end-of-life, and environmental externalities.
Confirm whether environmental externality costs can be monetized and verified.

regulations.regulation_name: Directive 2014/24/EU on public procurement - Award criteria linked to subject-matter and Member State discretion on sole price/cost criteria

description.brief_summary: These extracted provisions state that Member States may restrict use of price-only or cost-only as the sole award criterion, and define when award criteria are considered linked to the subject-matter of the contract, including life-cycle stages and production or trading processes even where such factors are not part of the material substance.
description.detailed_explanation: The section includes two specific procurement rules. First, Member States may provide that contracting authorities may not use price only or cost only as the sole award criterion, or may restrict such use to certain categories of contracting authorities or certain types of contracts. This is a discretionary enabling provision for Member States rather than a direct universal prohibition. Second, award criteria are deemed linked to the subject-matter of the public contract where they relate to the works, supplies, or services to be provided under the contract in any respect and at any stage of their life cycle. This includes factors involved in the specific process of production, provision, or trading of those works, supplies, or services, or a specific process for another stage of their life cycle, even where such factors do not form part of their material substance. This broadens the permissible connection between award criteria and the contract subject-matter.
description.purpose: To ensure award criteria are substantively connected to the contract and to allow Member States to limit overreliance on lowest-price or lowest-cost-only awards.
description.legislative_intent: The intent is to support quality-based procurement and clarify that process-related and life-cycle-related factors can legitimately form part of award criteria.

regulations.regulation_name: Directive 2014/24/EU on public procurement - Abnormally low tenders

description.brief_summary: These provisions require contracting authorities to assess information provided by tenderers when a tender appears abnormally low, limit rejection to cases where the evidence does not satisfactorily explain the low price or costs, mandate rejection where the abnormally low tender results from non-compliance with applicable obligations under Article 18(2), regulate rejection where State aid is involved, require Commission notification in certain State aid rejection cases, and impose Member State administrative cooperation duties.
description.detailed_explanation: The extracted text sets out a procedural and substantive framework for handling abnormally low tenders. The contracting authority must assess the information provided by consulting the tenderer. Rejection is permitted only where the evidence supplied does not satisfactorily account for the low level of price or costs proposed, taking into account the listed explanatory elements in paragraph 2. The text specifically identifies two paragraph 2 elements in the excerpt: compliance with obligations referred to in Article 71, and the possibility of the tenderer obtaining State aid. In addition, contracting authorities are under a mandatory duty to reject a tender where they have established that it is abnormally low because it does not comply with applicable obligations referred to in Article 18(2). The section further provides that where a contracting authority establishes that a tender is abnormally low because the tenderer has obtained State aid, the tender may be rejected on that ground alone only after consultation with the tenderer and only where the tenderer is unable to prove, within a sufficient time limit fixed by the contracting authority, that the aid was compatible with the internal market within the meaning of Article 107 TFEU. If the contracting authority rejects the tender in those circumstances, it must inform the Commission. Finally, upon request, Member States must make available to other Member States, by means of administrative cooperation, any information at their disposal relating to the evidence and documents produced in relation to the details listed in paragraph 2, such as laws, regulations, universally applicable collective agreements, or national technical standards.
description.purpose: To prevent unfairly low bids that result from unlawful practices or incompatible State aid while preserving procedural fairness through consultation and evidence assessment.
description.legislative_intent: The lawmakers intended to balance competition and value for money with protection against social dumping, unlawful non-compliance, and distortive State aid, while facilitating cross-border verification through administrative cooperation.

regulations.regulation_name: Contract performance requirement on abnormally low tenders

description.brief_summary: Contracting authorities must require economic operators to explain the price or costs proposed in a tender when the tender appears abnormally low in relation to the works, supplies, or services being procured.
description.detailed_explanation: The section imposes a mandatory procedural obligation on contracting authorities during procurement evaluation. Where a submitted tender appears abnormally low compared with the subject matter of the procurement, the authority is not permitted to ignore the issue; instead, it must require the economic operator to provide an explanation of the proposed price or costs. The trigger is the appearance of abnormal low pricing in relation to the relevant works, supplies, or services. The obligation is directed at the contracting authority, while the practical burden of responding falls on the economic operator. The provision establishes a review and clarification mechanism intended to scrutinize suspiciously low bids before further procurement decisions are made.
description.purpose: To ensure that unusually low tenders are examined and justified, helping protect procurement integrity and reducing the risk of unsustainable, unrealistic, or distortive pricing.
description.legislative_intent: The lawmakers intended to require active scrutiny of potentially abnormal bids so that contracting authorities assess whether low pricing is legitimate rather than automatically accepting or disregarding such tenders.

industry_sectors: Utilities where applicable under procurement frameworks

description.brief_summary: Contracting authorities are permitted to impose special conditions governing the performance of a public contract, but only where those conditions are linked to the subject-matter of the contract and are disclosed in the call for competition or procurement documents.
description.detailed_explanation: The section establishes a conditional authorization for contracting authorities to include special contract performance conditions in procurement procedures. This authority is not unrestricted. Two explicit legal conditions must be satisfied: first, the performance conditions must be linked to the subject-matter of the contract within the meaning of Article 67(3); second, those conditions must be indicated in the call for competition or in the procurement documents. The provision further clarifies the permissible subject areas of such conditions by stating that they may include economic, innovation-related, environmental, social, or employment-related considerations. The text also provides a specific example under paragraph 2(a), namely that explanations may relate to 'the economics of the manufacturing process, of the services provided or of the construction method.' This indicates that performance-related conditions or explanatory material may legitimately address process economics connected to how goods are manufactured, services are delivered, or works are constructed, provided the overarching linkage and disclosure requirements are met.

regulations.regulation_name: Directive 2014/24/EU on public procurement - Article 71 (Subcontracting)

industry_sectors: Utilities where applicable under procurement frameworks

description.brief_summary: Article 71 establishes specific rules governing subcontracting in public procurement, including oversight of subcontractor compliance with Article 18(2), disclosure of intended subcontracting, optional direct payment arrangements to subcontractors, mandatory post-award disclosure of subcontractor identity information in certain contracts, verification of exclusion grounds, and replacement of subcontractors where exclusion grounds are established.
description.detailed_explanation: The section imposes a structured compliance framework for subcontracting in public contracts. Competent national authorities must ensure, through appropriate action within their remit, that subcontractors observe the obligations referred to in Article 18(2). Contracting authorities may, or where required by Member States must, request tenderers to identify in their tenders the share of the contract intended for subcontracting and the proposed subcontractors. Member States may establish direct payment mechanisms allowing subcontractors, upon request and where the contract nature permits, to receive payments directly from the contracting authority for work, services, or supplies provided to the main contractor; such mechanisms may include safeguards allowing the main contractor to object to undue payments, and the payment arrangements must be stated in procurement documents. The article expressly preserves the main contractor’s liability notwithstanding these measures. For works contracts and certain services performed at a facility under the direct oversight of the contracting authority, the authority must require the main contractor, after award and no later than commencement of performance, to provide the names, contact details, and legal representatives of subcontractors involved, insofar as known, and to notify any changes and any new subcontractors during contract execution. Where national law provides for joint liability between subcontractors and the main contractor, Member States must ensure those rules comply with Article 18(2). Contracting authorities may, or where required by Member States must, verify whether subcontractors are subject to exclusion grounds under Article 57, in accordance with Articles 59, 60, and 61. If compulsory exclusion grounds are found, the economic operator must replace the subcontractor; if non-compulsory grounds are found, replacement may be required. Member States may adopt stricter liability rules and broader direct payment rules, including direct payment without subcontractor request. Member States implementing measures under paragraphs 3, 5, or 6 must specify implementing conditions by law, regulation, or administrative provisions, while respecting Union law, and may limit applicability by contract type, authority category, operator category, or contract amount.
description.purpose: To increase transparency, accountability, and legal compliance in subcontracting chains within public procurement, while enabling Member States to strengthen protections for subcontractors and ensure compliance with labor, social, and environmental obligations referenced in Article 18(2).
description.legislative_intent: The lawmakers intended to prevent abuse and opacity in subcontracting arrangements, ensure subcontractors are subject to compliance and exclusion screening, protect subcontractors through possible direct payment mechanisms, and preserve the responsibility of the main contractor for contract performance.

what_it_covers: Subcontracting in public procurement contracts
Disclosure of intended subcontracting in tenders
Post-award identification of subcontractors

entity_types: Private companies participating in public tenders
who_it_applies_to.geographic_presence: Applies within EU Member States to procurement governed by Directive 2014/24/EU and national implementing measures.

what_it_does_not_cover: The section does not define Article 18(2) obligations themselves; it only requires observance of them by subcontractors.
The section does not remove or reduce the main contractor’s liability.
Direct payment to subcontractors is not universally mandatory; it depends on Member State provision, subcontractor request, and contract nature unless national law goes further.
Mandatory post-award subcontractor disclosure is limited to works contracts and services provided at a facility under the direct oversight of the contracting authority.

mandatory_obligations: Competent national authorities must ensure, through appropriate action within the scope of their responsibility and remit, observance by subcontractors of the obligations referred to in Article 18(2).

Where the contracting authority requires subcontractor information under paragraph 5, the main contractor must indicate to the contracting authority the name, contact details, and legal representatives of subcontractors involved in the relevant works or services, insofar as known at that time.

In the case of works contracts and services to be provided at a facility under the direct oversight of the contracting authority, the contracting authority shall require the main contractor to provide the required subcontractor information after award and at the latest when contract performance commences.
The main contractor must notify the contracting authority of any changes to subcontractor information during the course of the contract.
The main contractor must notify the contracting authority of the required information for any new subcontractors subsequently involved in the relevant works or services.
Where verification shows compulsory grounds for exclusion of a subcontractor pursuant to Article 57, the contracting authority shall require the economic operator to replace that subcontractor.

Where a Member State provides for a mechanism of joint liability between subcontractors and the main contractor, that Member State shall ensure the relevant rules are applied in compliance with the conditions set out in Article 18(2).

Where Member States choose to provide for measures pursuant to paragraphs 3, 5, or 6, they must specify the implementing conditions by law, regulation, or administrative provisions, having regard for Union law.
Arrangements concerning direct payment to subcontractors must be set out in the procurement documents where such payment mode is provided.
prohibited_actions: Contracting authorities and Member States must not implement joint liability mechanisms in a manner inconsistent with the conditions set out in Article 18(2).

Where compulsory exclusion grounds are established for a subcontractor, the economic operator may not retain that subcontractor if replacement is required by the contracting authority under the article.
conditional_requirements: In the procurement documents, the contracting authority may ask, or may be required by a Member State to ask, the tenderer to indicate in its tender any share of the contract it may intend to subcontract to third parties and any proposed subcontractors.

Member States may provide that, at the request of the subcontractor and where the nature of the contract so allows, the contracting authority shall transfer due payments directly to the subcontractor for services, supplies, or works provided to the main contractor.
Direct payment measures may include appropriate mechanisms permitting the main contractor to object to undue payments.

Contracting authorities may, in accordance with Articles 59, 60 and 61, verify, or may be required by Member States to verify, whether there are grounds for exclusion of subcontractors pursuant to Article 57.

Where verification shows non-compulsory grounds for exclusion, the contracting authority may require, or may be required by a Member State to require, the economic operator to replace the subcontractor.
Member States may impose the obligation to deliver the required information directly on the main contractor, notwithstanding the first subparagraph referenced in the text.
Where necessary for the purposes of point (b) of paragraph 6, the required information shall be accompanied by the subcontractors’ self-declarations as provided for in Article 59.

Implementing measures pursuant to paragraph 8 may provide that subcontractors presented after the award of the contract shall provide certificates and other supporting documents instead of the self-declaration.
Member States may provide for more stringent liability rules under national law.
Member States may go further under national law on direct payments to subcontractors, including by providing for direct payments without requiring the subcontractor to request such payment.

Member States may limit the applicability of measures adopted under paragraphs 3, 5, or 6, for instance by contract type, category of contracting authority, category of economic operator, or contract amount.
documentation_requirements: Tender submissions may be required to include the share of the contract intended to be subcontracted.
Tender submissions may be required to identify proposed subcontractors.
Procurement documents must set out the arrangements concerning direct payment to subcontractors where that payment mode is used.
The main contractor must provide the names of subcontractors involved in covered works or services.
The main contractor must provide contact details of subcontractors involved in covered works or services.
The main contractor must provide the legal representatives of subcontractors involved in covered works or services.
Updates to subcontractor information during contract performance must be notified.
Information relating to newly involved subcontractors must be provided.
Where necessary for exclusion verification under paragraph 6(b), required information must be accompanied by subcontractors’ self-declarations under Article 59.
Under implementing measures, subcontractors presented after award may be required to provide certificates and other supporting documents instead of self-declarations.
