The main contractor must notify the contracting authority of required information for any new subcontractors subsequently involved in the relevant works or services.
timeline_requirements: For works contracts and covered services, subcontractor identity information must be provided after the award of the contract and at the latest when performance of the contract commences.
Changes to subcontractor information must be notified during the course of the contract.
Information on new subcontractors must be provided when they are subsequently involved in the works or services.
Direct payment arrangements, where applicable, must be established in the procurement documents before contract execution.

general_restrictions: Direct payment to subcontractors is subject to Member State provision and the nature of the contract allowing such payment.
Mandatory subcontractor disclosure under paragraph 5 is restricted to works contracts and services provided at a facility under the direct oversight of the contracting authority.
Verification and replacement obligations are tied to exclusion grounds under Article 57 and procedures under Articles 59, 60, and 61.
data_restrictions: Only specified subcontractor information is expressly required: name, contact details, and legal representatives, insofar as known at the relevant time.
operational_restrictions: Economic operators may be required to replace subcontractors where exclusion grounds are established.
Main contractors remain liable notwithstanding direct payment or other subcontracting measures.
technical_restrictions: No specific technical system requirements are stated in this section.
geographic_restrictions: Implementation conditions must be specified by Member States and may be limited nationally by contract type, authority category, operator category, or amount.

organizational_rights: Contracting authorities may request tenderers to indicate intended subcontracted shares and proposed subcontractors.
Contracting authorities may verify subcontractors for exclusion grounds, or may be required by Member States to do so.
Contracting authorities may require replacement of subcontractors where non-compulsory exclusion grounds are established, if permitted or required by Member State law.
Main contractors may be given mechanisms to object to undue direct payments to subcontractors.

Subcontractors may, where Member State law provides and the nature of the contract allows, request direct payment from the contracting authority for services, supplies, or works provided to the main contractor.
how_to_exercise_rights: A subcontractor exercises the possible right to direct payment by making a request, where national law provides such a mechanism and the contract nature allows it.
A main contractor exercises objection rights through the payment objection mechanisms established in the direct payment arrangements.
A contracting authority exercises verification rights in accordance with Articles 59, 60, and 61 when assessing exclusion grounds under Article 57.

general_exceptions: Post-award mandatory subcontractor disclosure under paragraph 5 applies only 'in the case of works contracts and in respect of services to be provided at a facility under the direct oversight of the contracting authority.'
Required subcontractor information under paragraph 5 is limited to subcontractors 'in so far as known at this point in time.'
conditional_exemptions: Direct payment to subcontractors applies only where Member States provide for it, the subcontractor requests it, and the nature of the contract so allows, unless national law provides broader direct payment rights.
Member States may limit the applicability of measures under paragraphs 3, 5, or 6 to certain contract types, categories of contracting authorities or economic operators, or certain amounts.
public_interest_exceptions: Competent national authorities act within the scope of their responsibility and remit when ensuring subcontractor observance of Article 18(2) obligations.
size_based_exceptions: Member States may limit applicability of implementing measures by reference to certain amounts.

technical_measures: Implement mechanisms in procurement administration to collect subcontractor identity and contact information.
Implement processes to track subcontractor changes during contract performance.
Implement verification workflows for exclusion checks under Articles 57, 59, 60, and 61 where applicable.
If direct payment is adopted, implement payment control mechanisms and objection procedures for undue payments.
organizational_measures: Establish procurement document templates that include subcontracting disclosure requirements where used.
Establish procedures requiring main contractors to submit subcontractor details after award and before commencement where paragraph 5 applies.
Maintain procedures for ongoing notification of subcontractor changes and additions.
Adopt internal controls to ensure replacement of subcontractors subject to compulsory exclusion grounds.
Where national law provides, establish and apply joint liability rules in compliance with Article 18(2).
Member States adopting measures under paragraphs 3, 5, or 6 must enact implementing conditions through law, regulation, or administrative provisions.
training_requirements: Procurement and contract management personnel should be trained on when subcontractor disclosure is mandatory, when exclusion verification is required or permitted, and how direct payment mechanisms operate under national law.
audit_requirements: Authorities should be able to evidence that subcontractor information was requested and updated where required.
Authorities should be able to evidence exclusion verification decisions and replacement actions where applicable.
Authorities should be able to evidence that direct payment arrangements were set out in procurement documents where such mechanisms are used.

enforcement.regulatory_authority: Contracting authorities, competent national authorities, and Member State authorities responsible for implementing and enforcing public procurement law

penalties.administrative_penalties: Not specified in this section; enforcement occurs through procurement controls such as mandatory replacement of subcontractors, compliance oversight, and national implementing measures.

enforcement_mechanisms: Appropriate action by competent national authorities to ensure subcontractor observance of Article 18(2) obligations.
Contracting authority requests for subcontracting information in tenders.
Mandatory post-award disclosure and ongoing notification obligations for subcontractor information in covered contracts.
Verification of subcontractor exclusion grounds under Article 57 in accordance with Articles 59, 60, and 61.
Mandatory replacement of subcontractors where compulsory exclusion grounds are established.
Possible required replacement where non-compulsory exclusion grounds are established.
National laws, regulations, or administrative provisions specifying implementing conditions.

implementation_steps: Determine whether national law requires or permits requesting subcontracting details in tenders.
Include in procurement documents any requirement for tenderers to disclose intended subcontracted shares and proposed subcontractors.
If national law provides for direct payment, include detailed payment arrangements and objection mechanisms in procurement documents.

For works contracts and covered services, require the main contractor after award and no later than contract commencement to submit subcontractor names, contact details, and legal representatives, insofar as known.
Set up a process for the main contractor to notify changes to subcontractor information and additions of new subcontractors throughout contract performance.
Assess whether subcontractor self-declarations under Article 59 or supporting certificates are required for exclusion verification.
Verify subcontractors against Article 57 exclusion grounds where permitted or required.
Require replacement immediately where compulsory exclusion grounds are found; assess whether replacement should be required for non-compulsory grounds under national rules.
Ensure internal records preserve evidence that the main contractor’s liability remains unaffected by subcontracting measures.
Where Member State measures exist under paragraphs 3, 5, or 6, apply national implementing conditions and any scope limitations.
common_violations: Failing to request or collect subcontractor information where mandatory under paragraph 5 or national law.
Omitting direct payment arrangements from procurement documents when such a payment mode is used.
Failing to update subcontractor records when changes occur during contract performance.
Allowing a subcontractor subject to compulsory exclusion grounds to remain on the contract.
Not obtaining required self-declarations or supporting documents for subcontractor verification.
Assuming direct payment removes the main contractor’s liability.
Applying joint liability rules without ensuring compliance with Article 18(2).
best_practices: Use standardized subcontractor disclosure forms in tender and post-award phases.
Maintain a live subcontractor register for each covered contract.
Include contractual clauses obligating prompt notification of subcontractor changes.
Create a documented exclusion-screening process for subcontractors.
Define clear escalation procedures for replacement of excluded subcontractors.
Document all national-law conditions affecting direct payment, liability, and verification obligations.
compliance_checklist: Has the authority determined whether tenderers must disclose intended subcontracted shares and proposed subcontractors?
Do procurement documents specify direct payment arrangements where applicable?
For works contracts and covered services, has the main contractor provided subcontractor names, contact details, and legal representatives after award and by contract commencement at the latest?
Is there a process for notifying and recording subcontractor changes and new subcontractors during contract performance?
Have subcontractor self-declarations or supporting documents been collected where necessary?
Have subcontractors been checked for exclusion grounds under Article 57 where required or permitted?
Has any subcontractor subject to compulsory exclusion grounds been replaced?
Where non-compulsory exclusion grounds exist, has the authority assessed whether replacement is required under national law?
Are national implementing conditions under paragraphs 3, 5, or 6 identified and applied?
Is it documented that the main contractor’s liability remains unaffected?

key_definitions.subcontractor: A third party engaged by the economic operator or main contractor to perform part of the public contract.
key_definitions.main contractor: The economic operator to whom the public contract has been awarded.
key_definitions.contracting authority: The public authority or body conducting the procurement and managing the contract.
key_definitions.economic operator: The tenderer or contractor participating in the procurement procedure or awarded the contract.
key_definitions.direct payment: A payment mechanism under which the contracting authority transfers due payments directly to the subcontractor for services, supplies, or works provided to the main contractor.
key_definitions.compulsory grounds for exclusion: Grounds under Article 57 that require exclusion and trigger mandatory replacement of the subcontractor when established through verification.
key_definitions.non-compulsory grounds for exclusion: Grounds under Article 57 that may justify exclusion and may lead to replacement of the subcontractor where required or permitted.
key_definitions.joint liability: A national-law mechanism under which subcontractors and the main contractor may share liability, subject to compliance with Article 18(2).
key_definitions.required information: Subcontractor name, contact details, legal representatives, and where necessary self-declarations or supporting documents for exclusion verification.

regulations.regulation_name: Directive 2014/24/EU on public procurement - Article 72: Modification of contracts during their term

industry_sectors: Utilities where applicable under procurement frameworks

description.brief_summary: Article 72 sets out the circumstances in which contracting authorities may modify public contracts and framework agreements during their term without conducting a new procurement procedure. It also defines when a modification is considered substantial and therefore impermissible without re-tendering, unless a specific exception applies.
description.detailed_explanation: The provision establishes a closed set of lawful modification routes. A contract or framework agreement may be modified without a new procurement procedure where: the modification was clearly provided for in the original procurement documents through review clauses or options; additional works, services, or supplies by the original contractor become necessary and changing contractor is not feasible for economic or technical reasons and would cause significant inconvenience or substantial duplication of costs; the need for modification arises from unforeseeable circumstances that a diligent contracting authority could not foresee; a new contractor replaces the original contractor in narrowly defined circumstances such as a valid review clause, corporate succession, or where the contracting authority assumes obligations toward subcontractors under national law; or the modification is not substantial. Separately, low-value modifications are permitted if they remain below both the applicable Article 4 thresholds and percentage caps tied to the initial contract value. The article also prescribes how to calculate price where indexation clauses exist, requires publication of a notice in the Official Journal of the European Union for certain modifications, and defines substantial modifications by reference to changes that materially alter the contract's character, competitive conditions, economic balance, scope, or contractor identity.
description.purpose: To balance flexibility in contract performance with transparency, equal treatment, and competition in public procurement by preventing authorities from materially changing awarded contracts in ways that circumvent procurement rules.
description.legislative_intent: The lawmakers intended to prevent abuse of post-award contract changes while allowing practical adjustments where they were foreseen, objectively necessary, low in value, or otherwise non-substantial. The article seeks to preserve the integrity of the original competition and avoid hidden renegotiations that would have affected bidder participation or outcomes.

what_it_covers: Modification of public contracts during their term
Modification of framework agreements during their term
Review clauses and options in procurement documents
Additional works, services, or supplies by the original contractor
Modifications due to unforeseeable circumstances
Replacement of the original contractor
Low-value modifications
Assessment of whether a modification is substantial
Publication of modification notices

target_entities: Economic operators involved in public procurement
entity_types: Economic operators contracting with public authorities
who_it_applies_to.size_thresholds: Applies subject to procurement thresholds referenced in Article 4 for low-value modification calculations; no entity-size threshold stated in this section.
who_it_applies_to.geographic_presence: Applies within EU Member States to procurements governed by Directive 2014/24/EU.

what_it_does_not_cover: Modifications outside the cases listed in paragraphs 1 and 2, which require a new procurement procedure
Supplier obligations under the first subparagraph where the text states: 'The first subparagraph shall not apply to suppliers.'

mandatory_obligations: Contracting authorities may modify contracts or framework agreements without a new procurement procedure only in the cases expressly permitted by Article 72.
Where modifications are based on review clauses or options, those clauses must be included in the initial procurement documents and must be 'clear, precise and unequivocal'.
Review clauses or options must state the scope and nature of possible modifications or options and the conditions under which they may be used.
Review clauses or options must not provide for modifications or options that would alter the overall nature of the contract or framework agreement.

For additional works, services, or supplies by the original contractor, the change of contractor must be impossible for economic or technical reasons such as interchangeability or interoperability requirements, and changing contractor must cause significant inconvenience or substantial duplication of costs for the contracting authority.
For additional works, services, or supplies under paragraph 1(b), any increase in price must not exceed 50% of the value of the original contract.

For modifications due to unforeseeable circumstances under paragraph 1(c), the need for modification must have been brought about by circumstances which a diligent contracting authority could not foresee.
For modifications due to unforeseeable circumstances under paragraph 1(c), the modification must not alter the overall nature of the contract.
For modifications due to unforeseeable circumstances under paragraph 1(c), any increase in price must not exceed 50% of the value of the original contract or framework agreement.
Where several successive modifications are made under the 50% cap rules, the limitation applies to the value of each modification.
For low-value modifications under paragraph 2, the value of the modification must be below both the Article 4 thresholds and the applicable percentage threshold of the initial contract value.
For low-value modifications, the modification must not alter the overall nature of the contract or framework agreement.
Where several successive low-value modifications are made, the value must be assessed on the basis of the net cumulative value of the successive modifications.
For price calculations under paragraph 2 and points (b) and (c) of paragraph 1, the updated price must be used as the reference value when the contract includes an indexation clause.
Where a new contractor replaces the original contractor under paragraph 1(d)(ii), the successor economic operator must fulfil the criteria for qualitative selection initially established.
Replacement of the contractor under paragraph 1(d)(ii) must not entail other substantial modifications to the contract.
Replacement of the contractor under paragraph 1(d)(ii) must not be aimed at circumventing the application of the Directive.
Contracting authorities that modify a contract under paragraph 1(b) or 1(c) must publish a notice to that effect in the Official Journal of the European Union.
The notice for modifications under paragraph 1(b) and 1(c) must contain the information set out in Annex V part G.
The notice for modifications under paragraph 1(b) and 1(c) must be published in accordance with Article 51.
A new procurement procedure in accordance with the Directive is required for modifications other than those permitted under paragraphs 1 and 2.
prohibited_actions: Contracting authorities must not rely on review clauses or options that alter the overall nature of the contract or framework agreement.
Contracting authorities must not exceed a 50% price increase for a modification under paragraph 1(b).
Contracting authorities must not exceed a 50% price increase for a modification under paragraph 1(c).
Successive modifications must not be aimed at circumventing the Directive.

Contracting authorities must not treat as permissible a modification that alters the overall nature of the contract or framework agreement where the relevant exception requires preservation of overall nature.

A new contractor must not replace the original contractor in cases other than those expressly permitted under paragraph 1(d) without triggering a substantial modification analysis and, if substantial, a new procurement procedure.
Contracting authorities must not make other modifications during the term of a public contract or framework agreement without a new procurement procedure unless they fall within paragraphs 1 or 2.
conditional_requirements: If a modification is based on an initial review clause or option, the clause must be clear, precise, unequivocal, and define scope, nature, and conditions of use.

If additional works, services, or supplies become necessary and were not included in the initial procurement, the original contractor may perform them only if changing contractor is not possible for economic or technical reasons and would cause significant inconvenience or substantial duplication of costs.
If the need for modification arises from unforeseeable circumstances, the contracting authority must be able to show that a diligent contracting authority could not have foreseen those circumstances.
If a contract includes an indexation clause, the updated price becomes the reference value for calculating the thresholds in paragraph 2 and points (b) and (c) of paragraph 1.
If several successive modifications are made under paragraph 2, their net cumulative value must be used to assess compliance with the low-value thresholds.

If several successive modifications are made under paragraph 1(b) or 1(c), the 50% limitation applies to each modification individually, but the modifications must not be used to circumvent the Directive.

If a new contractor replaces the original contractor due to corporate restructuring, takeover, merger, acquisition, or insolvency, the successor must satisfy the original qualitative selection criteria and the replacement must not involve other substantial modifications or circumvention.

If national legislation pursuant to Article 71 provides for it, the contracting authority may assume the main contractor's obligations toward its subcontractors, and this may justify contractor replacement under paragraph 1(d)(iii).
If a modification is not substantial within the meaning of paragraph 4, it may be made without a new procurement procedure irrespective of value.
documentation_requirements: Initial procurement documents must contain any review clauses or options relied upon for later modification.
Review clauses or options must document the scope and nature of possible modifications or options and the conditions for their use.
For modifications under paragraph 1(b) and 1(c), a notice must be prepared containing the information set out in Annex V part G.
Where indexation applies, documentation should support the updated reference price used for threshold calculations.
Where contractor replacement occurs under paragraph 1(d)(ii), documentation should evidence corporate succession and compliance with the original qualitative selection criteria.
Where unforeseeable circumstances are invoked, documentation should support why a diligent contracting authority could not have foreseen them.

Where additional works, services, or supplies are invoked, documentation should support the economic or technical reasons preventing contractor change and the significant inconvenience or substantial duplication of costs that would result.
reporting_requirements: Publication of a modification notice in the Official Journal of the European Union is required for modifications under paragraph 1(b) and paragraph 1(c).
The published notice must contain the information specified in Annex V part G.
Publication must be carried out in accordance with Article 51.
timeline_requirements: The rules apply to modifications 'during [the contract's] term'.
No specific publication deadline is stated in the provided text, but publication is mandatory when modifications are made under paragraph 1(b) and 1(c).
Compliance with the requirement for a new procurement procedure arises before implementing any modification not covered by paragraphs 1 or 2.

general_restrictions: Permissible modifications without a new procurement procedure are limited to the cases expressly listed in Article 72.
Any permitted modification must comply with the specific conditions attached to the relevant legal basis.
Low-value modifications are restricted by dual thresholds: Article 4 thresholds and percentage caps tied to initial contract value.
Certain modifications are restricted by a 50% cap on price increase.
Modifications must not be used to circumvent the Directive through successive changes.
operational_restrictions: Contracting authorities cannot freely renegotiate awarded contracts in ways that materially change their character.
Changing contractor is restricted and only allowed in narrowly defined circumstances.
The scope of the contract cannot be considerably extended without the modification being treated as substantial.
The economic balance of the contract cannot be shifted in favor of the contractor unless such change was provided for in the initial contract or framework agreement.
technical_restrictions: Economic or technical reasons justifying retention of the original contractor may include requirements of interchangeability or interoperability with existing equipment, services, or installations procured under the initial procurement.
geographic_restrictions: Publication of certain modification notices must occur in the Official Journal of the European Union.

organizational_rights: Contracting authorities are permitted to modify contracts without a new procurement procedure where one of the Article 72 grounds is satisfied.
Contracting authorities may rely on clear review clauses, low-value thresholds, unforeseeable circumstances, additional necessary works/services/supplies, or certain contractor replacement scenarios.

Member States may require contracting authorities to extend certain obligations referenced in the first subparagraph to additional categories such as supply contracts, certain service contracts, suppliers involved in works or services contracts, and subcontractors further down the chain.
how_to_exercise_rights: A contracting authority exercises the right to modify without re-tendering by ensuring the modification falls within one of the permitted categories and by satisfying all associated conditions, thresholds, and publication obligations.

A contracting authority exercises the right to replace a contractor only through a valid review clause, qualifying corporate succession, or assumption of obligations toward subcontractors where national legislation permits.

general_exceptions: A new procurement procedure is not required where the modification falls within paragraph 1 or paragraph 2.
The first subparagraph does not apply to suppliers.
conditional_exemptions: Modifications provided for in the initial procurement documents through clear, precise, and unequivocal review clauses or options are exempt from the need for a new procurement procedure.

Additional works, services, or supplies by the original contractor are exempt where they become necessary, were not included initially, and changing contractor is not feasible for economic or technical reasons and would cause significant inconvenience or substantial duplication of costs, subject to the 50% cap.

Modifications necessitated by unforeseeable circumstances are exempt where a diligent contracting authority could not have foreseen them, the overall nature is unchanged, and the 50% cap is respected.

Replacement of the original contractor is exempt where it results from an unequivocal review clause or option, qualifying universal or partial succession, or assumption by the contracting authority of the main contractor's obligations toward subcontractors under national legislation pursuant to Article 71.
Modifications that are not substantial within the meaning of paragraph 4 are exempt irrespective of value.
Low-value modifications are exempt where they remain below both the Article 4 thresholds and the applicable percentage threshold and do not alter the overall nature of the contract.
public_interest_exceptions: Member States may require contracting authorities to extend certain obligations to additional categories mentioned in the text.
size_based_exceptions: Low-value modifications are permitted below the specified monetary and percentage thresholds.

technical_measures: Maintain systems or calculations capable of determining whether a modification remains below Article 4 thresholds and the applicable percentage thresholds.
Where indexation clauses exist, implement a method for calculating the updated reference price for threshold assessment.
Track cumulative and successive modifications to assess compliance with net cumulative value and anti-circumvention rules.
organizational_measures: Include compliant review clauses and options in initial procurement documents where future flexibility may be needed.
Establish internal procedures for legal review of proposed contract modifications against Article 72 grounds.
Document justification for economic or technical reasons preventing contractor change.
Document unforeseeable circumstances and diligence analysis before relying on paragraph 1(c).
Verify and record whether a replacement contractor satisfies the original qualitative selection criteria.
Implement publication workflows for notices required under paragraph 1(b) and 1(c).
training_requirements: Procurement and contract management staff should be trained to identify substantial versus non-substantial modifications.
Staff should be trained on threshold calculations, anti-circumvention principles, and publication obligations.
audit_requirements: Authorities should audit contract modifications to ensure they fall within paragraphs 1 or 2 and are not used to circumvent procurement rules.
Authorities should review successive modifications for cumulative impact and compliance with applicable caps and overall-nature restrictions.

enforcement.regulatory_authority: Enforcement authority not specified in the provided text; generally implemented and enforced by Member State procurement oversight bodies, review bodies, courts, and relevant public procurement authorities.

penalties.administrative_penalties: Not specified in the provided text. The section states that a new procurement procedure is required for non-qualifying modifications, implying legal invalidity or procurement challenge risk if not followed.
penalties.reputational_consequences: Publication in the Official Journal of the European Union may expose modifications to public and competitor scrutiny.

enforcement_mechanisms: Mandatory publication of notices for certain modifications in the Official Journal of the European Union
Requirement to conduct a new procurement procedure for non-qualifying modifications
Assessment of whether a modification is substantial under paragraph 4
Potential review through procurement challenge mechanisms under Member State law

dates.compliance_deadline: Applies at the time any contract or framework agreement is modified during its term.
amendment_history: Official Journal citation in provided text: 28.3.2014

implementation_steps: Review the proposed modification and classify it under one of the permitted grounds in paragraph 1 or paragraph 2.
Check whether the initial procurement documents contain a compliant review clause or option covering the modification.
If relying on additional works/services/supplies, document why the need arose, why the original contractor must be retained, and confirm the 50% cap is not exceeded.
If relying on unforeseeable circumstances, document the unforeseeable event, diligence analysis, unchanged overall nature, and compliance with the 50% cap.

If relying on low-value modification, verify that the modification is below both the Article 4 threshold and the applicable percentage threshold, and assess cumulative value where successive modifications exist.
If the contract includes indexation, calculate the updated reference price before applying thresholds.
If replacing the contractor, confirm the replacement falls within one of the permitted scenarios and that the successor meets the original qualitative selection criteria where required.
Assess whether the modification is substantial under paragraph 4 even if another ground is being considered.
Publish a notice in the Official Journal of the European Union for modifications under paragraph 1(b) and 1(c), including Annex V part G information and following Article 51.
If no permitted ground applies, initiate a new procurement procedure before implementing the change.
common_violations: Using vague or overly broad review clauses that do not clearly define scope, nature, and conditions of modifications
Treating a materially different contract as a permissible modification
Exceeding the 50% cap for additional works/services/supplies or unforeseeable circumstances
Failing to assess cumulative value of successive low-value modifications
Structuring consecutive modifications to avoid procurement rules
Replacing the contractor outside the permitted scenarios
Failing to publish the required notice for paragraph 1(b) or 1(c) modifications
Changing the economic balance in favor of the contractor without prior provision in the initial contract
best_practices: Draft precise review clauses at procurement stage to preserve lawful flexibility.
Maintain a modification register tracking legal basis, value, cumulative impact, and publication status.
Perform a written substantial-modification assessment for every proposed change.
Use legal review before approving contractor replacement or major scope changes.
Retain evidence supporting unforeseeability, technical necessity, and cost/inconvenience justifications.
compliance_checklist: Is the modification during the term of a public contract or framework agreement?
Does the modification fall under paragraph 1(a), 1(b), 1(c), 1(d), 1(e), or paragraph 2?
If relying on a review clause, is it clear, precise, unequivocal, and included in the initial procurement documents?
Does the modification alter the overall nature of the contract or framework agreement?
If relying on paragraph 1(b), are economic or technical reasons documented and is contractor change impracticable?
If relying on paragraph 1(b) or 1(c), is the price increase within the 50% cap for each modification?
If relying on paragraph 2, is the value below both Article 4 thresholds and the applicable 10% or 15% threshold?
Have successive modifications been assessed cumulatively where required?
If indexation applies, was the updated price used as the reference value?
If replacing the contractor, does the scenario fit paragraph 1(d) and, where applicable, does the successor meet original qualitative selection criteria?
Has a substantial-modification analysis been completed under paragraph 4?
If modification is under paragraph 1(b) or 1(c), has the OJEU notice been prepared and published with Annex V part G information in accordance with Article 51?
If none of the permitted grounds apply, has a new procurement procedure been initiated?

key_definitions.review clauses: Clauses provided in the initial procurement documents in clear, precise and unequivocal terms that may include price revision clauses or options and that state the scope, nature, and conditions of possible modifications.
key_definitions.overall nature of the contract: The essential character of the contract or framework agreement, which must not be altered under certain permitted modification grounds.
key_definitions.substantial modification: A modification that renders the contract or framework agreement materially different in character from the one initially concluded, including where one or more paragraph 4 conditions are met.
key_definitions.materially different in character: A change significant enough to alter the contract or framework agreement from what was originally concluded.
key_definitions.additional works, services or supplies: Works, services, or supplies by the original contractor that become necessary and were not included in the initial procurement.
key_definitions.economic or technical reasons: Reasons such as requirements of interchangeability or interoperability with existing equipment, services or installations procured under the initial procurement that prevent changing contractor.
key_definitions.unforeseeable circumstances: Circumstances that a diligent contracting authority could not foresee and that create the need for modification.
key_definitions.updated price: The reference value used for threshold calculations where the contract includes an indexation clause.
key_definitions.net cumulative value: The aggregate value basis used to assess several successive modifications under paragraph 2.
key_definitions.universal or partial succession: Replacement of the initial contractor following corporate restructuring, including takeover, merger, acquisition or insolvency, by another economic operator meeting the original qualitative selection criteria.
key_definitions.substantial duplication of costs: A level of duplicated expenditure for the contracting authority that helps justify retaining the original contractor for additional works, services, or supplies.

regulations.regulation_name: Directive 2014/24/EU on public procurement - Article 73 (Termination of contracts)

industry_sectors: Utilities and suppliers participating in public tenders

description.brief_summary: Article 73 requires Member States to ensure that contracting authorities have the possibility, under national-law conditions, to terminate a public contract during its term in specified circumstances linked to unlawful modification, contractor exclusion grounds existing at award stage, or serious infringement of EU law and the Directive as declared by the Court of Justice of the European Union.
description.detailed_explanation: The provision imposes a legislative obligation on Member States to create a legal framework under which contracting authorities may terminate public contracts while they are still in force. The minimum mandatory circumstances are expressly listed. First, termination must be possible where the contract has undergone a substantial modification that would have required a new procurement procedure under Article 72. Second, termination must be possible where the contractor, at the time of award, was in one of the exclusion situations referred to in Article 57(1) and therefore should have been excluded from the procurement procedure. Third, termination must be possible where the contract should not have been awarded because of a serious infringement of obligations under the Treaties and the Directive, where that infringement has been declared by the Court of Justice of the European Union in proceedings under Article 258 TFEU. The section also includes a specific exception stating that the first subparagraph does not apply where a negotiated procedure without prior publication could have been used in conformity with Article 32 for the award of a public service contract.
description.purpose: To preserve the integrity of public procurement procedures and ensure that contracts tainted by unlawful modification, ineligible contractors, or serious EU-law infringements can be brought to an end.
description.legislative_intent: The lawmakers intended to prevent contracting authorities and contractors from maintaining contracts that undermine procurement transparency, equal treatment, competition, and compliance with EU procurement law.

what_it_covers: Termination of public contracts during their term
Substantial contract modifications
Award-stage exclusion issues concerning contractors
Contracts awarded in breach of EU Treaties and procurement rules
National-law conditions governing termination powers

who_it_applies_to.geographic_presence: Applies within EU Member States to public procurement governed by the Directive

what_it_does_not_cover: Detailed national procedural rules for exercising termination rights, which are left to applicable national law

mandatory_obligations: Member States shall ensure that contracting authorities have the possibility, at least under the listed circumstances and under the conditions determined by applicable national law, to terminate a public contract during its term.
Termination possibility must exist where 'the contract has been subject to a substantial modification, which would have required a new procurement procedure pursuant to Article 72'.

Termination possibility must exist where 'the contractor has, at the time of contract award, been in one of the situations referred to in Article 57(1) and should therefore have been excluded from the procurement procedure'.

Termination possibility must exist where 'the contract should not have been awarded to the contractor in view of a serious infringement of the obligations under the Treaties and this Directive that has been declared by the Court of Justice of the European Union in a procedure pursuant to Article 258 TFEU'.
prohibited_actions: Maintaining a public contract without a legally available termination mechanism in the minimum circumstances listed by the Article.
Allowing a contract affected by a substantial modification requiring a new procurement procedure to continue without the possibility of termination, subject to the stated exception.
Allowing a contract awarded to a contractor who should have been excluded under Article 57(1) to continue without the possibility of termination.
Allowing a contract that should not have been awarded due to a serious infringement declared by the Court of Justice of the European Union to continue without the possibility of termination.
conditional_requirements: The termination possibility applies 'under the conditions determined by the applicable national law'.
The first subparagraph shall not apply where 'a negotiated procedure without prior publication could have been used in conformity with Article 32 for the award of a public service contract'.
documentation_requirements: Evidence and legal assessment showing whether a contract modification is substantial and would have required a new procurement procedure under Article 72.
Records demonstrating whether the contractor was in an Article 57(1) exclusion situation at the time of award.
Documentation of any Court of Justice of the European Union declaration under Article 258 TFEU relevant to the award.
National-law documentation required to exercise termination rights.
reporting_requirements: No standalone reporting duty is expressly stated in Article 73 itself for termination decisions.
timeline_requirements: Termination must be possible 'during its term' for the listed circumstances.

general_restrictions: Termination rights are subject to 'the conditions determined by the applicable national law'.
The listed circumstances are minimum mandatory grounds ('at least under the following circumstances').
operational_restrictions: Contracting authorities must operate within national-law conditions when terminating contracts.
The exception limits application of the first subparagraph where Article 32 would have permitted a negotiated procedure without prior publication for a public service contract.
geographic_restrictions: Applies within EU Member States implementing the Directive.

organizational_rights: Contracting authorities must be given the legal possibility to terminate a public contract during its term in the listed circumstances.
how_to_exercise_rights: Exercise of the termination possibility must occur under the conditions determined by applicable national law.

general_exceptions: The first subparagraph does not apply where a negotiated procedure without prior publication could have been used in conformity with Article 32 for the award of a public service contract.
conditional_exemptions: Exemption from the first subparagraph is conditional on Article 32 conformity and the contract being a public service contract.

organizational_measures: Member States should implement national legal mechanisms enabling termination in the listed circumstances.
Contracting authorities should establish procedures to review contract modifications for Article 72 significance.
Contracting authorities should verify and retain evidence of contractor eligibility at award stage.
Contracting authorities should monitor relevant CJEU judgments under Article 258 TFEU affecting awarded contracts.
training_requirements: Procurement and legal staff should be trained on Article 72 substantial modifications, Article 57(1) exclusion grounds, and Article 258 TFEU infringement consequences.
audit_requirements: Periodic procurement audits should assess whether contracts have been substantially modified without a new procedure and whether award-stage exclusion checks were properly performed.

enforcement.regulatory_authority: Primarily enforced through Member State implementation and judicial/administrative procurement oversight; serious infringement trigger expressly references the Court of Justice of the European Union in Article 258 TFEU proceedings

penalties.administrative_penalties: Potential contract termination and procurement-law remedies under national law; specific penalties are not stated in the section.
penalties.reputational_consequences: Potential public scrutiny and loss of confidence in procurement integrity if unlawful awards or modifications are identified.

enforcement_mechanisms: National-law termination mechanisms
Judicial review and procurement remedies under Member State law
Court of Justice of the European Union declarations in Article 258 TFEU infringement proceedings

complementary_regulations: National public procurement laws implementing Directive 2014/24/EU

implementation_steps: Embed termination clauses or statutory references in procurement contracts reflecting Article 73 grounds.
Review all in-term contract changes against Article 72 to determine whether they are substantial.
Maintain award-stage due diligence files proving contractor eligibility and exclusion-ground checks.
Establish escalation procedures when a CJEU infringement ruling may affect an awarded contract.
Align termination decisions with applicable national-law conditions and procedural safeguards.
common_violations: Failing to provide a legal mechanism for termination in the listed circumstances.
Treating a substantial modification as permissible without assessing whether a new procurement procedure was required.
Awarding or maintaining a contract with a contractor who should have been excluded under Article 57(1).
Ignoring the implications of a CJEU declaration of serious infringement.
best_practices: Use formal modification review committees for contract changes.
Document legal reasoning for whether Article 32 could have applied as an exception.
Conduct pre-award exclusion screening and post-award compliance monitoring.
Coordinate procurement, legal, and audit functions on termination-risk assessments.
compliance_checklist: Has national law given contracting authorities the possibility to terminate during the contract term?
Has the contract been substantially modified in a way requiring a new procedure under Article 72?
If yes, does the Article 32 negotiated-procedure exception apply for a public service contract?
Was the contractor in an Article 57(1) exclusion situation at the time of award?
Has a serious infringement under the Treaties and the Directive been declared by the CJEU under Article 258 TFEU?

regulations.regulation_name: Directive 2014/24/EU on public procurement - Publication of results for services referred to in Article 74

description.brief_summary: The quoted provision requires contracting authorities that award public contracts for services referred to in Article 74 to publish the results of the procurement procedure through a contract award notice containing Annex V Part J information, using standard forms under Article 51. Notices may be grouped quarterly, but grouped notices must be sent within 30 days of the end of each quarter. The Commission is tasked with establishing the standard forms by implementing acts, and notices must be published in accordance with Article 51.
description.detailed_explanation: This provision imposes a concrete transparency obligation on contracting authorities after awarding public contracts for the services covered by Article 74. The authority must make known the results of the procurement procedure by means of a contract award notice. That notice must contain the information specified in Annex V Part J and must follow the standard forms referred to in Article 51. The provision allows an administrative simplification: instead of sending individual notices immediately, authorities may group such notices on a quarterly basis. If they choose this option, they must send the grouped notices within 30 days after the end of each quarter. The section also states that the Commission shall establish the standard referred to in paragraphs 1 and 2 by implementing acts adopted under the advisory procedure in Article 89(2), and that notices referred to in the Article must be published in accordance with Article 51.
description.purpose: To ensure transparency and standardized publication of procurement outcomes for certain services while allowing limited administrative flexibility through quarterly grouping.
description.legislative_intent: The lawmakers intended to make procurement results publicly known in a harmonized format and within a defined timeframe, thereby supporting transparency, oversight, and comparability across Member States.

regulations.regulation_name: Additional termination and lifecycle consistency points

applicable_regions: Not expressly specified; presented in the provided section text

description.brief_summary: The provided text includes five explicit lifecycle consistency constraints relating to publication, participation, start and end dates, and prior award before termination. These appear as operational validation rules rather than formal legislative text from the Directive, but they are stated as mandatory propositions in the section provided.
description.detailed_explanation: The section lists additional points framed as consistency requirements for contract lifecycle events. They state that a contract must not end before publication of its corresponding call; must not end immediately after publication without candidate participation and subsequent selection of an awarded candidate; if a contract starts, it must have a conclusion date; if a contract has ended, it must have started beforehand; and if a contract is terminated, it must previously have been awarded to a participant. Each point is accompanied by a note indicating a violation by a numbered point. These statements function as explicit process and data integrity rules for procurement lifecycle management and may be relevant for compliance controls or system validation, although they are not clearly identified as official legislative provisions in the quoted text.
description.purpose: To ensure logical and procedurally coherent sequencing of procurement and contract lifecycle events.
description.legislative_intent: Not clearly identifiable from the text; likely intended to enforce internal consistency and prevent impossible or procedurally invalid contract states.

what_it_covers: Sequencing of publication and contract end events

Requirement that ended contracts must have started

what_it_does_not_cover: Formal statutory penalties
Detailed procedural steps for remediation

Contract end and termination status records.
timeline_requirements: Publication must precede contract end.
Candidate participation and award selection must occur before a contract can validly end in the scenario described.
Contract start must be associated with a conclusion date.

general_restrictions: Lifecycle events must follow a logically consistent sequence.
Termination is restricted to contracts previously awarded to a participant.
data_restrictions: Contract status data must not reflect impossible states such as ended-before-started or started-without-conclusion-date.
operational_restrictions: Operational closure of a contract is restricted until publication and participation/award milestones have occurred where applicable.
technical_restrictions: Systems should prevent invalid status transitions that violate the listed lifecycle rules.

technical_measures: Implement system validation rules preventing contract end before call publication.
Implement workflow controls requiring candidate participation and award selection before closure in the relevant process stage.
Require mandatory conclusion-date fields when a contract start date is entered.
Prevent end-status assignment unless a prior start date exists.
Prevent termination-status assignment unless a prior award record exists.

Perform data quality checks on contract status transitions.
Maintain traceable links between call publication, participation, award, start, end, and termination events.
training_requirements: Train procurement and contract administration staff on valid lifecycle sequencing and recordkeeping.
audit_requirements: Audit contract records for invalid event sequences and missing prerequisite milestones.

penalties.reputational_consequences: Invalid lifecycle records may indicate control weaknesses and undermine procurement integrity.

Internal audit

implementation_steps: Map all procurement lifecycle states in the contract management system.

Review historical records for violations of the listed consistency points.
Create exception-handling and remediation procedures for invalid records.
common_violations: Contract marked ended before publication of the call.
Contract closed without any candidate participation or award selection.
Missing conclusion date for an active/started contract.
Contract marked ended without a prior start date.

best_practices: Use automated workflow gates rather than manual checks alone.

regulations.regulation_id: Directive 2014/24/EU - Chapter on social and other specific services award rules
regulations.regulation_name: Directive 2014/24/EU on public procurement - Award of contracts for social and other specific services

industry_sectors: Other specific services listed in Annex XIV

description.brief_summary: This provision governs how Member States must regulate the award of public contracts for social and other specific services. It imposes a duty on Member States to create national rules that ensure contracting authorities comply with transparency and equal treatment principles, while allowing procedural flexibility tailored to the nature of the services. It also establishes that contracts for Annex XIV services are subject to this Chapter when their value reaches or exceeds the threshold in Article 4(d).
description.detailed_explanation: The section contains two operative rules. First, Member States are required to establish national rules for awarding contracts covered by this Chapter. Those national rules must be designed to ensure that contracting authorities comply with the procurement principles of transparency and equal treatment of economic operators. At the same time, Member States retain discretion to define the procedural rules, provided that those procedures allow contracting authorities to account for the specific characteristics of the services being procured. Second, the section defines the applicability threshold for this Chapter: public contracts for social and other specific services listed in Annex XIV must be awarded in accordance with this Chapter where the contract value is equal to or greater than the threshold specified in Article 4(d). The provision therefore combines a mandatory compliance baseline with procedural flexibility and a monetary trigger for applicability.
description.purpose: To create a procurement regime for social and other specific services that preserves core EU procurement principles while allowing procedures to be adapted to the distinctive nature of such services.
description.legislative_intent: The lawmakers intended to ensure fair and transparent procurement for sensitive or specialized services without imposing unnecessarily rigid procedures, while also limiting the Chapter's application to contracts above a defined monetary threshold.

what_it_covers: National rulemaking for the award of contracts subject to this Chapter

who_it_applies_to.geographic_presence: Applies within EU Member States to contracting authorities conducting covered procurements.

This Chapter does not apply under this provision to services not listed in Annex XIV.
conditional_exemptions: Procedural rules may vary nationally, as long as they preserve transparency, equal treatment, and the ability to consider service-specific characteristics.

regulations.regulation_name: Directive 2014/24/EU on public procurement - Article 75 Publication of notices

description.brief_summary: This provision governs how contracting authorities must publicize their intention to award public contracts for services covered by Article 74, and sets out Member State obligations regarding procurement criteria for such services.
description.detailed_explanation: The section imposes a concrete publication obligation on contracting authorities that intend to award a public contract for services referred to in Article 74. Such authorities must make known their intention by one of the prescribed means. One expressly stated means is publication of a contract notice containing the information referred to in Annex V Part H and prepared in accordance with the standard forms referred to in Article 51. In addition, the section imposes an obligation on Member States to ensure that contracting authorities may take into account a range of service-related qualitative and user-centered considerations, namely quality, continuity, accessibility, affordability, availability, comprehensiveness, the specific needs of different categories of users including disadvantaged and vulnerable groups, user involvement and empowerment, and innovation. The section further permits Member States to provide that service providers may be selected on the basis of the tender presenting the best price-quality ratio, taking into account quality and sustainability criteria for social services.
description.purpose: To ensure transparency in the award of public contracts for Article 74 services and to allow procurement decisions to reflect the special characteristics and public-interest nature of social and similar services.
description.legislative_intent: The lawmakers intended to create a lighter but still transparent procurement regime for social and other specific services, while enabling contracting authorities to prioritize service quality, continuity, accessibility, user needs, and sustainability rather than relying solely on price.

what_it_covers: Publication of intention to award public contracts for services referred to in Article 74
Use of contract notices for such procurements
Required content of notices by reference to Annex V Part H
Use of standard forms referred to in Article 51
Permissible award considerations for social and related services
Member State rules enabling qualitative and sustainability-based selection criteria

entity_types: National governments and competent legislative/regulatory bodies in Member States
who_it_applies_to.geographic_presence: Applies within EU Member States to contracting authorities conducting procurements for services referred to in Article 74.

what_it_does_not_cover: Detailed content of Annex V Part H itself
The full list of services referred to in Article 74
Specific enforcement penalties
Detailed procedural rules beyond the publication and criteria points expressly stated in this section

mandatory_obligations: Contracting authorities intending to award a public contract for the services referred to in Article 74 must make known their intention.
Where the intention is made known by contract notice, the notice must contain the information referred to in Annex V Part H.
Where a contract notice is used, it must be issued in accordance with the standard forms referred to in Article 51.
Member States must ensure that contracting authorities may take into account the need to ensure quality, continuity, accessibility, affordability, availability and comprehensiveness of the services.
Member States must ensure that contracting authorities may take into account the specific needs of different categories of users, including disadvantaged and vulnerable groups.
Member States must ensure that contracting authorities may take into account the involvement and empowerment of users and innovation.
conditional_requirements: If a contracting authority intends to award a public contract for services referred to in Article 74, it must publicize that intention by one of the permitted means.
If the contracting authority uses a contract notice as the publication method, the notice must include Annex V Part H information and follow Article 51 standard forms.
If a Member State chooses to legislate or provide accordingly, the choice of service provider may be made on the basis of the tender presenting the best price-quality ratio.
If best price-quality ratio is used for social services, quality and sustainability criteria may be taken into account.
documentation_requirements: Contract notice containing the information referred to in Annex V Part H.
Use of the standard forms referred to in Article 51 for the contract notice.
reporting_requirements: Publication of a notice making known the intention to award the contract.
timeline_requirements: The intention must be made known when the contracting authority is intending to award the public contract; no further deadline is specified in the provided text.

general_restrictions: Contracting authorities cannot proceed under this provision without making known their intention to award a public contract for Article 74 services.
When using a contract notice, the authority is limited to the prescribed content and format requirements by reference to Annex V Part H and Article 51.
operational_restrictions: Publication must occur through one of the authorized means under the article.
Notice content is constrained by Annex V Part H.
technical_restrictions: The contract notice must be prepared in accordance with the standard forms referred to in Article 51.
geographic_restrictions: Applies within EU Member States.

organizational_rights: Contracting authorities are permitted to take into account quality, continuity, accessibility, affordability, availability, comprehensiveness, user-specific needs, user involvement and empowerment, and innovation in procurement decisions for the covered services.
Where Member States so provide, contracting authorities may choose the service provider on the basis of the tender presenting the best price-quality ratio.
Where best price-quality ratio is permitted, contracting authorities may take into account quality and sustainability criteria for social services.
how_to_exercise_rights: Contracting authorities exercise these rights through procurement design and award criteria, subject to national rules established by Member States.
Member States exercise their discretion by providing in national law or procurement rules that provider selection may be based on best price-quality ratio.

conditional_exemptions: The best price-quality ratio basis is optional at Member State level, as indicated by 'Member States may also provide'.
public_interest_exceptions: The provision expressly accommodates public-interest considerations in social services, including quality, continuity, accessibility, affordability, availability, comprehensiveness, vulnerable users' needs, user empowerment, and innovation.

technical_measures: Use the standard forms referred to in Article 51 when issuing a contract notice.
organizational_measures: Establish procurement procedures ensuring that intention to award Article 74 service contracts is formally publicized.
Ensure procurement teams include Annex V Part H information in the contract notice.
Member States should maintain legal or administrative frameworks allowing contracting authorities to consider the listed qualitative and user-centered criteria.
training_requirements: Procurement personnel should be trained on Article 74 service procurements, Annex V Part H notice content, and Article 51 standard forms.

Procurement personnel should understand how to evaluate quality, continuity, accessibility, affordability, availability, comprehensiveness, user needs, empowerment, innovation, and sustainability criteria where permitted.
audit_requirements: Authorities should be able to demonstrate that publication occurred through a permitted means.
Authorities should be able to evidence that the contract notice contained Annex V Part H information and used the proper standard form.
Where qualitative criteria are used, authorities should be able to show that such criteria were considered consistently with national rules.

enforcement.regulatory_authority: Not specified in the provided text; generally enforced through Member State procurement oversight bodies, review bodies, and courts under the EU public procurement framework.

penalties.reputational_consequences: Non-compliant procurement publication or award practices may expose contracting authorities to procurement challenges and public scrutiny, though not specified in the provided text.

enforcement_mechanisms: Not specified in the provided text.
Likely through procurement review and remedies mechanisms under applicable EU and national public procurement law.

implementation_steps: Determine whether the contemplated contract concerns services referred to in Article 74.
Before award, make known the intention to award the contract using one of the permitted publication methods.
If using a contract notice, prepare the notice using the standard forms referred to in Article 51.
Ensure the notice includes all information required by Annex V Part H.

Design procurement criteria to reflect service quality, continuity, accessibility, affordability, availability, comprehensiveness, user needs, user involvement, empowerment, and innovation where relevant.
Check national law to confirm whether best price-quality ratio may be used for selecting the service provider.
If permitted, incorporate quality and sustainability criteria into the evaluation of tenders for social services.
common_violations: Failing to publicize the intention to award an Article 74 service contract.
Using a contract notice that omits information required by Annex V Part H.
Failing to use the standard forms referred to in Article 51.
Applying award criteria that ignore the specific needs of disadvantaged or vulnerable groups where relevant.
Using best price-quality ratio without a national legal basis where Member State provision is required.
best_practices: Use a compliance checklist tied to Annex V Part H before publication.
Document the rationale for qualitative and user-centered criteria in the procurement file.
Engage service users or stakeholder representatives where appropriate to identify relevant accessibility and continuity needs.
Include sustainability and quality metrics in tender evaluation for social services where national law permits.
Maintain records showing the publication method, date, form used, and notice contents.
compliance_checklist: Is the contract for services referred to in Article 74?
Has the contracting authority made known its intention to award the contract?
Was the publication made by a permitted means?
If by contract notice, does the notice contain the information referred to in Annex V Part H?
Was the contract notice prepared in accordance with the standard forms referred to in Article 51?
Have quality, continuity, accessibility, affordability, availability, and comprehensiveness been considered where relevant?
Have the needs of different user categories, including disadvantaged and vulnerable groups, been considered?
Have user involvement, empowerment, and innovation been considered where relevant?
Does national law permit selection on the basis of best price-quality ratio?
If so, were quality and sustainability criteria appropriately incorporated for social services?

key_definitions.contracting authorities: Public bodies or entities subject to the procurement rules that intend to award public contracts.
key_definitions.services referred to in Article 74: The category of social and other specific services governed by the special procurement regime established in Article 74.
key_definitions.contract notice: A formal procurement publication used to make known the intention to award a public contract, containing the information referred to in Annex V Part H and issued using Article 51 standard forms.
key_definitions.best price-quality ratio: An award basis allowing selection of the tender offering the optimal balance between price and quality, and, for social services where permitted, taking into account quality and sustainability criteria.

regulations.regulation_id: Directive 2014/24/EU Article 75(b) and Article 77(1)-(2) (excerpted section titled 'Reserved contracts for certain services')
regulations.regulation_name: Directive 2014/24/EU on public procurement - reserved contracts for certain services and prior information notice requirements

description.brief_summary: The excerpt sets out two specific procurement rules. First, where a prior information notice is used, it must be published continuously, contain Annex V Part I information, specifically identify the service types concerned, indicate that contracts will be awarded without further publication, and invite interested economic operators to express interest in writing. Second, Member States may allow contracting authorities to reserve participation in award procedures exclusively for organisations when awarding certain health, social, and cultural services identified by Article 74 and specified CPV codes.
description.detailed_explanation: The section imposes concrete procedural content requirements for a prior information notice used as the publication mechanism for certain service contracts. The notice must be continuously published and must include the information required by Annex V Part I. It must also specifically identify the types of services that will be covered by the contracts, expressly state that the contracts will be awarded without further publication, and invite interested economic operators to submit written expressions of interest. In addition, the section provides an enabling rule for Member States: they may legislate so that contracting authorities can reserve participation in procurement procedures exclusively to organisations for a defined category of services. Those services are limited to health, social, and cultural services referred to in Article 74 and further delimited by an explicit list of CPV codes. The excerpt also states that an organisation benefiting from such reservation must satisfy all conditions listed in paragraph 2, but the actual conditions are not present in the provided text and therefore cannot be extracted.
description.purpose: To regulate transparent publication and participation mechanisms for certain service contracts and to permit socially oriented reservation of procurement opportunities for qualifying organisations in specified service categories.
description.legislative_intent: To balance procurement transparency with simplified publication for certain services, while allowing Member States to support organisations active in health, social, and cultural services through reserved participation mechanisms.

regulations.regulation_name: Directive 2014/24/EU - CPV-limited reservation for certain health, social and cultural services

description.brief_summary: This provision limits the services eligible for reserved participation to health, social and cultural services referred to in Article 74 and covered by a specific list of CPV codes.
description.detailed_explanation: The excerpt provides a closed list of CPV codes that define the service categories for which Member States may allow contracting authorities to reserve participation exclusively for organisations. The listed codes are: 75121000-0, 75122000-7, 75123000-4, 79622000-0, 79624000-4, 79625000-1, 80110000-8, 80300000-7, 80420000-4, 80430000-7, 80511000-9, 80520000-5, 80590000-6, from 85000000-9 to 85323000-9, 92500000-6, 92600000-7, 98133000-4, 98133110-8. This means the reservation authority is not open-ended and must be tied to these classifications.
description.purpose: To narrowly define the service categories eligible for reserved procurement participation.
description.legislative_intent: To prevent overbroad use of reserved procedures by confining them to specified socially significant service categories.

what_it_covers: Classification of eligible services for reserved participation
Use of CPV codes to delimit procurement scope

who_it_applies_to.geographic_presence: EU Member States

what_it_does_not_cover: Services not falling within the listed CPV codes

conditional_requirements: The CPV limitation applies only where a Member State has provided for reserved participation.

operational_restrictions: Contracting authorities must classify the procurement within the listed CPV codes before using the reservation.

how_to_exercise_rights: Participate in procedures reserved under national law for contracts mapped to the listed CPV codes.

training_requirements: Train procurement personnel on correct CPV classification.
audit_requirements: Audit reserved procedures for correct CPV code assignment.

enforcement_mechanisms: Not specified in the excerpt.

implementation_steps: Map the contract subject matter to the relevant CPV code.
Confirm the code is one of the listed eligible codes or within the stated range.
Retain evidence of the classification decision.

Using the reservation for mixed or unrelated services without proper classification.
best_practices: Use internal legal review for borderline CPV classifications.
Document why the service falls within Article 74 and the listed CPV code.

regulations.regulation_name: Directive 2014/24/EU on public procurement - Article 79 Notices

description.brief_summary: Article 79 establishes mandatory notice and publication rules for design contests conducted by contracting authorities. It requires advance publication of a contest notice, post-contest publication of results, inclusion of specified information in standard forms, and allows limited withholding of outcome information where publication would harm law enforcement, public interest, legitimate commercial interests, or fair competition.
description.detailed_explanation: The section imposes procedural transparency obligations on contracting authorities running design contests. Before carrying out a design contest, the authority must make its intention known through a contest notice. If the authority intends to award a subsequent service contract under Article 32(4), that intention must be expressly stated in the contest notice. After the design contest has been held, the authority must send a notice of the results in accordance with Article 51 and must be able to prove the date on which that notice was dispatched. The section also creates a limited exception to publication where disclosure of contest outcome information would impede law enforcement, be contrary to the public interest, prejudice the legitimate commercial interests of a particular enterprise, or prejudice fair competition between service providers. In addition, the notices referred to in paragraphs 1 and 2 must be published in accordance with Article 51(2) to (6) and Article 52, and must include the information specified in Annex V Parts E and F using standard forms. Finally, the Commission is tasked with establishing those standard forms by implementing acts under the advisory procedure in Article 89(2), and with assessing the effects of the Article and reporting to the European Parliament and the Council by 18 April 2019.
description.purpose: To ensure transparency, procedural regularity, and standardized publication in EU public procurement design contests while preserving limited confidentiality where publication would cause specified harms.
description.legislative_intent: The lawmakers intended to create a harmonized EU-wide notice regime for design contests, enabling market awareness, fair competition, traceable publication, and standardized reporting, while balancing transparency against law enforcement, public interest, and commercial sensitivity concerns.

what_it_covers: Pre-contest publication of design contest intentions
